rows.title: Environment - components; ecology, ecosystem, food chain and food web, energy flow, ecological pyramids
sub: Group-II M2-B-47: Basic concepts of ecology - habitat, niche, population, community and biome
Group-II M2-B-48: Ecosystem - components (biotic and abiotic), structure and function
Group-II M2-B-49: Types of ecosystems - forest, grassland, desert, aquatic (freshwater, marine, estuarine, wetland)
Group-II M2-B-50: Energy flow, food chains, food webs and ecological pyramids

secs.t: Environment — meaning, categories and functions

x: Environment comprises
the surroundings and conditions in which organisms live
Lithosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere constitute the physical category.
A habitat is a living place suited to a species, whereas environment is broader and may include conditions without life.
The primary functions of the environment are providing resources, assimilating wastes and serving as a habitat for biodiversity.

secs.t: Ecology — levels of organisation, habitat and niche

x: The ecological order is organism, population, community, ecosystem, biome and biosphere.
The complete sequence proceeds from atoms to molecules, protoplasm, cells, tissues, organs, organisms, populations, communities, ecosystems, biomes and biosphere.
Ernst Haeckel
coined the term 'ecology' (1869; the ecologists table gives 1866).
Fundamental niche is the potential range of conditions and resources available to a species when competition and other biological limitations are absent.
The niche is the functional role ('profession') of a species, set by habitat, food, reproduction and physical-chemical factors.

secs.t: Ecologists → contributions

x: Charles Elton
wrote *Animal Ecology* in 1927 and is associated with food chains and the pyramid of numbers.

Cowles studied succession on Lake Michigan sand dunes; Clements developed phases of succession and monoclimax theory; Tansley coined ecosystem; Odum contributed to ecosystem ecology and authored Fundamentals of Ecology.
Fundamentals of Ecology (1953) is by
Eugene P. Odum
, father of modern ecosystem ecology.

secs.t: Ecogeographic rules → trait

x: Jordan's rule relates temperature to the number of vertebrae in fish; colder conditions are associated with a greater number of vertebrae.
Bergmann, Allen and Rensch respectively describe body size, appendage length and sexual size dimorphism.
Gloger’s rule relates climate to
colouration
; warm and humid environments are generally associated with darker colouration.

secs.t: Population attributes — terms → meaning

x: The J-curve represents exponential growth, expressed as dN/dt = rN, when resources are assumed to be unlimited.
The S-curve represents logistic growth, in which population growth slows as it approaches carrying capacity K; it is expressed as dN/dt = rN(K-N)/K.
All three statements are correct. r-selected species include many insects and weeds, whereas elephants and humans illustrate the K-selected strategy of fewer offspring and greater care.

secs.t: Ecosystem — concept, structure vs function, open vs closed

x: In 1935, Arthur Tansley described an ecosystem as a system resulting from the integration of all living and non-living factors of the environment.
The
ecosystem
- a biotic community plus its non-living surroundings linked by energy flow and nutrient cycling - is the basic functional unit of ecology (APPSC PYQ).

secs.t: Abiotic factors — types and limiting-factor laws

x: An abiotic factor is
any non-living component that affects organisms or their environment
, such as light, temperature, water or soil.
Climatic factors include light, temperature and rainfall; edaphic factors relate to soil; topographic factors include altitude, slope and aspect.
Abiotic factors can either enable the distribution of organisms or limit it when conditions fall outside suitable ranges.

secs.t: Biotic components — producers, consumers, autotroph types

x: Humans are omnivores, saprotrophs feed on dead matter, reptiles are cold-blooded, and camels are adapted to desert conditions.
Chemoautotrophic bacteria in deep ocean trenches can use
hydrogen sulphide
released from cracks on the sea floor as an energy source.
Nitrifying bacteria are chemoautotrophs, and many chemoautotrophic archaea such as methanogens inhabit extreme environments.

secs.t: Decomposers and decomposition — steps and factors

x: Decomposers release inorganic nutrients from dead organic matter, making them available again to producers and linking living and non-living components.
Bacteria and fungi are the principal decomposers, while earthworms, nematodes and arthropods act as helpers.
Decomposition is rapid when detritus contains nitrogen and sugars and the climate is warm and moist.

secs.t: Food chains and trophic levels — Grazing vs detritus chains

x: Grazing chains begin with living producers, whereas detritus chains begin with dead leaves, remains or other dead organic matter.
A grassland chain begins with grass, followed by herbivores such as grasshoppers or rabbits, and then predators such as snakes or hawks.

secs.t: Food chains and trophic levels — Trophic levels

x: Exam angle: a "missing second trophic level" means no herbivore in the chain (e.g. tiger, grass, snake, frog); "correct grazing chain" means it starts with a producer and moves up in order.
A
detritus food chain
starts with dead organic matter such as leaf litter and proceeds through detritivores such as earthworms to higher consumers.

secs.t: Food webs and ecosystem stability — terms

x: A complex food web provides alternative pathways for energy and feeding relationships, increasing ecosystem stability.
Warming and ocean acidification
can cause coral bleaching and disrupt marine food chains.
Homeostasis is the self-regulatory capacity by which an ecosystem resists stress through feedback up to a limit.
Diverse and complex systems such as
rainforest
s are generally more stable than simple systems such as tundra, deserts and monoculture croplands.

secs.t: Energy flow — productivity and ten percent law — Nature of energy flow

x: Less than 50% of incident sunlight is photosynthetically active radiation, and plants fix only about 2–10% of that PAR.
Primary production efficiency is the share of incoming solar energy captured and used in photosynthesis.
GPP is the total organic matter produced through photosynthesis; NPP is GPP minus producer respiration; secondary productivity is new organic matter formed by consumers.

secs.t: Energy flow — productivity and ten percent law — Ten percent law

x: Exam angle: "most productive ecosystem" = tropical rainforest in APPSC keys.
Both statements are true, and the large energy loss at each transfer leaves insufficient energy to support many successive trophic levels.
Tropical rainforest
s are the standard highest-productivity ecosystem among the alternatives.
Open oceans have low productivity per unit area, but their enormous area gives them a large total output.

secs.t: Ecological pyramids — types, inverted cases, limitations

x: Exam angle: "which pyramid is inverted": pyramid of numbers in a parasitic chain; "which can never be inverted": the energy pyramid.
Parasitic food chains can have fewer hosts supporting numerous parasites, resulting in an inverted pyramid of numbers.
Ecological pyramids cannot place one species at two trophic levels, generally omit decomposers and may ignore organism size; counting organisms is also difficult.

secs.t: Biomagnification vs bioaccumulation — terms and examples

x: DDT, mercury and PCBs are persistent, fat-soluble and non-biodegradable pollutants, which are the characteristics favouring biomagnification.
DDT causes thinning of bird eggshells and has been associated with crashes in seabird populations.
Methyl mercury concentrates through the food chain and reaches high levels in
apex predators such as dolphins and orcas
Methylmercury
concentrated up the marine food chain and caused Minamata disease in Japan.

secs.t: Biotic interactions → sign → example

x: Orchid on mango is commensalism, Cuscuta is parasitism and Penicillium inhibiting bacteria is amensalism.
The fig wasp pollinates the fig and obtains a breeding site, making the association a coevolved mutualistic relationship.
The Ophrys orchid attracts bees through sexual deceit, thereby facilitating pollination.
Resource partitioning permits competing species to coexist by using different portions of a resource, such as different parts of the same plant.

secs.t: Species roles → meaning → example

x: A
keystone species
has an ecological effect far larger than its abundance; its removal may cause the community to collapse.
Pisaster ochraceus is a keystone sea star that
controls mussels in intertidal zones
Foundation species create or shape the habitat itself;
coral
s and kelp are examples.
Lichens can indicate environmental health and are particularly used as indicators of
sulphur dioxide pollution

secs.t: Ecotone and edge effect — meaning and places

x: An ecotone is a transition zone between two biological communities or biomes, generally having intermediate conditions.
A uniform stand of one forest type is a single community, not an ecotone.
Grassland is identified as an ecotonal region between
forest and desert
conditions.
The edge effect is the increased number of species and increased density of some species in an ecotone.

secs.t: Ecosystem types — classification, forests and deserts

x: Tropical rainforest
s have the highest species richness among terrestrial ecosystems.
Rapid litter decay in tropical rainforests leaves the soil relatively thin and nutrient-poor.
In mature forests, photosynthesis and respiration approximately balance with respect to net oxygen production, but the forests continue to function as important carbon sinks.
Low precipitation is common to hot and cold deserts; the Thar occurs in western Rajasthan and Kutch, while Ladakh and the Gobi are cold deserts.

secs.t: Grasslands → region

x: Shola consists of high-altitude grasslands and stunted forests in
the Western Ghats of Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu
Terai refers to tall wet grasslands along the Himalayan foothills, including areas of Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh and Assam.
Banni is in Kutch, Gujarat, at the edge of a salt marsh, one of Asia's largest natural grasslands.

secs.t: Aquatic ecosystems — freshwater, marine, estuaries — Freshwater

x: Lentic ecosystems contain still water, including
pond
s, lakes, pools, ditches and marshes.
The
littoral zone
is the shallow edge of a lake where light reaches the bottom and rooted plants commonly grow.
Oligotrophic
lakes are nutrient-poor, clear and oxygen-rich.
Eutrophic lakes are nutrient-rich and may develop algal blooms.

secs.t: Aquatic ecosystems — freshwater, marine, estuaries — Marine

x: Exam angle: "which does NOT belong to marine ecosystems": rivers and freshwater lakes do not; coral reefs, hydrothermal vents and tidal zones do.
The profundal zone lies below the limnetic zone, is deep and dark, does not support photosynthesis, and is associated with decomposers.
The epipelagic is the upper layer of the pelagic, or open-water, zone and contains the greatest number of marine habitats.

secs.t: Aquatic ecosystems — freshwater, marine, estuaries — Estuaries and mangroves

x: An estuary is formed where a river meets the sea, creating a transition between freshwater and saltwater.
Salinity generally increases from near-freshwater conditions upstream to approximately 35 ppt near the sea-facing mouth.
Mangroves buffer cyclones and storm surges, reduce coastal erosion and store carbon.
Narmada and Tapi
are major west-coast estuaries.

secs.t: Wetlands — functions, Ramsar Convention, rules and day

x: Flood moderation, water purification, biodiversity conservation and carbon storage are all important wetland functions.
The
Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017
provide the specific legal framework for wetland protection in India.
World Wetlands Day is on
2 February
, the date the Ramsar Convention was signed in 1971 at Ramsar, Iran.

secs.t: Plant adaptations to habitat — halophytes, xerophytes, hydrophytes

x: Xerophytes are adapted to deserts through features such as thick cuticles, sunken stomata, spines, succulence and CAM; Opuntia is an example.
Rhizophora is a salt-tolerant mangrove plant, Opuntia is a desert plant, and Hydrilla is an aquatic plant.
Halophytes tolerate saline conditions, and salt-excreting glands, succulent leaves, pneumatophores and vivipary are important adaptations found among estuarine and mangrove plants.

secs.t: AP ecosystems — Kolleru, Pulicat, Coringa, Eastern Ghats

x: Kolleru is the freshwater lake, Pulicat the brackish lagoon, Coringa the mangrove-estuary sanctuary and the Eastern Ghats the forest-to-thorn-forest transition region.
Andhra Pradesh has a 1,053 km coastline and the second-largest mangrove ecosystem in India, concentrated in the Godavari and Krishna estuaries.
Coringa is a mangrove-estuary in the Godavari delta, designated as a wildlife sanctuary and associated with marine turtles.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Nallamala and Seshachalam forests provide habitat for tigers, leopards, sloth bears and elephants.
Ecosystem function includes processes such as energy flow and nutrient cycling.
Structure describes the components present in an ecosystem, whereas function describes the processes or activities performed by it.
India launched its first guide to Open Natural Ecosystems at UNCCD COP17 in Ulaanbaatar.
The AP State Biodiversity Board is planning OECMs
outside protected areas
as part of broader conservation efforts.
Gujarat released 20 blackbucks into the
Banni
grassland of Kutch, one of Asia's largest natural grasslands.

rows.title: Biogeochemical cycles, ecological succession, ecosystem services
sub: Group-II M2-B-51: Biogeochemical cycles, ecological succession and ecosystem services

secs.t: Functions of the environment — resources, waste, life, aesthetics

x: Exam angle: match function with description (waste decomposition = breakdown of organic waste into simpler compounds; cultural heritage = source of tradition).

Waste decomposition is the breakdown of organic waste into simpler compounds (iii); cultural heritage is a source of traditional practices and identity (iv); recreation and aesthetics give scenic and leisure value (i); medicinal resources supply drugs and herbal remedies (ii).

secs.t: Ecosystem functions and services — MEA categories

x: Provisioning services supply food and water; regulating services include climate regulation; cultural services include recreation; supporting services include soil formation.
Groundwater recharge and flood moderation are ecological services.
Carbon sequestration
removes and stores carbon from the atmosphere.
Cultural services such as spiritual value, heritage and aesthetics are difficult to price accurately.

secs.t: Reports and frameworks → valuation of nature

x: Costanza et al. estimated the annual value of global ecosystem services at approximately US$33 trillion in 1997.
TEEB stands for
The Economics of Ecosystems and Biodiversity
TEEB was launched in 2007 in the G8+5 context at Potsdam, hosted by UNEP, and aims to make the economic and other values of nature visible in decisions.

secs.t: Biogeochemical cycles — basics, types and human disruption

x: The classification is based on the main reservoir of the nutrient input: the atmosphere and oceans for gaseous cycles, and the Earth’s crust for sedimentary cycles.
Forests regulate water flow, conserve soil and moisture, recharge groundwater and moderate floods.
Fossil-fuel burning raises CO2, and nitrogen and phosphorus runoff can cause algal blooms and eutrophication.

secs.t: Carbon and nitrogen cycles — processes → agents

x: Respiration, decomposition, fossil-fuel combustion and volcanic activity
all add CO2.
Carbon is held in the atmosphere, oceans, forests and soils, while carbonate rocks and fossil fuels store carbon over long periods.
Both statements are true, and the release of stored carbon through fossil-fuel burning and deforestation explains the rise in atmospheric CO2 and associated climate change.
Ammonification
is the conversion of organic nitrogen in dead matter into ammonia by decomposer bacteria and fungi.

secs.t: Nitrogen fixers and biofertilisers → organism → crop

x: Azotobacter and Azospirillum are free-living nitrogen fixers used with crops.
Cyanobacteria and Azolla in rice fields fix nitrogen and add organic matter to the soil.
Azolla is an aquatic fern associated with Anabaena and supplies nitrogen in paddy systems.
VAM is a fungus-root association that improves
phosphorus and water
uptake by plants.

secs.t: Ecological succession — terms, persons and types

x: Frederic Clements
first proposed the sequence of nudation, invasion, competition and co-action, reaction, and stabilisation in 1916.
Pioneer communities colonise first, seral communities occupy intermediate stages, and the climax community is the stable terminal community related to the prevailing climate.
A newly formed volcanic island lacks a pre-existing community and soil, so its colonisation represents primary succession.

secs.t: Succession — Clements' phases and sere sequences

x: Reaction
is the most important phase: organisms modify soil, water, light and temperature, making the site suitable for later species.
The xerosere sequence on bare rock proceeds from crustose lichens to foliose lichens, mosses, herbs, shrubs and finally forest.
Hydrosere proceeds from phytoplankton through submerged and floating plants, reed-swamp, sedge-meadow, woodland and finally forest.
Lake sediments preserve a permanent record of ecological changes, making hydroseres better studied than xeroseres.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The invasive Prosopis juliflora spreads in response to changes in hydrology and soil chemistry, leading to its description as an ecological first responder.
The
Godavari and Krishna estuaries
are the principal locations associated with Andhra Pradesh’s mangrove ecosystem in the stated context.
Andhra Pradesh forests act as carbon sinks, regulate water flow and conserve soil and moisture, thereby providing important intangible ecosystem services.

rows.title: Environmental issues and concerns - land degradation, desertification, deforestation, soil erosion
sub: Group-II M2-B-94: Other environmental challenges - desertification, land degradation and urban heat islands

secs.t: Land degradation — terms → meaning

x: Desertification involves land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas due to climatic variation and human activity; it is not merely the spread of existing deserts.
Over-use of a commonly shared pasture is described as the
Tragedy of the Commons
, a concept associated with Garrett Hardin in 1968.
Cool roofs use white or reflective, high-reflectance coatings that reduce heat absorption and lower the indoor cooling load.

secs.t: Causes → effects of degradation — Deforestation

x: The highest forest loss is concentrated in tropical forests, especially in the Amazon, Congo Basin and Southeast Asia.
Overgrazing strips vegetation, deforestation exposes soil, water erosion removes topsoil and causes sedimentation, and wind erosion blows topsoil away in dry areas.
Poor drainage and over-irrigation
cause salinisation and waterlogging, including in delta regions.

secs.t: Causes → effects of degradation — Agriculture-driven degradation

x: Excess use of urea has skewed the nitrogen-phosphorus-potassium balance in the soils of
Punjab and Haryana
The most conspicuous effects of modern agriculture are
soil degradation, pollution and ecological imbalance
Synthetic chemicals contaminate soil and water; over-irrigation with poor drainage causes waterlogging and salinity; and the projected affected share by 2050 is 50% of global arable land.

secs.t: Data — forest loss and degraded land — Global forest data

x: Exam angle: fill-in-the-blank on FAO net-loss figures; check which FRA edition the question uses.
The FRA 2025 figures record a decline in annual net forest loss from 10.7 million hectares in the 1990s to 4.12 million hectares per year during 2015–2025.
About 94% of the reported forest loss was in tropical forests, while the world was 63% off track for zero deforestation by 2030.

secs.t: Data — forest loss and degraded land — India - Desertification and Land Degradation Atlas 2021

x: The 2021 Atlas (ISRO-SAC) gives 97.85 Mha = 29.77%.
The UNCCD Global Land Outlook estimates that land degradation costs more than
of global GDP through lost ecosystem services.
Africa, especially the Sahel region, and Asia are identified as the worst-hit regions in relation to desertification.
The Desertification and Land Degradation Atlas was published by ISRO's Space Applications Centre located at Ahmedabad.

secs.t: Data — forest loss and degraded land — AP data (APSES 2024-25)

x: Under SDG 15 (SDG India Index 2023-24), degraded land is
of AP, about ten times Punjab's 3.15%.

secs.t: UNCCD, days and conferences

x: Sand and dust storms commonly affect drylands of north-western India, including Rajasthan, as well as West Asia and the Sahel.
The related day is observed on
12 July
, while 2025–2034 has been declared the UN Decade on Combating Sand and Dust Storms.
The World Day to Combat Desertification and Drought is observed on
17 June
, following a 1994 UNGA decision.

secs.t: Restoration initiatives and programmes → aim — Green walls and pledges

x: The Aravalli Green Wall concerns the Aravallis; the Great Green Wall is the Sahelian belt; and the Bonn Challenge has the specified restoration targets.
SPSR Nellore targets
green cover by 2047 (Jul 2026) under the Great Green Wall of Andhra Pradesh, which aims to raise green cover and combat desertification.

secs.t: Restoration initiatives and programmes → aim — India's programmes

x: The Mitti Bachao Abhiyan began in Madhya Pradesh in the Tawa dam area of Hoshangabad in 1977 and opposed waterlogging and salinity.
Watershed development under the PMKSY Watershed Development Component follows the '
ridge to valley
' approach, treating the upper catchment first and moving downstream.
The Namo Van–Nagar Van Scheme promotes urban forests with the aim of reducing the urban heat island effect.

secs.t: Places → degradation feature

x: Anantapur and Sri Sathya Sai are associated with drought-induced degradation, desertification, wind erosion of topsoil and groundwater depletion.
Uppada in Kakinada is associated with coastal erosion.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The cited figure is only
of the Union budget, which was presented as a reason for advocating a national environmental survey.
China's Three-North Protective Forest Program, also called the Great Green Wall of China, has checked desert spread but needs decades more to mature and achieve its broader objectives.

rows.title: Environmental legislation in India - Water Act 1974, Air Act 1981, Environment (Protection) Act 1986
sub: Group-II M2-B-79: Pollution control regulation - CPCB and SPCBs, the Water Act, Air Act and Environment (Protection) Act

secs.t: Environmental Acts → year (chronology)

x: Exam angle: "arrange in chronological order" - Water 1974 → Water Cess 1977 → Forest 1980 → Air 1981 → EPA 1986 → NGT 2010; Water (1974) always precedes Air (1981) and EPA (1986).
The Water Cess Act imposed a cess on water consumed by
industries and local bodies
Air Act 1981 -> EPA 1986 -> PLI Act 1991 -> NGT Act 2010, so 4, 1, 3, 2.

secs.t: Water Act 1974 and Water Cess Act 1977 — provisions

x: Article 252 permits Parliament to legislate on a State subject when States adopt the required resolution; the law applies in the States adopting it.
The
Central Board for the Prevention and Control of Water Pollution
, created in 1974, was renamed the CPCB by the 1988 amendment.
The Water Cess Act provided a 25 per cent rebate for installing treatment plants, encouraging reduction and treatment of polluted discharges.

secs.t: Air Act 1981 — provisions

x: The State Government
may declare an air pollution control area under Chapter IV, particularly Sections 19 to 31, of the Air Act.
The Water Act deals with effluent-discharge standards; the Air Act deals with air-control areas and emissions; the Cess Act funds the Boards; and the 1987 amendment added noise.

secs.t: Environment (Protection) Act 1986 — background, powers, authorities

x: The Central Government’s powers include prescribing emission and discharge standards, regulating industrial locations, managing hazardous wastes and protecting public health.
Section 5 empowers the Central Government to issue directions, including directions for
closure of an industrial unit
EPA 1986 rests on Article 253 (laws to implement international agreements) and gives effect to the Stockholm Conference (1972) decisions.

secs.t: Notifications and rules under EPA → provision

x: The CRZ notification of 1991 regulates coastal stretches and prohibits ash and waste dumping in the regulated areas.
The EIA notification was issued in 1994 and was subsequently revised in 2006; it provides for prior environmental clearance.
Eco-Sensitive Zone notifications, the Plastic Waste Management Rules and the Green Credit Rules are all instruments notified under the Environment (Protection) Act.
The Green Credit Rules, 2023 provide
Green Credits
for voluntary tree planting on degraded land.

secs.t: Penalties and decriminalisation — Jan Vishwas Act 2023

x: The original penalty was imprisonment up to five years or a fine up to Rs 1 lakh, with an additional Rs 5,000 per day for a continuing offence.
The PLI Act mentioned in this context is the
Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991
, which was amended by the Jan Vishwas Act, 2023.

secs.t: Organisations → role (MoEFCC, CPCB, SPCBs, APPCB)

x: The Forest Survey of India is one of the bodies under MoEFCC (with BSI, ZSI and NTCA), not unrelated to it.
The APPCB implements the Water Act, Air Act and Environment (Protection) Act, along with rules relating to hazardous, biomedical, plastic and solid waste.
The APPCB issues siting guidelines for industries and also prepares SOPs for marine outfall monitoring and hazardous waste.
The system allocates inspections based on risk, with
high-risk industries
inspected more often.

secs.t: Consent mechanism — CTE/CTO and industry colour categories

x: The White category covers industries with a CPCB score of 20 or less and is described as practically non-polluting, requiring no consent or environmental clearance.
The basis of the colour categories is the pollution potential represented by
emissions, effluents and hazardous waste generated
The January 2026 reform provides for a single application for Air and Water consents plus waste authorisations, while consent to operate remains valid until cancelled.

secs.t: Cases and NGT orders → holding

x: The power to levy compensation has been upheld, but its exercise must be connected with clear or imminent environmental harm.
The Court held that administrative orders cannot override the EIA Notification, 2006, and its ruling was prospective.
The National Green Tribunal issued the suo motu notice to
Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh
regarding sewage entering drinking water.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Water Act of 1974 is regarded as India’s first pollution-control law, while the National Green Tribunal Act of 2010 is the latest in the stated legislative chain.
The APPCB was set up in 1976 under the Water Act.
The
Central Pollution Control Board
was established in 1974, before the enactment of the Air Act.

rows.title: Environmental Impact Assessment - process, EIA notification, public hearing, criticism
sub: Group-II M2-B-80: Environmental Impact Assessment and the National Green Tribunal

secs.t: EIA — origin, FIRSTs and amendment chronology

x: The global origin of EIA is associated with the United States National Environmental Policy Act, enacted in 1969.
India's EIA process began in
when the Planning Commission asked DST to examine river-valley projects.
The first use of EIA in India is dated to 1978 in connection with
river-valley projects
Large public-sector projects requiring
Public Investment Board
clearance became another early area of EIA application.

secs.t: Terms → meaning (EIA and related tools)

x: EIA concerns a project before it starts; LCA covers a product or process through its life cycle; cumulative impact assessment examines combined effects; and an environmental audit checks an operating unit after the fact.
The 12 principles of green chemistry (prevent waste, atom economy, safer solvents, renewable feedstocks, design for degradation) were set out by Anastas and Warner in 1998.

secs.t: EIA process — stages

x: Baseline environmental conditions are surveyed, alternatives are compared during impact prediction, and mitigation planning includes an Environmental Management Plan.
Appraisal is evaluation of the EIA report by the expert committee (a-ii); Decision is EC granted with conditions or rejected (b-i); Monitoring checks EMP implementation (c-iii).
The sequence is Screening, Scoping, Appraisal and Decision; public consultation occurs before appraisal.

secs.t: EIA Notifications 1994, 2006 and Draft 2020 — provisions

x: The 2006 notification shifted the test from investment size to impact potential and made clearance compulsory for 39 project categories.
Category B1 projects require an EIA, while Category B2 projects do not; both are associated with state-level appraisal and clearance arrangements.
Category A projects do not undergo screening; they always require full EIA, are appraised by EAC and cleared by MoEFCC.

secs.t: Public hearing — notice, conduct, exemptions

x: Public consultation is
a mandatory two-fold process
involving public hearing and written responses for scheduled projects.
The State Pollution Control Board conducts the hearing, while
the District Collector
presides over it.
The notice period is at least 30 days, and the hearing is to be completed within 45 days.
'strategic' is determined by the Central Government, which is criticised as arbitrary; the SPCB only conducts the hearing.

secs.t: Clearance bodies — EAC, SEIAA, SCEIA/SAEIA, PARIVESH

x: The amendment permits the Centre to remove members of EAC, SEAC or SEIAA mid-term for persistent delays.
The stated backup bodies are SAEIA in place of SEIAA and SCEIA in place of SEAC.
The tenure was raised to
four years, with a maximum of two terms and an age limit of 70
years for members of SEIAA, EAC and SEAC.

secs.t: Cases on post-facto clearance → holding — Cases

x: Common Cause (2017) dealt with Odisha mining without or beyond EC and ordered compensation of 100% of the value of illegally extracted minerals.

The May 2025 ruling struck down the specified instruments, was recalled in November 2025 by a 2:1 majority, relied on the cited earlier cases, and affected projects valued at approximately ₹20,000 crore.

secs.t: Cases on post-facto clearance → holding — Final Vanashakti verdict, 29 July 2026

x: Exam angle: "primary issue in case X" - match case to the exemption or post-facto question it decided.
Exam angle: prior EC is mandatory under EIA 2006; post-facto approval only as a narrow exception.
The Court held that ex post facto EC must meet Articles 14 and 21 (a proportionality test), while the Supreme Court keeps its power under Article 142.

secs.t: NGT orders and AP project disputes → place

x: Following the Visakhapatnam styrene leak in May 2020, the NGT took suo motu cognisance and ordered an interim deposit of Rs 50 crore.
A High-Powered Committee was set up on the directions of the
National Green Tribunal
in relation to the Great Nicobar project.
The Polavaram inter-state dispute concerns submergence in neighbouring
Odisha and Chhattisgarh
and was raised before the Supreme Court.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: All four statements describe identified criticisms of the EIA process: proponent-paid consultants, absence of a central baseline data bank, weak emergency plans and exemptions from hearings.
Telangana sought Supreme Court review of the Polavaram EIA, while the APPCB hearing on the Prakasam Barrage water aerodrome drew criticism from the Human Rights Forum for an error-ridden draft EIA.

rows.title: Environmental institutions - MoEFCC, CPCB and SPCBs, National Green Tribunal, National Biodiversity Authority

secs.t: MoEFCC and CPCB — evolution, FIRSTs, functions

x: All three statements are correct according to the stated current information: the allocation is 0.07%, MoEFCC is nodal for India’s NR7 biodiversity report, and it runs Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan.
PRANA is the portal tracking NCAP; daily bulletins come from the National AQI launched in 2015.
The CPCB coordinates SPCBs, provides technical help, supports research and training, and performs monitoring and regulatory functions.

secs.t: SPCBs and APPCB — functions

x: It reverses the two; Consent to Operate is needed before production or discharge.
All four statements describe stated APPCB responsibilities, including enforcement, waste-management rules, siting guidance, SOPs and cleaner production.
The APPCB was established in 1976 by the
Government of Andhra Pradesh under the Water Act, 1974

secs.t: Acts → NGT (predecessors, Acts covered, exclusions)

x: Exam angle: bench-to-city matching; "which Act is NOT under NGT" (Wildlife Act).
The National Environment Tribunal Act, 1995 provided for strict liability in cases of accidents involving hazardous substances.
The National Environment Tribunal Act, 1995 was never brought into force and was repealed by the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010.
The NGT combines original jurisdiction over environmental disputes with the appellate role earlier performed by the NEAA.

secs.t: National Green Tribunal — establishment, procedure, benches — Establishment and nature

x: The NGT gives effect to the right to a healthy environment, which is treated as part of the
right to life under Article 21
The NGT deals with environmental protection, conservation of forests and natural resources, enforcement of environmental legal rights, and relief and compensation for damage.

secs.t: National Green Tribunal — establishment, procedure, benches — Procedure and composition

x: Exam angle: APPSC 2018 asked for the date it was set up (
18 October 2010
). APPSC 2025 asked its purpose (environmental and pollution-control cases).
The Principal Bench is at New Delhi; Pune is a zonal bench location; and Jodhpur and Shillong are circuit bench locations.
The NGT consists of a Chairperson who is a retired Supreme Court judge, along with Judicial and Expert Members, with 10 to 20 members in each category.

secs.t: National Biodiversity Authority and APSBB — provisions

x: The three tiers are the National Biodiversity Authority at the national level, State Biodiversity Boards at the State level and Biodiversity Management Committees at the local level.
Foreigners require NBA approval to access bio-resources or associated traditional knowledge, and such approval precedes the grant of intellectual property rights.
The City Biodiversity Index, biodiversity parks on the flood plains of five polluted rivers and the Gloriosa superba cultivation pilot are APSBB initiatives.

secs.t: Other statutory bodies → basis

x: The
Commission for Air Quality Management
(CAQM), established under the CAQM Act, 2021, replaced EPCA in the NCR and adjoining areas.
NMCG is the successor set-up to the National Ganga River Basin Authority (
NGRBA
), which was established in 2009 under the Environment (Protection) Act.
The National River Conservation Plan covers pollution abatement in
38 rivers in 16 States outside the Ganga basin

secs.t: Institutes → location

x: The Wildlife Institute of India is at Dehradun, the Botanical Survey of India is at Kolkata and GBPNIHE is at Kosi-Katarmal, Almora.
SACON is located at Coimbatore, IITR at Lucknow, CMLRE at Kochi and ZSI at Kolkata.
ENVIS is the MoEFCC’s network of environmental-information centres and is now known as EIACP.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The NGT directed southern States and Puducherry to execute action plans under the
National Clean Air Programme
(NCAP).
The Environmental (Protection) Fund Rules, 2026 provide for financing CPCB and State Pollution Control Boards.
Guntur stood second in the
towns category
of Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan 2026, which covered 130 cities.
A stated criticism is that MoEFCC is underfunded and operates in silos.

rows.title: International environmental treaties - Stockholm 1972, Rio 1992, Ramsar, CITES, CBD and its protocols
sub: Group-II M2-B-58: Recent plans and targets - Convention on Biological Diversity, Nagoya and Cartagena Protocols
Group-II M2-B-59: Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework and India's biodiversity targets
Group-II M2-B-60: Wildlife conservation - CITES: structure, appendices and species listings relevant to India

secs.t: Conferences → year, venue, outcome (Stockholm, Rio, Rio+) — Stockholm Conference, 1972

x: Exam angle: match conference with year and output
The UN Conference on the Human Environment was held in
Stockholm, Sweden
, from 5 to 16 June 1972.
The Stockholm Conference produced the 26-principle Stockholm Declaration and an Action Plan, led to the establishment of UNEP and resulted in 5 June being observed as World Environment Day.

secs.t: Conferences → year, venue, outcome (Stockholm, Rio, Rio+) — Rio Earth Summit, 1992

x: Exam angle: "Agenda 21 / Rio Declaration came from which summit" - Earth Summit 1992.
The 1972 Stockholm Conference was the UN Conference on the Human Environment, while the 1992 Rio Summit was UNCED, focused on environment and development.
The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change and the Convention on Biological Diversity were opened for signature at Rio in 1992.

secs.t: Conferences → year, venue, outcome (Stockholm, Rio, Rio+) — Follow-up summits

x: Rio+5 was a special session of the United Nations General Assembly held in New York in 1997 to review the implementation of Agenda 21.
Rio+20, held in Rio de Janeiro in 2012, produced “The Future We Want”, launched the Sustainable Development Goal process and was associated with the High-Level Political Forum.

secs.t: Ramsar Convention, 1971 — provisions and India's sites

x: The Ramsar Convention Secretariat is located at
Gland, Switzerland
Chilika Lake
, along with Keoladeo National Park, was among the first Indian Ramsar sites, designated on 1 October 1981.
Udaipur and Indore became India's first accredited Wetland Cities in January 2025.
The Montreux Record lists Ramsar sites under threat; India's sites on it are Keoladeo NP and Loktak Lake.

secs.t: CITES, 1973 — provisions and appendices

x: CITES was adopted on 3 March 1973, entered into force on 1 July 1975, and has a UNEP-administered Secretariat in Geneva.
CITES prohibits commercial trade for approximately 3 per cent of the species covered and regulates the remaining 97 per cent; the statement reverses these proportions.
The walrus is an example associated with Appendix III, where Canada’s protection and request for cooperation are relevant.
CITES
was signed at Washington D.C. on 3 March 1973, hence 'Washington Convention', and 3 March is World Wildlife Day.

secs.t: CITES in India — law, bodies, monitoring

x: CITES is implemented in India through the
Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972
The Zoological Survey of India hosts a CITES Cell and is an authorised wildlife-forensic body.
WCCB assists Customs and builds the wildlife-crime database.
ICCWC links CITES with INTERPOL, the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime and the World Customs Organization.
Statement 3 is a trap: invasive alien species are regulated under a separate new section, not Schedule IV.

secs.t: CITES COPs → venue and highlights

x: India proposed changes concerning
rosewood, otters, tortoises, Tokay gecko and wedgefish
CoP3 was held in 1981, CoP18 in 2019, CoP19 in 2022 and CoP20 in 2025.
CoP3 was held in New Delhi in 1981 and is the only CITES COP hosted by India.
At CoP20, India defeated the European Union proposal for a stricter listing of Guggul, scientifically known as Commiphora wightii.

secs.t: Species → CITES appendix (incl. red sanders of Seshachalam)

x: Indian and Chinese pangolins are in Appendix I. The striped hyena is in Appendix II, rosewood (Dalbergia) is in Appendix II, and the AP-endemic golden gecko is in Appendix II, not III.
Pterocarpus santalinus is endemic to the Seshachalam and southern Eastern Ghats and is classified as Endangered by IUCN.
Red sanders contributes
of India’s ABS income, stated as Rs 120 crore.

secs.t: CMS and wildlife bodies → mandate and status

x: CMS Appendix I contains endangered migratory species requiring strict protection.
CMS Appendix II covers migratory species whose conservation requires international cooperation agreements.
The
Great Indian Bustard, Asian elephant and Bengal florican
were added to CMS Appendix I at COP-13.
TRAFFIC is an NGO network of WWF and IUCN that works to ensure wildlife trade does not become a threat to conservation.

secs.t: CBD — objectives, COPs, protocols

x: The CBD was opened at Rio in 1992, entered into force in 1993, has its Secretariat in Montreal and was ratified by India in 1994.
CBD COP-16 was held at Cali, Colombia, in October–November 2024 and resumed at Rome in February 2025.
The
Global Environment Facility
serves as a financial mechanism for both the CBD and the UNFCCC.
The Nagoya-Kuala Lumpur Supplementary Protocol on Liability and Redress is supplementary to the
Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety
and is therefore connected to the CBD framework.

secs.t: Cartagena and Nagoya Protocols — provisions — Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety

x: The Cartagena Protocol deals with the safe transfer, handling and use of
Living Modified Organisms resulting from modern biotechnology
AIA needs the importing country's informed consent, and LMO shipments carry identifying documentation.
MoEF&CC is India's nodal ministry, and the
Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee
handles approvals for genetically engineered organisms.

secs.t: Cartagena and Nagoya Protocols — provisions — Nagoya Protocol on ABS - subject and nature

x: Its full name is the
Nagoya Protocol on Access to Genetic Resources and the Fair and Equitable Sharing of Benefits Arising from their Utilization
The Nagoya Protocol is a legally binding supplementary agreement to the Convention on Biological Diversity; it is not merely voluntary.
The pillars are prior informed consent, Mutually Agreed Terms for benefit-sharing, and compliance against illegal acquisition.

secs.t: Cartagena and Nagoya Protocols — provisions — Nagoya - India's law and report

x: Implementation:
Biological Diversity Act, 2002
(amended 2023) +
BD Rules 2024.
NBA regulations:
ABS/BD Regulations in April 2025
, incl. rules on
Digital Sequence Information.
1st National Report on Nagoya:
Certificates of Compliance (
of global total)

secs.t: CBD implementation in India — NBA, BMCs, PBRs, APSBB

x: The AP State Biodiversity Board constitutes BMCs, prepares PBRs, processes ABS applications and performs several biodiversity-related functions.
The objectives mirror the CBD: conservation of biodiversity, sustainable use of its components and fair sharing of benefits.

Both are correct: the NBA at Chennai handles regulation, advice and ABS approvals for foreign users and IPR, and BMCs can levy collection fees on access to bio-resources in their area (UPSC 2023 key).

secs.t: Aichi Targets vs KMGBF — adoption, goals, structure — Aichi Biodiversity Targets, 2011-2020

x: The 20 Aichi Biodiversity Targets were adopted at CBD COP10, held at Nagoya in 2010.
The five broad goals included addressing underlying causes, reducing direct pressures, safeguarding ecosystems and species, enhancing benefits, and participatory implementation.
Cartagena concerns biosafety, Nagoya concerns access and benefit-sharing, the Aichi Targets numbered 20 for 2011–2020, and the Kunming-Montreal GBF contains four 2050 goals and 23 targets for 2030.

secs.t: Aichi Targets vs KMGBF — adoption, goals, structure — KMGBF goals (2050)

x: Goal A is the tenfold cut in extinction (iii), Goal B sustainable use (i), Goal C fair benefit-sharing from genetic resources (iv), Goal D finance and technology closing the US$700 bn gap (ii).

secs.t: KMGBF 2030 targets → content

x: Target 2 calls for effective
restoration of 30% of degraded land and water ecosystems
Target 3 is 30x30 conservation (iv), Target 6 cuts invasive alien species by at least 50% (ii), Target 7 halves excess nutrients and pesticide risk (iii), Target 16 halves food waste (i).
India’s route includes
Biodiversity Management Committees, People’s Biodiversity Registers and access and benefit-sharing
mechanisms to connect conservation benefits with local and tribal communities.

secs.t: Biodiversity finance and monitoring — GBF Fund, Cali Fund, NBSAP

x: The Cali Fund was associated with COP16 at Cali in October 2024 and addresses benefit-sharing from DSI use, with the stated contribution expectations for large users.
COP16 at Cali, resumed at Rome, was associated with the Cali Fund for DSI, implementation of the KMGBF including 30x30, and a permanent subsidiary body on Indigenous peoples under Article 8(j).
India’s updated NBSAP contains
23 national targets
matching the 23 targets of the KMGBF.
Progress is tracked through
headline indicators
of the KMGBF monitoring framework.

secs.t: Other treaties → year, secretariat, India's status

x: The BBNJ Agreement (High Seas Treaty) concerns marine biodiversity in areas beyond national jurisdiction, i.e. the high seas.
India hosted UNCCD COP-14 in 2019, ratified the World Heritage Convention in 1977 and is a member of the IWC.
The Montreal Protocol was adopted at Montreal in 1987, its Ozone Secretariat is at Nairobi, and India is a Party.
UNCCD COP-17 is hosted by
Mongolia
and has the theme “Restoring Land.

secs.t: Days and observances → date

x: International Day for Biological Diversity is observed annually on
22 May
World Environment Day on 5 June commemorates the opening of the
Stockholm Conference
World Wetlands Day is 2 February, the day the Ramsar Convention was adopted.
2010 was the International Year of Biodiversity (PYQ 2018).

secs.t: Universal angles

x: UNFCCC, CBD and UNCCD are the three Rio Conventions addressing climate, biodiversity and land-related concerns respectively.
The Ramsar Convention dates from 1971, the Stockholm Conference from 1972 and the Rio Earth Summit from 1992.
The amendment has been criticised for diluting access and benefit-sharing, increasing biopiracy risks and reducing the role of local communities.
CMS COP15 in Campo Grande, Brazil
, launched the Global Initiative on the Taking of Migratory Species.
The NBA SOP under Section 38 of the Biological Diversity Act has notified 159 plant and 173 animal species (some sources give 175 animals).

rows.title: Sustainable development - meaning, nature, scope and components
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I F-72

secs.t: Sustainable development — scope and pillars

x: Sustainable development includes meeting present needs, equity within and across generations, and inclusion.
Economic development, social equity and environmental protection are interlinked pillars that must be balanced rather than pursued in isolation.
The triple bottom line is commonly expressed as
People, Planet and Profit
, corresponding broadly to social, environmental and economic concerns.

secs.t: Principles → meaning

x: The precautionary principle states that lack of full scientific certainty is no reason to postpone cost-effective preventive measures, making statement 2 false.
CBDR recognises shared responsibility while assigning greater duties to developed nations in view of their capacities and historical contribution.
Carrying capacity refers to the level of human use that ecosystems can support without losing their ability to function and regenerate.

secs.t: Summits → year, venue, outcome (Rio 1992 to 2030 Agenda)

x: The 2012 UNCSD at Rio de Janeiro was known as Rio+20, adopted The Future We Want and decided to frame the SDGs.
The 2015 UN Sustainable Development Summit was held in
New York
during the 70th session of the UN General Assembly.
Agenda 21 is
a comprehensive action plan for sustainable development at local, national and global levels

secs.t: Measures → meaning and India's rank

x: An ecological footprint estimates the productive land and sea area required to supply consumption and absorb generated wastes, expressed in global hectares.
Earth Overshoot Day marks the point in a year when humanity's demand on ecological resources exceeds Earth's regenerative capacity for that year.
The Sustainable Development Report and its SDG Index are associated with UN SDSN, whereas NITI Aayog's SDG India Index ranks Indian States.

secs.t: Cases and Tribunal → principle applied

x: Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum v. Union of India
(1996) recognised sustainable development, the precautionary principle and the polluter-pays principle in Indian environmental law.
The NGT must apply the principles of sustainable development, precautionary action and polluter pays.
The NGT is headquartered at New Delhi and aims to dispose of cases within six months.

secs.t: AP — Swarna Andhra @2047 sustainability components

x: The pillar includes
renewable energy, green mobility and sustainable urban planning
The sustainability framework is guided by
Ten Sutras under APSES 2024-25
The July 2026 AP-UN-Habitat MoU envisages a Centre of Excellence for Urban Affairs in
Amaravati
Andhra Pradesh signed an MoU with UN-Habitat for SDG-11 urban goals; UN-Habitat is headquartered in Nairobi.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The first Earth Summit was held at Rio in 1992, while the first definition is associated with the Brundtland Commission in 1987.
India was ranked
99th
in the Sustainable Development Report 2025.
APFDC is cited as a sustainability model involving
49,743 hectares of plantations
SDG targets have been built into
Swarna Andhra @2047
, Andhra Pradesh's long-term vision.

rows.title: Goals of sustainable development - the 17 SDGs, targets and India's SDG Index performance
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I F-72

secs.t: Agenda 2030 — origin, adoption, nature

x: The SDGs were adopted in the document titled “
Transforming our World: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development
Agenda 2030 is guided by the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted in 1948, together with international human-rights treaties.
The Rio+20 outcome document titled “
The Future We Want
” called for global goals to follow the MDGs.

secs.t: MDGs to SDGs — chronology and comparison

x: The SDGs have a broader social, economic and environmental focus and are guided by the principle of leaving no one behind.
The correct sequence is Rio+20 in 2012, Agenda 2030 adoption in 2015, SDGs coming into force in 2016 and the first SDG India Index in 2018.
The First Five Year Plan belongs to 1951–56, the Millennium Declaration to 2000, Rio+20 to 2012 and Agenda 2030 adoption to 2015.

secs.t: SDG number → theme

x: Exam angle: "How many targets?" answer
; "Goal 4?" answer
Quality Education
; "Goal 5?" answer
Gender Equality
SDG 4 concerns quality education, SDG 7 affordable and clean energy, SDG 12 responsible consumption and production, and SDG 16 peace, justice and strong institutions.
Green Economy
is not one of the 17 SDG titles.

secs.t: Goal-specific targets — Goal 4, Goal 5, Goal 10

x: Goal 4 includes
affordable technical, vocational and tertiary education
, along with equitable schooling, early-childhood care and literacy.
All four statements describe areas covered by SDG 5, Gender Equality.
SDG 10 targets inequality within and among countries and seeks a greater voice for developing countries.

secs.t: SDG → Indian scheme

x: SDG 1 is associated with MGNREGA, SDG 2 with the National Food Security Act, SDG 3 with Ayushman Bharat and SDG 4 with Samagra Shiksha.
SDG 5 matches Beti Bachao Beti Padhao, SDG 6 Jal Jeevan Mission, SDG 7 Saubhagya and SDG 11 Smart Cities Mission.
India’s National Action Plan on Climate Change, comprising eight missions, is associated with SDG 13.

secs.t: Indices and reports → publisher and data

x: MoSPI develops the NIF, NITI Aayog coordinates, and the 2026 report tracks 277 indicators.
The SDG-NIF Progress Report 2026 records multidimensional poverty falling from 24.85% (2015-16) to 14.96% (2019-21).
The NER District SDG Index is associated with NITI Aayog and the Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region (MoDoNER), with support from UNDP.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Andhra Pradesh is associated with a score of 74, the Front Runner category, ninth position and rank one in SDG 7.
India's best-ever rank is
94th
, in SDR 2026.

rows.title: Sustainable development in practice - green economy, circular economy and ESG
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I F-72

secs.t: Terms → meaning (green economy to greenwashing)

x: A green economy decouples growth from resource use and pollution and fosters green industries and jobs.
High cost is a major barrier to green technology, particularly for developing countries; it is not necessarily inexpensive.
Green Pharmacy applies green chemistry to the
design, use and disposal of medicines
Greenwashing is the practice of making false or exaggerated environmental claims about a product, firm or investment.

secs.t: Programmes and initiatives → year and aim — India

x: The Green Hydrogen Mission has an outlay of Rs 19,744 crore, targets 5 MMT annually and is linked with the net-zero target for 2070.
The programme trains youth in biodiversity conservation, pollution monitoring, waste management, forestry, wildlife and allied environmental sectors.
NITI Aayog and MoEFCC committees drew up action plans for priority streams including
plastics, e-waste, batteries, tyres and metals

secs.t: Programmes and initiatives → year and aim — International

x: Farm to Fork concerns a sustainable food system; the Circular Economy Action Plan concerns resource efficiency and recycling; the Biodiversity Strategy protects and restores ecosystems; and the Just Transition Fund supports affected regions.
PAGE was launched in 2013 in response to the call made at Rio+20 for action towards greener and more inclusive economies.

secs.t: Green Chemistry and Cleaner Production — persons and principles

x: Paul Anastas and John Warner
introduced the 12 Principles of Green Chemistry in 1998.
All four statements describe principles or features included among the 12 Principles of Green Chemistry.

Green chemistry and cleaner production minimise waste and pollution and promote sustainability throughout the product life cycle, supporting the objectives of Environmental Impact Assessment and Life-Cycle Assessment.

secs.t: Green finance instruments → fact

x: The European Investment Bank pioneered green bonds in 2007, followed by the World Bank in 2008, and the proceeds support environment-friendly projects.
The Sovereign Green Bonds were announced in Budget 2022–23, their framework was issued in 2022, and the first issue in 2023 amounted to Rs 8,000 crore.
The RBI Green Deposit Framework allows banks to raise deposits specifically earmarked for green lending.

secs.t: ESG regulation — BRSR, ratings, taxonomy as remedy

x: A clear taxonomy helps regulators identify and curb greenwashing as well as transition washing.
BRSR is set by SEBI, not RBI.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: SEBI BRSR and the taxonomy gap were discussed at the
Bonn Climate Conference 2026
Without a final green taxonomy, the classification of genuinely green activities may be unclear, increasing the risk of
greenwashing
Urban local bodies cannot issue municipal green bonds because
they lack credit ratings
, which are important for such borrowing.

rows.title: International treaties on chemicals and waste - Basel, Rotterdam, Stockholm POPs, Minamata; Montreal Protocol and Kigali Amendment
sub: Group-II M2-B-92: Ozone layer depletion - causes, ozone hole, effects; Montreal Protocol and Kigali Amendment

secs.t: Ozone layer and ozone hole — terms, location, FIRSTs, UV effects

x: UV-B exposure can cause DNA damage, skin cancer, eye cataracts and suppression of the human immune system.
The Antarctic ozone hole is a seasonal phenomenon, with maximum thinning during
Southern Hemisphere spring, approximately August to November
In the extremely cold polar vortex, polar stratospheric clouds provide surfaces that convert stable chlorine into active forms.

secs.t: Ozone-depleting substances → use

x: Exam angle: "which gas causes ozone depletion", ODS matched to its use, assertion-reason on CFCs.
Halons (bromine) are used in fire extinguishers, methyl bromide is a fumigant/quarantine agent, and CTC and methyl chloroform are solvents.
Their use in appliances and aerosols does not explain their greenhouse effect and ozone-depleting action; those arise from their atmospheric chemical properties.
CFCs are associated with refrigeration and aerosols; halons with fire extinguishers; methyl bromide with fumigation; and HCFCs with transitional substitution.

secs.t: Vienna Convention and Montreal Protocol — provisions, results, World Ozone Day

x: The Protocol covers approximately 100 man-made ozone-depleting chemicals, including CFCs, halons, HCFCs and methyl bromide.
The Multilateral Fund supports developing countries through technical and financial assistance for implementing ODS phase-out obligations.
The Protocol is estimated to avoid approximately
of warming by 2050 because many ODS are also potent greenhouse gases.
The Vienna Convention was adopted in 1985, the Montreal Protocol in 1987, the Multilateral Fund in 1991, and the Kigali Amendment in 2016.
16 September marks the signing of the Montreal Protocol in 1987; the UN General Assembly proclaimed the Day in 1994.

secs.t: Kigali Amendment, 2016 — HFC phase-down schedule

x: Kigali phases down HFCs, which do not deplete ozone but have very high global warming potential; HCFCs are handled by the Montreal phase-out itself.
HFCs replaced ODS in cooling equipment, do not deplete ozone, and possess high global warming potential.
The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change directed Central and State authorities to stop granting environmental clearances for new or additional HFC production after 31 December 2027.

secs.t: India's ozone and cooling action — Ozone Cell, ODS Rules, HPMP, ICAP — Ozone Cell and ODS phase-out

x: The dates are 1 January 2001 for halons, 2003 for CFCs in manufacturing, 2010 for CTC, methyl chloroform and CFCs in MDIs, and 2015 for methyl bromide.
Under Stage-II, India became the first developing country to fully phase out HCFC-141b in rigid foam, achieving a 44 percent reduction against the 35 percent target by January 2020.

secs.t: India's ozone and cooling action — Ozone Cell, ODS Rules, HPMP, ICAP — India Cooling Action Plan (ICAP)

x: ICAP has a 20-year horizon extending to
The six thematic areas are space cooling in buildings, cold chain, servicing sector, domestic or indigenous production, research and development, and transport.
ICAP targets a 20-25% cut in cooling demand and a 25-30% cut in refrigerant demand by 2037-38, plus training 1 lakh servicing technicians.

secs.t: Basel Convention, 1989 — provisions, Ban Amendment

x: Exam angle: match Basel to hazardous waste, Montreal to the ozone layer and Kyoto to greenhouse gases. "Biodiversity" is the usual wrong option for Basel.
The Basel Convention controls the transboundary movement of hazardous wastes and their disposal, while promoting environmentally sound management.
India implements the Basel Convention through the Prior Informed Consent mechanism under the
Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2016

secs.t: Rotterdam and Stockholm Conventions — PIC, POPs, annexes — Rotterdam Convention

x: POPs are toxic chemicals that persist for long periods, build up in living tissue and travel long distances.
The
POPs Review Committee
, or POPRC, assesses candidate chemicals for possible listing.
The Stockholm Convention was adopted in 2001, entered into force in 2004, India ratified it in 2006, and India ratified seven additional POPs in 2020.

secs.t: Rotterdam and Stockholm Conventions — PIC, POPs, annexes — Stockholm - chemicals listed

x: The Convention initially covered 12 POPs, popularly known as the ‘dirty dozen’.
DDT, PCBs, dioxins and furans were among the initial 12 POPs.
Aldrin and dieldrin are associated with Annex A, while dioxins and furans are Annex C examples.
The Convention is stated to list 34 chemicals, although some reference sources continue to mention lower figures.

secs.t: Minamata Convention — mercury, sources, origin of name

x: The Minamata Convention protects human health and the environment from anthropogenic emissions of mercury and mercury compounds across the mercury lifecycle.
Major sources include coal-fired power plants, artisanal and small-scale gold mining, industrial processes and waste.
The Convention is named after Minamata, Japan, where factory wastewater contaminated local fish with mercury and poisoned people in the 1950s.

secs.t: Treaties → focus (matching)

x: The Vienna Convention was adopted in 1985, the Basel Convention in 1989, the Kyoto Protocol in 1997 and the Cartagena Protocol in 2000.
Basel concerns waste, Rotterdam concerns prior consent in trade, Stockholm concerns persistent chemicals, and Minamata concerns mercury.
All three pairs are correctly matched.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: India’s national cooling plan is referred to as
ICAP
and is counted among the world’s first national cooling plans.
World Ozone Day 2026 marked ten years of the Kigali Amendment.
Both the Montreal Protocol and the Vienna Convention are associated with protection of the ozone layer.
MOP37 focused on
implementation of the Kigali Amendment

rows.title: Biodiversity - levels, values, measurement; India as a megadiverse country
sub: Group-II M2-B-52: Biodiversity - meaning and components: genetic, species and ecosystem diversity
Group-II M2-B-53: Values and significance of biodiversity; India as a megadiverse country

secs.t: Biodiversity — definition, levels and FIRSTs

x: The CBD definition covers organisms from terrestrial, marine and other aquatic sources, together with the ecological complexes to which they belong.
Genetic diversity is
variation within a species
and is the basic source of biodiversity.
One ecosystem cannot simply replace another; boreal conifers cannot do the job of tropical deciduous trees in every context.
Tropical rainforests or tropical moist forests are the richest terrestrial ecosystems, while coral reefs are the richest marine ecosystems.

secs.t: Persons → contributions on biodiversity

x: Rosen coined the word (1985) and E.O. Wilson popularised it.

secs.t: Terms → meaning: measuring biodiversity

x: The Shannon-Wiener and Simpson indices are measures of species diversity.
Functional richness refers to the niches occupied, functional evenness to the spread of abundance across niches, and functional divergence to the dominance of extreme traits.
Species richness rises with area, the relation is log S = log C + Z log A, and Z is 0.1-0.2 for most areas.
Alexander von Humboldt proposed the species-area relationship.

secs.t: Species richness patterns — features and causes

x: Exam angle: A/R that butterflies peak in the tropics because they cannot tolerate low temperature: both true, and R explains A.
Tropical richness is associated with long evolutionary time without glaciation, stable climate, solar energy and productivity.
The Himalayas bring together different biogeographical zones, creating varied habitats and high species richness.

secs.t: Values of biodiversity — types and hypothesis

x: Productive use value concerns biodiversity products that are commercially marketed, such as timber, fibre, medicines and genetic material for crops.
The hypothesis compares an ecosystem to an aeroplane and species to its
rivets
; the loss of a key rivet may cause system failure.
Biodiversity underpins sustainable development by supporting ecosystem services such as food, water and air quality.

secs.t: Data — species estimates, India's share, ranks and new records — Global estimates

x: All four estimates are stated figures: about 1.5 million described living species, 300,000 described fossil species, Wilson’s 10–50 million estimate and May’s estimate of about 7 million.
Over 70% of recorded species are animals, plants account for about 22%, and insects are the richest group among animals.
India ranks 10th among plant-rich countries, 11th for endemic higher vertebrates and 6th among centres of crop origin and diversity.

secs.t: Data — species estimates, India's share, ranks and new records — New discoveries (BSI + ZSI)

x: The figures were released in Kolkata by the Botanical Survey of India (BSI) and the Zoological Survey of India (ZSI).
The order was Kerala with 98, West Bengal with 76, Karnataka with 67 and Arunachal Pradesh with 65 new animal species.
The night frog Mewasingi was discovered in
Kozhikode, Kerala

secs.t: Organisations, reports and agreements on biodiversity

x: TEEB, or The Economics of Ecosystems and Biodiversity, seeks to make nature’s values visible and bring them into decision-making at every level.
ABS began with the CBD in 1992 and was made operational through the Nagoya Protocol in 2010.
The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 regulates access to bio-resources and traditional knowledge and implements the
Nagoya Protocol

secs.t: Organisations, reports and agreements on biodiversity — Megadiverse countries

x: India, Brazil, China, Colombia, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Ecuador, Indonesia and Madagascar are all among the 17 megadiverse countries.
India
is reported as the world leader in issuing Internationally Recognized Certificates of Compliance under the Nagoya framework.
TKDL documents traditional knowledge so that patent offices can treat it as prior art, helping prevent wrongful patents.

secs.t: Places → India's biogeographic zones

x: The three biomes identified in the IYB classification are
tropical humid forests, tropical dry deciduous forests, and warm deserts or semi-deserts
The
Deccan Peninsula
is the largest biogeographic zone of India and covers about 42% of the country's land area.
The five provinces are
Central Highlands, Chotanagpur, Eastern Highlands, Central Plateau and Deccan South
The Deccan Peninsula is mainly a rain-shadow deciduous plateau, not a permanently snow-covered alpine zone.

secs.t: Species → natural range in India (zoogeography)

x: Exam angle: UPSC 2019 answer: only the Asiatic lion is found naturally in India alone.
The Nilgiri tahr is restricted to the Western Ghats, not the Eastern Ghats.
The
Asiatic lion
is naturally restricted to India, particularly the Gir region of Gujarat.
The hoolock gibbon is India’s only ape, while slow loris and pangolin are associated particularly with the North-East.

secs.t: Places → agro-biodiversity centres and crop wild relatives

x: The Hindustan or Indian centre is associated with
rice, sugarcane, mango, pigeon pea, brinjal, cucumber and black pepper
Borjuli was notified as a Biodiversity Heritage Site and protects Oryza rufipogon, ancestor of Oryza sativa.
India’s Citrus Gene Sanctuary is located in the Nokrek Biosphere Reserve in the Garo Hills of Meghalaya.

secs.t: Terms and cases → bioprospecting and biopiracy

x: Biopiracy is patenting resources or traditional knowledge WITHOUT consent or compensation.
The appetite-suppressant use of Hoodia was based on knowledge of
the San people of southern Africa
, and a benefit-sharing deal followed.

secs.t: AP biodiversity — Eastern Ghats, Seshachalam and the APSBB

x: The Eastern Ghats contain deciduous, semi-evergreen and evergreen forests, along with savanna, scrub and estuarine vegetation.
Some descriptions call the Eastern Ghats a biodiversity hotspot, but they are not included among the 36 global biodiversity hotspots.
The Board shares 5% of Red Sanders sale profits with farmers, works through People's Biodiversity Registers and is preparing a Marine ABS framework for fishers.
The Seshachalam Biosphere Reserve was notified in 2010, the corridors support major mammals, and the Chenchus are a PVTG living in the landscape.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: India’s fauna count passed 1.05 lakh species after 709 additions in 2025.
The Golden Gecko and Cycas beddomei of the Seshachalam hills are the threatened micro-endemics (by mining and fires).
ZSI-only counts and combined ZSI–BSI totals differ; therefore, the institution or combination of institutions behind a figure should be stated.
The OECM initiative is linked with the Kunming–Montreal target of conserving 30 percent by 2030.

rows.title: Biodiversity hotspots in India; endemism; Biological Diversity Act 2002 and access-benefit sharing
sub: Group-II M2-B-54: Biodiversity hotspots - criteria; global hotspots and the four in India

secs.t: Biodiversity hotspot — definition, criteria and FIRSTs

x: A hotspot needs both high endemism (at least 1,500 endemic vascular plants) and threat (loss of at least 70% of original habitat), so it is characterised by
endemic flowering plants and threat perception
(APPSC-G2 2017).

Norman Myers introduced the concept in 1988, quantitative criteria were set in 1999, Forests of East Australia became the 35th hotspot in 2011, and North American Coastal Plain became the 36th in 2016.

secs.t: Data — hotspot coverage and global count

x: Hotspots once covered 15.7% of Earth's land.

secs.t: Places → India's four hotspots and distractors

x: Exam angle: "which of these is NOT a hotspot in India" - the odd one out is usually a desert or the Eastern Ghats.
The Western Ghats–Sri Lanka hotspot has at least 6,000 vascular plants, with more than 3,000, or about 52%, being endemic.
The Eastern Himalayas (part of the Himalaya hotspot) and the Western Ghats (Western Ghats and Sri Lanka hotspot) are hotspots, the APPSC-G1 2018 answer.

secs.t: Western Ghats — profile, UNESCO status and threats by hotspot

x: The Western Ghats extend approximately 1,600 km through six States and are called the water tower of peninsular India, being associated with the Godavari, Krishna and Cauvery river systems.
The Western Ghats were inscribed in 2012 as a serial UNESCO World Heritage Site comprising 39 component areas in seven clusters.
Odonates are dragonflies and damselflies; their disappearance in the Western Ghats is treated as an early indication of ecological deterioration.

secs.t: Committees and notifications → Western Ghats ESA

x: The Gadgil-led WGEEP recommended the whole Western Ghats as an ESA, whereas the Kasturirangan-led High-Level Working Group limited the ESA to about 37%.
The High-Level Working Group headed by K. Kasturirangan was set up after
State opposition to the Gadgil recommendations
New mining, quarrying, thermal plants and red-category industries are banned or heavily restricted in the proposed ESAs.

secs.t: Species → endemic region or hotspot

x: The
Golden Gecko
is a micro-endemic species of the Seshachalam hills.
Podocarpus (Nageia) wallichianus is the only endemic gymnosperm tree of the Western Ghats.
Nilgiri marten and Malabar spiny dormouse are associated with the
Agasthyamalai
region of the Western Ghats.
The Hangul or
Kashmir
stag is endemic to Kashmir, found in Dachigam National Park (APPSC 2018).

secs.t: Acts → Biological Diversity Act 2002 and 2023 amendment

x: The National Biodiversity Authority performs the national regulatory role; State Boards and UT Councils regulate commercial use in their respective jurisdictions; and BMCs document biodiversity and prepare PBRs.
The Act works with the Biological Diversity Rules, 2024 and a statutory National Biodiversity Authority Fund, known as NBAF.
Section 38
of the Biological Diversity Act deals with notifying threatened species, under which 1,500+ plant species have been declared threatened.

secs.t: BMCs, People's Biodiversity Registers and Biodiversity Heritage Sites

x: BMCs document biodiversity, prepare PBRs and can levy collection fees for access to bioresources within their area.
BMCs contribute to the objectives of the Nagoya Protocol through local biodiversity governance and access-related collection fees.
Nallur Tamarind Grove is in Karnataka, Borjuli wetland in Assam, Kasampatty in Tamil Nadu and Ameenpur Lake in Telangana.

secs.t: Access and benefit sharing — concept, Kani model, earnings, fund rules

x: For an identifiable repository, 25–40% of ABS funds goes to it and 60–75% goes to local communities through SBBs or UTBCs.

India's ABS Regulations 2025 cover Digital Sequence Information, the APSBB plans a first-of-its-kind Marine ABS framework for fishermen, and the NBA sanctioned Rs 82 lakh for Red Sanders conservation.

secs.t: Hotspots vs Key Biodiversity Areas vs Global 200 ecoregions

x: Hotspots use endemic plant and habitat-loss criteria; KBAs are significant individual sites; Global 200 consists of representative priority ecoregions.
Conservation International set the hotspot criteria in 1999, WWF developed the Global 200 framework, and the KBA standard is associated with an IUCN-led partnership.
Global 200 selects representative terrestrial, freshwater and marine priority ecoregions, rather than relying only on endemism and habitat threat.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Agasthyamalai Biosphere Reserve extends across Kerala and Tamil Nadu and was included in UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere (MAB) programme in 2016.
The Supreme Court ordered the
immediate eviction of encroachers
from the Agasthyamalai Biosphere Reserve.
The hotspot approach focuses strongly on plant endemism and can therefore miss threatened systems with low endemism, including grasslands and coldspots.
