rows.title: Loss of biodiversity - causes, invasive alien species, IUCN Red List categories
sub: Group-II M2-B-55: Loss of biodiversity - causes, consequences and the role of invasive alien species
Group-II M2-B-61: Endangered species of India - IUCN Red List categories and flagship species

secs.t: Extinction — definitions, types and traits

x: The sixth extinction is the current human-driven episode, while the end-Cretaceous event about 66 million years ago was the fifth mass extinction and eliminated the dinosaurs.
Co-extinction
occurs when the loss of one species causes the decline or loss of dependent species, such as an obligate pollinator or a parasite dependent on a host.
Large body size, small population, low reproductive rate, narrow or specialised niche and endemism are high-risk traits.

secs.t: Causes of biodiversity loss — frameworks and PYQ answers

x: Exam angle: "which is NOT a cause" - pick the odd option (appetite, vegetarianism, protected-area expansion).
The Evil Quartet consists of
habitat loss and fragmentation, over-exploitation, invasive alien species and co-extinctions
Habitat destruction is not restricted to terrestrial species; destruction of aquatic habitats also causes biodiversity loss.
Global warming, habitat fragmentation and invasion by alien species are recognised threats to biodiversity.

secs.t: Drivers → effects: deforestation, fragmentation, climate change and consequences

x: Climate change causes coral bleaching, ocean acidification, shifts in ecosystem boundaries and disrupted migration.
Habitat fragmentation particularly affects
migratory animals and wide-ranging mammals and birds
because it disrupts movement and separates populations.
Agricultural expansion and urban development
are identified as primary drivers of deforestation and habitat loss.
The Amazon, often called the lungs of the planet, is cleared substantially for
soybean cultivation and cattle pasture
The edge effect exposes habitat boundaries to greater light, wind, heat, predators and weeds.
Biodiversity loss disrupts pollination, nutrient cycling, water and soil services.

secs.t: Invasive alien species — definition and scale

x: The three relevant tests are non-native origin, uncontrolled spread and measurable harm.
The estimated damage to India over 60 years is about US$127.3 billion, not US$12.7 billion.

secs.t: Invasive species → origin and impact

x: Parthenium hysterophorus originated in tropical America and came to India with
imported wheat in the 1950s
Prosopis juliflora, locally called Seema Chintakaya, lowers groundwater in Rayalaseema and raises soil salinity.
Prosopis juliflora has degraded the
Banni grasslands
and is also associated with groundwater depletion and increased soil salinity in Rayalaseema.
Water hyacinth
(Pontederia crassipes), from South America, is called the worst aquatic weed in the world because it chokes freshwater bodies (APPSC 2024).

secs.t: Acts, orders and actions on invasive species

x: The
Plant Quarantine (Regulation of Import into India) Order, 2003
requires pest risk analysis and phytosanitary checks.
The Directorate of Plant Protection, Quarantine and Storage deals with uncertified imports, which are fumigated with
methyl bromide
In Raimona National Park, Lantana and Chromolaena are invasive plants but also serve as major nectar sources for butterflies, illustrating the management debate surrounding their removal.

secs.t: Data — global assessments, recorded extinctions and new discoveries

x: IPBES found extinction rates to be tens to hundreds of times higher than the background rate.
The Living Planet Index, published through WWF's Living Planet assessment, measures the average change in
vertebrate populations since 1970
The IUCN Red List (2014) records 784 extinctions over the last 500 years, including the passenger pigeon, Steller's sea cow and the Bali, Javan and Caspian tigers.
The survey found only
about 65%
of historically recorded species, recording 143 species (40 endemic) across 144 sites in five States.

secs.t: Organisations and reports → IUCN, IPBES, WWF

x: The
Invasive Species Specialist Group
(ISSG), functioning under the IUCN Species Survival Commission, maintains the Global Invasive Species Database.

The Living Planet Report is published by WWF with the Zoological Society of London; the IUCN Red List by IUCN; the Global Invasive Species Database by the IUCN SSC Invasive Species Specialist Group; and the Global Assessment by IPBES.
The Global Invasive Species Database and the list of 100 of the World's Worst IAS are associated with the
IUCN SSC Invasive Species Specialist Group

secs.t: IUCN Red List categories → full forms and criteria

x: Exam angle: "CR stands for?" - Critically Endangered (not "critically extinct"); asked by APPSC in 2023 and 2025.
The criteria include declining population, geographic range, small population size, very small population or restricted distribution, and quantitative extinction-risk analysis.
CR stands for
Critically Endangered

, the category of extremely high risk of extinction in the wild (APPSC 2023 and 2025). 'Critically Extinct' is the usual trap; there is no such category. 'Conservation Required' and 'Critically Rare' are not IUCN categories either.

secs.t: Red List / Red Data Book — name, coverage, colour pages, latest figures

x: The Red List measures extinction risk, whereas the IUCN Green Status measures species recovery; they do not measure exactly the same parameter.
Version 2026-1, released in July 2026, recorded 175,909 species assessed and 49,505 threatened species, approximately 28 percent.
The IUCN's list of endangered species is the
Red List
(Red Data Book), also called the Barometer of Life (APPSC 2025).
The Red Data Book or Red List lists
threatened plant and animal species
and measures their extinction risk.

secs.t: Terms → flagship, keystone, umbrella, endemic species

x: A
flagship species
is a charismatic species used to generate public support for conservation; the tiger and Asiatic lion are examples.
A keystone species has an ecological effect disproportionately larger than its numerical abundance.
Protection of pygmy hog habitat also benefits the Bengal florican, hispid hare, hog deer and rhinoceros.

secs.t: Species in news → Red List category and habitat

x: The Great Indian Bustard and Gharial are Critically Endangered, while Red Sanders and Sangai deer are Endangered.
The Great Indian Bustard inhabits the Thar grasslands and Rollapadu Wildlife Sanctuary in Kurnool, Andhra Pradesh.
The Gharial is associated with the Chambal, has been recommended for species recovery, received suo motu judicial attention, and is a Project Crocodile species.
The Emperor penguin is classified as Endangered, having moved from Near Threatened, and its habitat is Antarctica.
The pygmy hog is the only surviving Porcula species and the world's smallest wild suid.
The Asiatic lion is now Endangered (improved from CR), and the Hangul is among the 22 CR species in the IDWH Species Recovery Programme.

secs.t: Andhra Pradesh species → category and habitat

x: Red Sanders occurs in the Seshachalam, Veligonda and Nallamala hills; Golden Gecko in Seshachalam micro-habitats; Jerdon’s Courser in Sri Lankamalleswara WLS; and Slender Loris in dry scrub forests.
Jerdon’s Courser is critically endangered and nocturnal, and its Andhra Pradesh habitat is Sri Lankamalleswara Wildlife Sanctuary in Kadapa.
Red Sanders (*Pterocarpus santalinus*) is Endangered and occurs naturally only in Andhra Pradesh, particularly in the Seshachalam, Veligonda and Nallamala hills.

secs.t: Andhra Pradesh — drivers and cases of biodiversity loss

x: Encroachment by fish and prawn tanks and unregulated aquaculture have converted wetland and mangrove areas into ponds, causing salinity and loss of breeding grounds.
Prosopis juliflora drains groundwater, crowds out native flora and shrinks grazing land in Rayalaseema and coastal areas.
Demand from
China and Japan
has driven Red Sanders smuggling, illegal logging and associated violence in the Seshachalam region.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Ujani reservoir in Maharashtra is associated with India’s first community-driven invasive-fish removal programme.
A cited study found that invasive alien species damage per species is higher in the Global South.
In Amrabad Tiger Reserve in the Nallamala region, Lantana is converted into biochar known as ‘Black Gold’ with the involvement of Joint Forest Management Committees.
Jerdon’s Courser is an Andhra Pradesh species of Eastern Ghats scrub, particularly associated with Sri Lankamalleswara Wildlife Sanctuary, not Antarctica.

rows.title: Conservation - in-situ (protected areas, biosphere reserves) and ex-situ (zoos, gene banks, seed banks)
sub: Group-II M2-B-56: Conservation of biodiversity - in-situ methods: protected areas, biosphere reserves, sacred groves
Group-II M2-B-57: Conservation of biodiversity - ex-situ methods: zoos, gene banks, botanical gardens, cryopreservation
Group-II M2-B-62: Biosphere reserves of India - list, features and those in Andhra Pradesh

secs.t: Conservation — definitions, types and FIRSTs — In-situ vs ex-situ

x: National Parks, sacred groves, biosphere reserves and OECMs conserve species in their natural or associated habitat and are in-situ methods.
A
field gene bank
is an ex-situ method because genetic resources are maintained away from their original natural habitat.
Captive breeding is suitable when a species' habitat has been permanently lost; bred animals may subsequently be released, as in the reintroduction of Gangetic gharials in several states.

secs.t: Conservation — definitions, types and FIRSTs — FIRSTs

x: The Cold Desert Biosphere Reserve is located in
Himachal Pradesh
and includes areas such as Pin Valley National Park, Kibber Wildlife Sanctuary and Chandratal.
The
Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve
extends across Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Karnataka and is India's only three-State Biosphere Reserve.
Palk Bay, covering about 448 square kilometres, is India's first
Dugong Conservation Reserve

secs.t: Protected area categories under the Act and India's PA network

x: Both are established under the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972, but human activity is regulated and permitted to an extent in a Wildlife Sanctuary; National Parks have higher protection.

A Conservation Reserve consists of State-owned land near or linking protected areas; a Community Reserve is on voluntarily offered private or community land; National Parks have strict restrictions; and tiger reserves are notified under the NTCA chapter.

secs.t: Protected area categories under the Act and India's PA network — BR vs NP vs sanctuary

x: The four protected area categories are National Park, Wildlife Sanctuary, Conservation Reserve and Community Reserve.
The 2026 count gives India 75 community reserves and 127 conservation reserves (with 109 NPs and 573 WLS).
India has 109 National Parks, 573 Wildlife Sanctuaries and 58 Tiger Reserves (along with 127 Conservation Reserves and 75 Community Reserves), making up 1,134 PAs.

secs.t: Data and targets — global PA coverage, 30x30 and OECMs

x: The WDPA is run by
UNEP-WCMC
, based in Cambridge, in collaboration with IUCN, and tracks progress towards the 30x30 target.
An OECM is outside the formal protected-area network but delivers long-term in-situ conservation outcomes and is recognised on the basis of its results.
30x30 (Target 3 of the KMGBF, CBD COP-15, 2022) aims to protect 30% of land and oceans by 2030.

secs.t: Acts and court orders → eco-sensitive zones

x: An ESZ functions as a shock absorber around a protected area, providing a transition from high protection to areas where regulated development may be permitted.
The Supreme Court held that mining is impermissible within 1 kilometre of every National Park and Wildlife Sanctuary; where a larger ESZ is notified, the larger buffer prevails.

secs.t: Biosphere reserves — MAB programme, criteria, zonation and funding

x: The Seville Strategy added social, cultural and economic needs, together with community participation, to Biosphere Reserve criteria.
The core zone is legally protected, often as a national park or sanctuary under the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972, and permits conservation and monitoring rather than ordinary human activities.
The
transition zone
is the outer interface between people and nature and permits settlements, agriculture, forestry and tourism.

secs.t: Places → biosphere reserves in and outside the UNESCO network

x: Exam angle: "All Indian BRs are in the UNESCO network" - false (13 of 18).
Nilgiri entered in 2000, Gulf of Mannar in 2001, Nanda Devi in 2004 and Nokrek in 2009.
Cold Desert became India’s 13th WNBR site in September 2025 at the 37th MAB Council meeting held at Hangzhou.

secs.t: Notable biosphere reserves — largest, multi-state and World Heritage links

x: Nilgiri lies within the Western Ghats World Heritage Site; Nanda Devi is linked with Nanda Devi and Valley of Flowers National Parks; Sundarbans with Sundarbans National Park; and Manas with Manas Wildlife Sanctuary.
The World Heritage Site is
Nanda Devi and Valley of Flowers National Parks
; the Biosphere Reserve itself is not the WHS (UKPSC 2025 key treated 'Nanda Devi BR is a WHS' as wrong).

secs.t: Places → marine conservation areas and Hope Spots

x: Hope Spots are ocean sites named by Mission Blue, an initiative associated with marine scientist Sylvia Earle, because of their importance to ocean health.
Under SDG 14, APSES identifies expansion of marine protected areas as a priority, and APSBB plans a Marine Access and Benefit-Sharing framework.
The National Centre for Marine Biodiversity is located at Jamnagar in Gujarat.

secs.t: Places → protected landscapes and Important Bird and Biodiversity Areas

x: Keibul Lamjao National Park
in Manipur is the world's only floating National Park, situated on the phumdis of Loktak Lake.
Keibul Lamjao National Park is famous for the
Sangai deer
, which is classified as Endangered.
IBAs are designated by BirdLife International.
Silent Valley National Park (tropical evergreen forest) is in Palakkad, Kerala.

secs.t: Community conservation — sacred groves, Bishnoi tradition, community reserves

x: Sacred groves are forest patches preserved by communities on religious grounds, where trees and wildlife are traditionally venerated.
In 1730, Amrita Devi Bishnoi and 363 other Bishnois died at Khejarli while protecting khejri trees from the men of the Jodhpur king.
The Citrus Gene Sanctuary in Nokrek Biosphere Reserve, Garo Hills, Meghalaya, conserves
crop wild relatives
in situ.

secs.t: Andhra Pradesh protected areas — Seshachalam BR, NSTR, Papikonda, Coringa — AP PA network

x: APSES lists one tiger reserve, Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam, and one biosphere reserve, Seshachalam.
Papikonda National Park protects the Papikondalu ranges situated along the Godavari River.
Coringa WLS in Kakinada, together with Krishna WLS, forms the Godavari-Krishna estuarine mangroves, described as India's
second-largest mangrove ecosystem
. ⚠ Sources differ: ISFR 2023 puts Gujarat second, so this ranking follows the AP sources.

secs.t: Andhra Pradesh protected areas — Seshachalam BR, NSTR, Papikonda, Coringa — Seshachalam BR

x: Seshachalam Biosphere Reserve was notified in 2010 and spans the Tirupati and Kurnool Circles.
Red Sanders, Cycas beddomei and the Golden Gecko are associated with Seshachalam.

secs.t: Institutions → gene banks and seed vaults — Gene banks

x: The second National Gene Bank was announced with a capacity of 10 lakh germplasm lines and is intended to function as a safety duplicate.
NBAGR deals with livestock, NBFGR with fish, NBAIM with agriculturally important microorganisms and NBPGR with plants and crops.
Field gene banks maintain living collections, especially of
vegetatively propagated crops and crops with recalcitrant seeds
, such as mango, coconut and banana.

secs.t: Institutions → gene banks and seed vaults — Seed vaults

x: Exam angle: statement questions on seed vaults (Svalbard and India's Ladakh vault), and "cryopreservation uses which medium".
Exam angle: statement-type questions on Svalbard's country and "largest" claims; APPSC G2 2017 key - Norway.
The International Rice Genebank is at Los Baños, NBRI is at Lucknow, the high-altitude seed vault is at Chang La and the Millennium Seed Bank is at Wakehurst in the United Kingdom.

secs.t: Cryopreservation and the LaCONES frozen zoo, Hyderabad

x: Cryopreservation is generally carried out in
liquid nitrogen at −196°C
, which halts metabolic activity and preserves viability for very long periods.
Cryopreservation can be applied to gametes, embryos, seeds, pollen, disease-free meristems, tissues and DNA.
LaCONES, the Laboratory for the Conservation of Endangered Species, is associated with CSIR-CCMB at Hyderabad and functions as
India’s frozen zoo using assisted reproduction and DNA banking

secs.t: Places → botanical gardens and conservation breeding centres

x: The Acharya Jagadish Chandra Bose Indian Botanic Garden, known for the Great Banyan and associated with the Botanical Survey of India, is at Shibpur in Howrah, West Bengal.

Vultures are associated with the Jatayu Conservation Breeding Centre at Pinjore, the Great Indian Bustard with Sam and Ramdevra in Jaisalmer, and the red panda with Padmaja Naidu Himalayan Zoological Park.

secs.t: Organisations and schemes → zoos and medicinal plants

x: The NMPB was established in 2000 under the
Ministry of AYUSH
and promotes the cultivation and conservation of medicinal plants.
The Phyto-Pharma Plant Mission is associated with CSIR and focuses on rare or threatened medicinal plants and phytopharmaceutical drug development.
The 2024 Rules encourage cultivated medicinal plants, provide faster NBA/SBB approvals, and mention 90 days generally and 180 days for IPR-related matters.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: OECMs can cover effectively conserved areas outside reserve forests, National Parks and Wildlife Sanctuaries, including sacred groves, greenbelts and wetlands, and thereby support the 30x30 objective.
Gulf of Mannar is the first marine Biosphere Reserve, Palk Bay is the first dugong reserve and Aravalli Biodiversity Park is the first OECM.
Ex-situ conservation serves as a fallback when habitats are lost or unsuitable, conserving species or their genetic material outside the natural ecosystem.

rows.title: Protected areas of Andhra Pradesh - national parks, sanctuaries, tiger reserve and Ramsar sites
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I F-77

secs.t: Places → national parks and endemic plants of AP

x: Rajiv Gandhi National Park
, also known as Rameswaram National Park, covers approximately 2.30 sq km and is the smallest national park in Andhra Pradesh.
Sri Venkateswara National Park is part of the Sri Venkateswara protected landscape in the Seshachalam hills and is associated with Cycas beddomei and red sanders.
Cycas beddomei is endemic to Andhra Pradesh and the Eastern Ghats and occurs in the Sri Venkateswara-Seshachalam region.

secs.t: Wetlands → Kolleru Ramsar site

x: Kolleru is a large freshwater lake situated between the
Godavari and Krishna
deltas.
Kolleru is a freshwater lake, supports pelicans and migratory waterfowl, and its sanctuary area is approximately 308.55 sq km.
Operation Kolleru in 2006 demolished illegal fish tanks inside the sanctuary up to the +5 ft contour.
Kolleru has been a Ramsar site since 2002.

secs.t: Places → mangrove and elephant habitats of AP

x: Coringa is associated with the mangroves of the Godavari estuary, whereas Krishna Wildlife Sanctuary protects mangroves of the Krishna estuary.
Avicennia and Rhizophora
are the mangrove genera specifically associated with the Andhra Pradesh coastal habitats.
Koundinya Wildlife Sanctuary is associated with the
Rayala Elephant Reserve
Koundinya is in Chittoor district, supports Asiatic elephants and borders Tamil Nadu.

secs.t: Acts and norms → eco-sensitive zones around AP protected areas

x: The 2002–16 Wildlife Action Plan suggested a 10 km zone around protected areas.
ESZs are notified by MoEF&CC under the
Environment (Protection) Act, 1986
, and not under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972.
There are 353 final eco-sensitive zone notifications covering 496 out of 688 protected areas nationally.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: A monsoon ban on safari vehicles
in the Nagarjuna-Srisailam Tiger Reserve was reported in June 2026.
Hope Island near Coringa was reported to face a threat from a satellite launch facility.

rows.title: Species-specific conservation projects - Project Tiger, Project Elephant, Gangetic dolphin, Great Indian Bustard, vulture, cheetah reintroduction
sub: Group-II M2-B-63: Indian wildlife conservation efforts - Project Tiger, Project Elephant and species recovery programmes
Group-II M2-B-64: Recent wildlife initiatives - cheetah reintroduction, dolphin and vulture conservation, marine conservation

secs.t: Species projects → launch year, new national projects and FIRSTs — Project → launch year

x: The correct order is Project Tiger (1973), Crocodile Project (1975), Indian Rhino Vision 2020 (2005), and Project Snow Leopard (2009).
Project Lion and Project Dolphin began in 2020, while Indian Rhino Vision 2020 began in 2005 for Assam's one-horned rhinoceros.
The five additions were dolphin, Asian elephant, gharial, Great Indian Bustard and Olive Ridley turtle.

secs.t: Species projects → launch year, new national projects and FIRSTs — FIRSTs and largest

x: Corbett
was the first tiger reserve under Project Tiger, formally included on 1 April 1973.
Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam Tiger Reserve
(NSTR) in the Nallamala hills of Andhra Pradesh is India's largest tiger reserve, with a core area of about 5,443 sq km.
India's first Dugong Conservation Reserve was established in
Palk Bay, Tamil Nadu

secs.t: Programmes, action plans and funds → coverage

x: Great Indian Bustard, Gangetic dolphin and dugong
are among the species covered by the programme.
The SC created ad hoc CAMPA in 2006 and the CAF Act, 2016 gave it statutory backing.
SAVE
, meaning Saving Asia’s Vultures from Extinction, is the partner consortium associated with these efforts.
MISHTI is a
mangrove restoration
initiative launched in 2023, covering approximately 22,561 hectares in 13 States and Union Territories.

secs.t: Project Tiger → launch, reserves, NTCA and AP

x: Project Tiger began with nine reserves covering 18,278 square kilometres.
Project Tiger was launched on the advice of Indira Gandhi’s task force, had WWF support, and included Palamau among its first nine reserves.
India has 58 tiger reserves in 18 States, covering about 84,488 sq km, or approximately 2.6% of the country’s area.
By 2022, 51 reserves had been evaluated; 12 were rated Excellent, with an average score of 78%.

secs.t: Organisations and alliances → HQ, logo, membership — Global tiger efforts

x: World Tiger Day is observed on 29 July, whereas World Wetlands Day is observed on 2 February.
TX2 was the goal of doubling the global population of wild tigers by 2022.
The summit was held in St Petersburg in November 2010, adopted TX2, and is associated with International Tiger Day on 29 July.
CA|TS stands for
Conservation Assured Tiger Standards

secs.t: Organisations and alliances → HQ, logo, membership — International Big Cat Alliance (IBCA)

x: The International Big Cat Alliance was launched in April 2023 to mark
50 years of Project Tiger
The seven big cats are tiger, lion, leopard, snow leopard, cheetah, jaguar and puma.
The IBCA was opened to 96 range and non-range countries, and 37 countries including India had consented to join.

secs.t: Organisations and alliances → HQ, logo, membership — Conservation organisations → logo and headquarters

x: IUCN and WWF are headquartered at Gland, Switzerland; BNHS at Mumbai; and WTI at Noida, Uttar Pradesh.
The Great hornbill is the logo of the
Bombay Natural History Society
(BNHS).
WTI was established in 1998, not 1982.

secs.t: Data — population counts and global shares

x: The reported figures were 891 Asiatic lions and 718 snow leopards.
The 2022 estimation recorded
3,682 tigers, with an upper estimate of 3,925
India holds approximately
of the world’s wild tigers.
India has about 60% of the world’s Asian elephants; conflict causes over 500 human deaths annually; and 29,964 is the older 2017 count for elephants in 33 reserves.

secs.t: Monitoring methods and terms → meaning

x: The All India Tiger Estimation's camera-trap survey, run by NTCA with WII, holds a Guinness World Record as the world's largest camera-trap survey.
The old pugmark technique was replaced by camera trapping and ExtractCompare software, which identifies tigers through stripe patterns.
Lakshadweep and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands are the Indian locations identified as IUCN and Mission Blue Hope Spots.

secs.t: Project Elephant → objectives, reserves and biology

x: Project Elephant was launched in
February 1992
as a Centrally Sponsored Scheme (some sources say 1991-92). '1990' is the trap: APPSC 2022 treated a 1990 launch as the incorrect statement.
Project Elephant covers wild elephants, their habitats and corridors, mitigation of conflict, and the welfare of captive elephants.
India has 33 Elephant Reserves in 14 States, and these areas can overlap tiger reserves, sanctuaries and reserved forests.

secs.t: Big cats → Project Cheetah and Project Lion — Project Cheetah - Kuno translocations

x: Project Cheetah brought African cheetahs to Kuno National Park and seeks to restore open forest and grassland ecosystems.
The introduced animals are African cheetahs.
Eight cheetahs came from Namibia in September 2022, twelve from South Africa in February 2023, and two females were released from Botswana in May 2026.
The cheetah was declared extinct in India in 1952.

secs.t: Big cats → Project Cheetah and Project Lion — Project Lion

x: Kuno was initially chosen as a second home for Gir's Asiatic lions.
Project Lion was launched in 2020 to conserve the world's last free-ranging Asiatic lions in Gir through surveillance, research and disease management.
Critics argue that Barda Wildlife Sanctuary is too close to Gir to function as an effective separate metapopulation safeguard.

secs.t: Birds → Great Indian Bustard, vultures, Amur falcon

x: The Great Indian Bustard is found mainly in
the Thar region of Rajasthan
, although its range also extends into parts of Gujarat, Maharashtra and Karnataka.
Collisions with overhead power lines are a major threat to the Great Indian Bustard, particularly in solar and wind-energy zones.

The Great Indian Bustard is included in the Species Recovery Programme and among the national species projects; it is also one of the five new national species projects of the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change.
Vultures declined sharply after feeding on cattle carcasses containing veterinary
diclofenac

secs.t: Aquatic and coastal species → status, range and sites — Gangetic dolphin

x: The Ganges River Dolphin is found in the Ganga-Brahmaputra-Meghna and Karnaphuli-Sangu systems across India, Nepal and Bangladesh.
Pollution, entanglement or bycatch in fishing nets, dams and barrages, poaching, killing for oil and boat traffic are recognised threats.
The
Ganges River Dolphin
(Platanista gangetica) was declared the National Aquatic Animal on 5 October 2009.

secs.t: Aquatic and coastal species → status, range and sites — Crocodiles and other captive-bred releases

x: Rushikulya in Ganjam, Odisha, and beaches in Srikakulam and Vizianagaram in Andhra Pradesh are associated with
Olive Ridley mass nesting
, known as arribada.

Gulf of Mannar is associated with coral reefs, islands and dugong; Malvan with corals and marine life; Coringa with mangroves and the Godavari estuary; and Bhitarkanika with saltwater crocodiles and mangroves.

secs.t: Cases, bans and conventions → year and outcome

x: All three statements correctly describe the proceedings concerning power lines in Great Indian Bustard habitat and the changes made in 2024.
The Supreme Court recognised a right against the adverse effects of climate change under Articles 14 and 21.
The Supreme Court took suo motu cognisance to protect
gharial
s in the National Chambal Sanctuary.
CMS is the Bonn Convention, was signed in 1979, operates under UNEP, and India is a party to it.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Andhra Pradesh launched Project HANUMAN on 3 March 2026, World Wildlife Day, to
reduce human-wildlife conflict
All three are reported concerns: tiger dispersal outside reserves, increasing conflict, and a railway line through the Satpura-Melghat corridor.

All three developments are correctly stated: the first captive-bred slender-billed vulture release occurred in Assam in August 2026, Botswana cheetahs were released at Kuno in May 2026, and the Nilgiris reintroduction failed after the bird's death.

rows.title: Forest and wildlife legal framework - Indian Forest Act 1927, Forest (Conservation) Act 1980, Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972
sub: Group-II M2-B-65: Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972 and its recent amendment; Biological Diversity Act 2002 and amendment

secs.t: Acts → year — enactment chronology

x: Exam angle: direct year questions (1865, 1927, 1972, 1980).
Transfer of forests and wildlife to the Concurrent List was associated with the 42nd Amendment in 1976, not the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act.
The 42nd Amendment inserted Article 48A, added Article 51A(g), and transferred forests and wildlife to the Concurrent List.
The 2023 amendment renamed it the
Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980

secs.t: Constitutional provisions and cases → ruling

x: Article 48A
, directing the State to protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife, was inserted by the 42nd Amendment in 1976.
Article 51A(g) is a Fundamental Duty requiring citizens to protect and improve the natural environment, including forests, lakes, rivers and wildlife.
Mining is barred within
1 kilometre
of every national park and sanctuary boundary unless a larger eco-sensitive zone is notified.

secs.t: Indian Forest Act 1927 → forest categories and sections

x: Section 26 lists prohibited acts in a reserved forest and makes trespass punishable.
Section 35 permits the State to regulate
forests that are not government property
Ordinance 2017, Act 2018, removing bamboo grown outside forests from 'tree' in Section 2(7).
The Act has been criticised for harming forest-dwellers’ livelihoods, contributing to reform efforts focused on community rights.

secs.t: National Forest Policy 1952 vs 1988 → targets and objectives

x: Exam angle: the statement "at least two-thirds of the country's land should be under forest" is
NOT true
. Two-thirds applies only to the hills.
The 1952 policy aimed at one-third of the total land under forest, with 60% forest cover in hills and 25% in plains.
The policy supports ecological stability, conservation, afforestation, social forestry and local needs.

secs.t: Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972 → purpose, structure and sections

x: Section 39 declares wild animals, trophies and articles derived from them to be
Government property
Section 9 prohibits hunting of scheduled animals, subject to exceptions provided by the Act.
Under Section 62, the Central Government may declare a wild animal not in Schedule I as vermin for a specified area and period by notification.

secs.t: WPA amendments 2002, 2006 and 2022 → changes

x: The 2022 amendment rationalised the schedules and added invasive alien species.
Sec. 38V(3) (2006 amendment) mandates
a Tiger Conservation Plan for every tiger reserve
The 2022 amendment incorporated
CITES
-related provisions, including provisions concerning management and scientific authorities.
African catfish
is an example of an invasive alien species referred to in connection with the amendment.

secs.t: WPA schedules → species, before and after 2022

x: Schedule I species receive the highest protection; hunting and trade are prohibited except in special cases permitted by the Act.
The mugger crocodile, rock eagle-owl and blackbuck are in Schedule I. The common crow was included in the former vermin Schedule V, not Schedule I.
A specified plant cannot be
picked, uprooted or traded without permission

secs.t: Forest (Conservation) Act 1980 / Van Adhiniyam → provisions and 2023 amendment

x: The amendment provides an exemption from central approval for strategic projects within
100 km
of international borders, among other specified exemptions.
Equal-area non-forest land is preferred; otherwise twice the degraded forest area is used, along with payment of NPV.
The 2025 rules treat
assisted natural regeneration and plantation
on leased forest land as forestry activities.

secs.t: Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act 2023 → provisions

x: Registered AYUSH practitioners and BMC-certified cultivated medicinal plants received exemptions relating to benefit-sharing.
The ordinary NBA approval period was reduced from 180 days to
90 days
Foreign nationals and foreign-incorporated entities
continue to require prior NBA approval.
The April 2025 ABS Regulations provide
25–40 percent
for identifiable source institutions and 60–75 percent for local communities through SBBs or UTBCs.

secs.t: Authorities → parent law, chair and HQ

x: The five regional offices are at
Delhi, Kolkata, Mumbai, Chennai and Jabalpur
Save Kurma concerns turtles, Softgold concerns shahtoosh, Clean Art targets mongoose-hair brushes, and Thunderbird is INTERPOL-led.
Operation Birbil deals with wildlife crime involving
wild cats and birds
The relevant years are Animal Welfare Board—1962, National Biodiversity Authority—2003, National Tiger Conservation Authority—2006, and Wildlife Crime Control Bureau—2007.

secs.t: Acts → what they protect, and NGT jurisdiction

x: The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 is an umbrella law for
environmental protection and pollution control
The NGT hears cases under seven specified laws, including the FCA 1980, EPA 1986 and BD Act 2002.
There is no Act called the
Nature (Protection) Act, 2000
The WPA 1972 protects wild animals, birds and plants and manages their habitats (APPSC 2025 key).

secs.t: Data — AP forest diversion and protected areas

x: The protected areas covered 1,75,169.42 square kilometres, corresponding to
5.32% of India’s land area

secs.t: Universal angles

x: All three statements correctly describe the reported current issue: the Delhi High Court PIL, the clearance rate of over 97%, and the 2025 full-Board meeting after a 13-year gap.
The criticism is that the 2023 amendment takes deemed forests out of the Act’s scope, potentially diluting the Godavarman protection and clashing with the Forest Rights Act.

rows.title: Forest Rights Act 2006, CAMPA, compensatory afforestation, joint forest management, agroforestry

secs.t: Afforestation and agroforestry → terms and meaning

x: The Miyawaki method creates dense, multi-layered mini-forests using native species, particularly in urban areas.
Farm forestry, community forestry, extension forestry and agroforestry are components of social forestry.
Social forestry has been criticised for drifting into
commercial monocultures
Seed balls are used to facilitate regeneration on degraded or inaccessible land.
Agroforestry integrates trees, crops and livestock on the same land.

secs.t: Origins, FIRSTs, persons and institutes

x: JFM began with the Arabari experiment in West Bengal in 1971-72.
India adopted the National Agroforestry Policy in
February 2014
and was the first country to do so.
The GROW report by NITI Aayog uses the expansion ‘Greening and Restoration of Wasteland with Agroforestry’ and places the agroforestry area at about 8.65% of India’s geographical area.

secs.t: CAMPA and compensatory afforestation → provisions

x: Exam angle: CAMPA exists at
both national and state levels
, which is correct. "People's participation is mandatory" under the 2016 Act is
wrong
The agency must pay for compensatory afforestation as well as the NPV of the lost forest ecosystem before the project begins.
CAMPA funds may support regeneration, wildlife management, catchment treatment, relocation from protected areas, human-wildlife conflict management and forest-fire prevention.

secs.t: Compensatory afforestation rules → land banks, Green Credit, consent

x: The FC Rules 2022 introduced Accredited CA.
The 2022 Rules dropped the clause requiring the consent of forest-dwellers before diversion, and the NCST disputed this with the MoEFCC.
Accredited Compensatory Afforestation permits developers to use plantations raised in advance, effectively creating land banks for meeting obligations.
The relevant guidelines were issued on
16 September 2025

secs.t: Schemes and programmes → body, target and funding — Nagar Van Yojana (NVY)

x: The
National Afforestation and Eco-development Board
(NAEB) runs the Nagar Van Yojana.
The scheme targets
600 Nagar Vans and 400 Nagar Vatikas

secs.t: Schemes and programmes → body, target and funding — Other national schemes

x: The ‘Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam’ campaign began on
5 June 2024
The revised framework targets the Aravallis, Western Ghats, Himalayas and mangroves.
The Green India Mission is one of the NAPCC missions, is implemented through JFMCs and receives partial funding from National CAMPA.
The Green India Mission works through JFMCs, VFCs and SHGs under the oversight of the Gram Sabha.

secs.t: Schemes and programmes → body, target and funding — State schemes

x: In Andhra Pradesh, the State Forest Development Agency federates 22 Forest Development Agencies and runs the NAP, GIM and NMPB schemes.
The State Forest Development Agency conducts capacity-building camps through
Vana Samrakshana Samithis
The Mukhyamantri Vriksharopan Protsahan Yojana is associated with Chhattisgarh.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Koya and Kondh communities oppose the Polavaram project over
land rights and rehabilitation
concerns.
The audit-related assessment stated that
convergence with CAMPA and MGNREGS, now VB-G RAM G
, never happened.
CAMPA money has been criticised for
funding exotic plantations on native grasslands
The Andhra Pradesh CAMPA prepares an
Annual Plan of Operations
every year.

rows.title: Climate change - greenhouse effect, greenhouse gases, radiative forcing, evidence and observed impacts
sub: Group-II M2-B-88: Global warming - greenhouse effect, greenhouse gases, radiative forcing and evidence

secs.t: Greenhouse effect → mechanism, natural vs enhanced

x: The atmosphere allows much incoming short-wave solar radiation to reach Earth’s surface but absorbs outgoing long-wave terrestrial infrared radiation through greenhouse gases.
CO2 and water vapour strongly absorb infrared radiation in the 14,000–25,000 nm range and re-radiate energy in all directions, including back towards the surface.
The primary cause of global warming is the increase in greenhouse gases (APPSC 2025 key): heat from sunlight re-radiated by the Earth is absorbed by CO2 and other gases.

secs.t: Greenhouse gases → contribution, GWP, lifetime, source — Largest contributor and contribution order

x: Water vapour is the most important greenhouse gas, and human influence on it is mainly indirect through warming.
Water vapour is the largest natural contributor, followed by carbon dioxide, methane, ozone and CFCs.
The textbook distribution given is approximately CO2 60%, methane 20%, CFCs 15% and nitrous oxide 5%.
A concentration of 423.9 ppm is approximately
0.04 percent
of the atmosphere.

secs.t: Greenhouse gases → contribution, GWP, lifetime, source — Gas → GWP, lifetime, source

x: GWP compares the heat absorbed over a specified period, generally 100 years, by a given mass of a greenhouse gas with that absorbed by the same mass of CO2.

CO2 is associated with fossil fuels, deforestation and cement production; methane with rice paddies, livestock and landfills; N2O with fertilisers and biomass or coal burning; and SF6 with dielectric fluid.

secs.t: Greenhouse gases → contribution, GWP, lifetime, source — Distractors and exam traps

x: Exam angle: "Deforestation is decreasing the amount of CO2" is the
incorrect
statement, because deforestation raises CO2.
N2, O2 and Ar are not greenhouse gases.
Deforestation does not decrease atmospheric CO2; it reduces carbon uptake and may release stored carbon, thereby raising atmospheric CO2.
Nitrogen
is a non-greenhouse gas and constitutes about 78.08 percent of the atmosphere.

secs.t: Climate science terms → meaning (forcing, sensitivity, feedbacks, tipping, records)

x: All three statements describe positive climate feedbacks: reduced ice albedo increases absorption, while additional atmospheric water vapour enhances heat trapping.
The Keeling curve is the continuous atmospheric CO2 record from Mauna Loa, Hawaii, begun in 1958 by Charles David Keeling.
Ice cores
preserve trapped air bubbles that provide evidence of past atmospheric CO2 concentrations and temperatures.

secs.t: Short-lived climate pollutants → source and lifetime

x: The Climate and Clean Air Coalition works to address
short-lived climate pollutants
such as black carbon, methane, HFCs and tropospheric ozone.
Tropospheric ozone is formed through reactions involving nitrogen oxides (NOx) and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) in sunlight.
Tropospheric ozone is a short-lived greenhouse gas, harms vegetation and cuts crop yields; its pollution is generally most severe in summer.

secs.t: Carbon accounting and removal → terms

x: Each carbon bomb can emit over 1 Gt CO2; LINGO identified 425, and their combined emissions would consume the 1.5°C carbon budget twice over.
This is the definition of carbon footprint.
Agriculture is left out because farm emissions are diffuse, making them unsuitable for treatment as a concentrated source in the CCUS road map.

secs.t: Emission sources → sector and top emitters

x: Deforestation and land-use change generally remove or reduce carbon sinks rather than increase them in all circumstances.
Black and brown carbon have a warming effect on the air, whereas sulphate droplets exert a cooling effect.
Synthetic fertilisers release nitrous oxide, while livestock digestion through enteric fermentation and rice paddies are important methane sources.
The draft rules frame emissions intensity as greenhouse gas emissions per unit of output, for example per tonne of cement.

secs.t: Data — CO2 ppm, WMO GHG Bulletin, radiative forcing shares

x: CH4 gives about 16% of long-lived GHG forcing.
The pre-industrial CO2 concentration is generally taken as approximately
CO₂ reached about 423.9 ppm in 2024, described as the highest concentration in approximately two million years; the pre-industrial level was around 280 ppm.
CO2 rose 3.5 ppm to 423.9 ppm, the biggest rise since 1957.

secs.t: Observed impacts → effect

x: Greenhouse gases and the ozone hole strengthened the westerlies, which lifted warm Circumpolar Deep Water and initiated a feedback loop that prevents new ice formation.
When oceans absorb carbon dioxide, carbonic acid forms, lowering ocean pH and causing acidification.
Climate change is associated with glacier melt, ocean acidification, extreme weather, coral bleaching, species loss and health risks.

secs.t: Pledges, reports and projections → body and finding

x: The Call to Action on Methane was launched at London Climate Action Week on 24 June 2026 and addresses waste, agriculture and fossil-fuel operations.
The UNEP Emissions Gap Report 2025 projected approximately
of warming even with updated NDCs.
‘Overshoot, peak and decline’ describes the trajectory in which warming or emissions exceed a level, reach a maximum, and then decrease.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: India sought clarity at the Bonn talks on how
tipping points
could be used for policy-making.
India's country-level social cost of carbon is reported as
$86 per tonne of CO2
, the highest globally.
The 2009 US 'endangerment finding' on six greenhouse gases, which let the EPA regulate vehicle GHG emissions, flowed from the Supreme Court's ruling in
Massachusetts v. EPA (2007)

rows.title: Ocean acidification - causes, effects on marine ecosystems and coral reefs
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I F-81

secs.t: Ocean acidification → cause, chemistry and terms

x: Ocean acidification is called the ‘evil twin of global warming’ or ‘the other CO2 problem’ because anthropogenic carbon dioxide produces a distinct chemical threat to marine systems.
The oceans absorb
about one-third
of anthropogenic carbon dioxide; the estimate is also expressed as roughly 30–40%.
Decay of algal blooms consumes dissolved oxygen, causing deoxygenation, and adds carbon dioxide, which worsens acidification.

secs.t: Organisms and ocean stressors → effect

x: Effects on calcifying organisms can disrupt marine food webs, which may reduce fish stocks and affect livelihoods dependent on fisheries.
Marine heatwaves
are identified as the strongest global driver of coral-cover decline.
Nutrient runoff promotes algal blooms; when the biomass decays, decomposition consumes oxygen and can create hypoxic dead zones.

secs.t: Coral restoration methods → technique and place

x: Biorock (mineral accretion) uses low-voltage current on steel frames to deposit limestone.
Coral translocation or transplantation involves moving colonies away from project sites as a conservation and protection measure.
The NGT asked MoEFCC to ensure coral protection and coral regeneration through a proved scientific method for the Great Nicobar project.

secs.t: Monitoring bodies, missions and targets → role

x: SDG 14.3 is about minimising and addressing ocean acidification.
Samudrayaan includes the three-member Matsya 6000 submersible, and the mission has surveyed about 25 seamounts and identified about 39 potentially new species.
Varaha is the deep-sea mining system trialled at 5,270 metres.
The National Centre for Coastal Research (NCCR), Chennai, monitors coral reef health through the D-COIN platform.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: SDG 14 is not ranked by NITI Aayog, while Andhra Pradesh has plans concerning expanded Marine Protected Areas and sustainable fishing.
Lakshadweep is made up entirely of atoll reefs.

rows.title: Impacts of climate change on India - monsoon, agriculture, Himalayan glaciers, sea-level rise, extreme events
sub: Group-II M2-B-89: Climate change - observed and projected impacts globally and on India
Group-II M2-B-90: Climate change and Indian agriculture, water resources, coasts and the Himalaya

secs.t: Reports and assessments → publisher and finding — Indian assessments

x: ; the MoES assessment places the rise at about 0.7°C.
The assessment covers
temperature, rainfall and monsoon, droughts, sea level, tropical cyclones and the Himalayan cryosphere
India's first national climate assessment was published in 2020 by the
Ministry of Earth Sciences
The IMD statement put India's 2020 average yearly temperature at
(APPSC 2021 key).

secs.t: Reports and assessments → publisher and finding — Global reports in news

x: The 2026 edition described the indicators as 'flashing red' and highlighted accelerating change.
The UK Met Office is the lead centre.
The Lancet Countdown 2025 reported a 23% rise in heat deaths since the 1990s and an 85% increase in dengue potential in India.
The theme of the UNEP Emissions Gap Report 2025 was ‘
Off Target

secs.t: Reports and assessments → publisher and finding — Bodies behind the reports

x: WMO was set up in 1950, became a UN specialised agency in 1951 and is headquartered in Geneva.
The IPCC was set up in 1988 by WMO and UNEP, assesses existing scientific literature rather than conducting its own research, and shared the 2007 Nobel Peace Prize.

secs.t: Heat waves, wet-bulb temperature and health → terms and hotspots — Terms

x: IMD declares a heat wave when the actual maximum temperature is at least 45°C, regardless of the normal maximum temperature.
Wet-bulb temperature is the lowest temperature that air can reach by evaporative cooling and combines the effects of heat and humidity.
When relative humidity is 100%, no further evaporative cooling is possible, so wet-bulb and dry-bulb temperatures become equal.

secs.t: Heat waves, wet-bulb temperature and health → terms and hotspots — Heat data and hotspots

x: Palnadu, Kurnool and Anantapur
are the Andhra Pradesh districts identified as experiencing increasingly frequent and intense heat waves.
At a wet-bulb temperature above about 35°C, sweat can no longer cool the body sufficiently, making human survival highly difficult.
Models may UNDERestimate urban warming by 0.5-2 C, not overestimate it.

secs.t: Heat waves, wet-bulb temperature and health → terms and hotspots — Health impacts

x: Rentachintala in Palnadu is the hottest place in Andhra Pradesh.
Warmer and wetter conditions expand dengue and malaria.
Urban waterlogging can spread
leptospirosis, typhoid and hepatitis A
Ahmedabad
prepared the first Heat Action Plan in South Asia in 2013.

secs.t: Monsoon, water and drought → changes

x: Extreme pre-monsoon rainfall events doubled between 1981 and 2020.
The
Brahmaputra, Ganga and Krishna
basins have experienced surging flash floods in the stated assessment.
Both statements are true, and the greater moisture-holding capacity of warmer air helps explain the intensification of extreme rainfall and associated flash floods.
Falling groundwater levels are reported in Punjab, Haryana and parts of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana.

secs.t: Agriculture → yield impacts and programmes

x: El Niño tends to weaken the south-west monsoon and reduce rice and sugarcane yields, whereas La Niña usually enhances monsoon rainfall.
The FAO–WMO report indicates that extreme heat can reduce dairy milk yield by about
15–25 percent
ACASA-India, the Atlas of Climate Adaptation in Indian Agriculture, uses GIS-based mapping to assess crop vulnerability.

secs.t: Himalayan glaciers → bodies, places and GLOF events — Monitoring bodies

x: The
Geological Survey of India
performs these monitoring, mapping and inventory-related functions for Himalayan glaciers.
Himansh is an NCPOR station situated above 4,000 metres in Lahaul-Spiti and established in 2016 for glacier studies.
As valley glaciers thin, tributary glaciers are left hanging on steep slopes.
ICIMOD has its headquarters in
Kathmandu

secs.t: Himalayan glaciers → bodies, places and GLOF events — GLOF events and places

x: Glacier melt threatens lean-season flows of rivers such as the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra and also affects hydropower.
The melting of the Gangotri glacier is attributed to
global warming
Gangabal and Nundkol lakes lie below Harmukh peak in Ganderbal and are highly GLOF-prone.
Permafrost thaw releases CH4 and CO2 and damages infrastructure.

secs.t: Sea-level rise, cyclones and fisheries → AP coast

x: Sea-level rise results mainly from thermal expansion of seawater and the addition of water from melting glaciers and ice sheets.
Cyclones can wreck paddy and aquaculture in deltas while supplying water beneficial to rabi crops and tanks.
Marine heatwaves can increase cyclone wind speeds by up to 20% and rainfall by up to 12%, thereby promoting rapid intensification.

secs.t: Data — climate vulnerability and Climate Risk Index

x: The AP SAPCC assessment identifies the northern and central regions as very highly vulnerable, the southern coast as moderately vulnerable, and the south-western areas as relatively low vulnerable.
India was ranked the ninth most climate-affected country, with
430 extreme events, losses of 170 billion US dollars and 1.3 billion people affected

secs.t: Adaptation measures → detail

x: Exam angle: "Climate change is increasing social tension in India" (A) with "extreme events threaten food security" (R):
both are true, and R explains A
The NDC 2031–35 adaptation focus includes
coasts, heat and infrastructure
Both statements are true, and threats to food security from extreme weather provide the reason why climate change can increase social tension.

secs.t: Observed global impacts → places, FIRSTs and data — Ice and oceans

x: Oceans hold over 90% of excess heat, 2025 saw marine heatwaves over about 90% of the ocean surface, and ocean heat records continued for nine straight years.
Quelccaya (Peru) is the largest tropical ice cap, retreating ~200 ft/yr.
The cited World Bank estimate is
45 million
Indians pushed into extreme poverty within 15 years.

secs.t: Observed global impacts → places, FIRSTs and data — Biodiversity

x: The Rutgers study found that warming could eliminate about twice as many ocean species from their habitats as land species.
~8 million species, up to 1 million threatened.
Species are shifting
poleward and upslope
as they track cooler climatic conditions.
Antarctic sea-ice loss disrupts krill populations and contributes to Emperor penguin breeding failure.

secs.t: Tipping points and 1.5 C vs 2 C → elements and projections

x: A tipping point is a threshold beyond which small changes may produce large, self-perpetuating and irreversible shifts in a non-linear system.
Warm-water coral reefs
are identified as the most fragile tipping element, with their critical threshold already crossed.
Arctic sea ice
is a recognised climate tipping element and is near record lows (APPSC-G2 2025 answer).

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The WMO decadal update and UNEP’s assessment indicate that 1.5°C is effectively breached, while a strong El Niño is considered likely in 2027.
The APSDMA Heatwave Action Plan 2026 identifies heatwaves as causing more deaths in Andhra Pradesh than any other natural disaster.
The criticism is that ‘loss and damage’ is being understood locally as merely
disaster relief
, although the concept concerns wider climate-related losses and damages.

Group-II M2-B-96: Recent Conference of the Parties outcomes and the loss and damage fund
Group-II M2-B-97: IPCC assessment reports - key findings and their significance for India
Group-II M2-B-98: India's participation and role in climate negotiations - equity, CBDR and the developing-country position

secs.t: Climate treaties → adoption, entry into force, parties and FIRSTs

x: Adopted 9 May 1992 (New York), opened for signature at Rio, in force 21 March 1994, and the COP is the supreme body meeting annually.
The objective of the UNFCCC is to stabilise greenhouse gas concentrations at a level that prevents dangerous anthropogenic interference with the climate system.
The Paris temperature goal is to hold warming well below 2°C and pursue efforts to limit warming to 1.5°C.

secs.t: UNFCCC → Annex groups, CBDR-RC and bodies

x: CBDR-RC recognises differentiated historical responsibility and capabilities; developed countries that caused most historical emissions are expected to take the lead.
CBDR-RC appears in Principle 7 of the Rio Declaration, Article 3.1 of the UNFCCC and Article 2.2 of the Paris Agreement ('in the light of different national circumstances').
The Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement are the two instruments associated with the UNFCCC; their governing meetings are referred to as CMP and CMA respectively.

secs.t: Negotiating blocs → members and stance

x: India requested dedicated agenda space for Article 9.1, which obliges developed countries to provide climate finance to developing countries.
India aligned with G77+China (largest developing-country group), the LMDC (of which India is a member, hard-line on equity and CBDR) and BASIC.
AOSIS
(Alliance of Small Island States) presses for the 1.5°C goal, as its members face existential threats from sea-level rise.

secs.t: Kyoto Protocol → commitment periods, mechanisms and gases

x: The original six gases were CO2, CH4, N2O, HFCs, PFCs and SF6.

International Emissions Trading involves allowances traded among Annex I countries; CDM generates CERs from developing-country projects; Joint Implementation generates ERUs from projects in other Annex I countries.
Both statements are true, and the differentiated treatment of industrialised and developing countries explains why binding targets were limited to Annex I parties.

secs.t: Carbon markets → CDM to Paris Article 6

x: The Article 6.4 mechanism replaces the Kyoto CDM, corresponding adjustments prevent double counting, and Article 6 was made fully operational at COP29.
CDM projects in developing countries such as India earned Certified Emission Reductions, or CERs.
The India-Japan Joint Crediting Mechanism, signed in August 2025, is a bilateral cooperative approach under
Article 6.2

secs.t: Paris Agreement → Articles, NDCs and withdrawals — Articles

x: Under the ratchet mechanism, each new NDC must represent progression beyond the previous one and is informed by the Global Stocktake.
Article 13 establishes the Enhanced Transparency Framework, including common reporting through Biennial Transparency Reports.
A party may give notice of withdrawal three years after the Agreement entered into force for it, and the withdrawal takes effect one year after the notice.

secs.t: Paris Agreement → Articles, NDCs and withdrawals — Data - India's NDC

x: The United States left the Paris Agreement for the second time in
January 2026
The United States announced withdrawal in 2017, its withdrawal became effective on 4 November 2020, and it rejoined on 19 February 2021.
The memorandum ended US participation in the UNFCCC, IPCC, International Solar Alliance and IRENA.

secs.t: COPs → year, host city and outcome

x: Exam angle: match the COP with its city and outcome (COP8 Delhi, COP21 Paris, COP26 Glasgow Pact, COP27 Loss and Damage Fund, COP29 NCQG, COP30 Belém).
COP22 was held at Marrakech, COP23 at Bonn under Fiji's presidency, and COP25 at Madrid under Chile's presidency.
COP8, held in New Delhi in 2002, adopted the
Delhi Ministerial Declaration on Climate Change and Sustainable Development

COP21 adopted the Paris Agreement, COP26 produced the Glasgow Climate Pact, COP27 established the Loss and Damage Fund, and COP29 is associated with the New Collective Quantified Goal on Climate Finance.

secs.t: COP27 and COP28 → decisions

x: Exam angle: multi-statement COP27 questions (APPSC-G1 2022: I, III, IV correct) - read each clause on dates and temperature targets.
The APPSC-GS 2024 key links Saraswathi of Malluvalasa (AP natural-farming practitioner) with '
Sustaina India 2025
'. ⚠ Sources differ: one guide links her to COP28 instead, so check the official key.
COP28 included pledges to triple renewable capacity to 11,000 GW and double energy-efficiency gains to 4 per cent per year by 2030.

secs.t: COP29 and COP30 → finance and adaptation decisions

x: The COP30 outcome was called the
Belém Political Package
and was framed in a ‘mutirão’ spirit.
NDC 3.0 calls for economy-wide, all-gas pledges aligned with the 1.5°C objective and due for COP30.
Adaptation finance target US$120 billion/year, 59 voluntary GGA indicators, and the Belém 4x pledge to quadruple sustainable fuels by 2035.

secs.t: Climate finance bodies → founded, HQ, board — Funds

x: The GCF has a 24-member Board, operates under the UNFCCC financial mechanism and is the largest dedicated climate fund.
The GEF finances the
UNFCCC, CBD, UNCCD, Stockholm Convention and Minamata Convention
, among others.
The Adaptation Fund was established under the Kyoto Protocol, is financed by a 2% share of CDM CER proceeds, and NABARD is India’s National Implementing Entity.

secs.t: Climate finance bodies → founded, HQ, board — Loss and Damage Fund (FRLD)

x: The Loss and Damage Fund was created at COP27 and became operational at COP28.
The Fund was agreed at COP27 in 2022, operationalised at COP28 in 2023, opened to applications at COP30, and the World Bank’s interim role extends until COP33 in 2028.
The Fund covers economic and non-economic losses resulting from both sudden-onset and slow-onset events.

secs.t: Climate initiatives → founders, launch and type — Initiatives launched at COPs

x: Exam angle: in APPSC 2024 both Global Shield statements were keyed
wrong
("None of the above"), so check who founded it and where it was launched.
The Global Methane Pledge was launched at COP26 by the United States and the European Union and aims to cut methane emissions by 30 per cent from 2020 levels by 2030.

secs.t: Climate initiatives → founders, launch and type — Other initiatives

x: Climate Action Tracker is an independent scientific analysis initiative of
Climate Analytics and the NewClimate Institute
The CCAC was launched in 2012 by UNEP and six countries, and it targets short-lived climate pollutants.
The New York Declaration on Forests was endorsed at the 2014 UN Climate Summit and is voluntary and non-binding, with the objective of halting deforestation.

secs.t: Environmental treaties → goal and whether they address GHGs

x: The Montreal Protocol addresses ozone-depleting substances, Basel concerns hazardous-waste movement, CBD concerns biodiversity and Ramsar concerns wetlands.
The Rotterdam Convention establishes the Prior Informed Consent procedure for certain hazardous chemicals and pesticides in international trade.

The Montreal Protocol has an indirect greenhouse-gas relevance because CFCs are greenhouse gases, while the other statements correctly identify the subjects of the Paris, Minamata and Stockholm instruments.

secs.t: IPCC → founding, working groups and assessment cycle — Founding and role

x: The IPCC has 195 member countries, its reports are policy-relevant but not policy-prescriptive, and it shared the 2007 Nobel Peace Prize with Al Gore.
WG I covers the physical science basis, WG II covers impacts, adaptation and vulnerability, and WG III covers mitigation.
Each IPCC assessment report carries a Summary for Policymakers, which presents the assessment findings in a form relevant to policymakers.

secs.t: IPCC → founding, working groups and assessment cycle — Assessment reports → year

x: The IPCC was set up in 1988 by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) and the World Meteorological Organization (WMO).
AR7 began in July 2023, but its Working Group reports are expected only from about mid-2028 and its Synthesis Report by late 2029; therefore AR6 remains the current authority in the interim.

secs.t: IPCC reports → key findings (SR1.5, SRCCL, SROCC, AR6) — SR1.5 (2018)

x: Exam angle: fill-in-the-blank on "2030-2052", "45% by 2030 from 2010 levels" and "net zero by 2050".
The pathways require cuts that are deep, rapid and sustained; gradual or limited cuts are not sufficient.
The Ocean and Cryosphere report highlighted that marine heatwaves became more frequent, along with coral bleaching and fisheries impacts.

secs.t: IPCC reports → key findings (SR1.5, SRCCL, SROCC, AR6) — AR6 Synthesis Report - global findings

x: The AR6 assessment states that the 1.5°C threshold is likely to be crossed in the
early 2030s
without immediate, deep cuts.
The stated pathway requires global emissions to peak before 2025, reach net zero by mid-century, and obtain 70–85% of electricity from renewables by 2050.
AR6 Working Group I placed the remaining carbon budget for a 50% chance of limiting warming to 1.5°C at about
500 GtCO2
from 2020.

secs.t: IPCC reports → key findings (SR1.5, SRCCL, SROCC, AR6) — AR6 - India-relevant findings

x: The IPCC AR6 indicates that
India is warming faster than the global average
and is experiencing more frequent and intense heatwaves.
AR6 associates erratic monsoons with severe floods, identifies risks to Mumbai and Chennai from sea-level rise, and reports that high mountains are warming at twice the global average.
Black carbon lowers the albedo of snow, causing it to absorb more solar energy and thereby accelerating melting.

secs.t: Scenarios → SSPs and RCPs

x: SSPs are narratives concerning future population, economic and policy conditions that are used with forcing levels in AR6 scenarios.
SSPs replaced the four
Representative Concentration Pathways
, or RCPs, used in AR5.
SSP3 represents Regional Rivalry.
is one of the AR6 illustrative scenarios.
There is still no plausible path below 1.5°C without overshoot.

secs.t: India at the COPs → stances, pledges not signed, hosting — India's stances

x: India did not sign the Global Methane Pledge and stayed out of the Glasgow Leaders' Declaration on Forests and Land Use
India advocated a
phase-down
, rather than a phase-out, of unabated coal power at COP26.
India criticised the US$300 billion annual NCQG target as
inadequate
India joined the TFFF only as an observer at COP30.

secs.t: India at the COPs → stances, pledges not signed, hosting — COP hosting

x: The Prime Minister announced India's bid for COP33 at COP28 on 1 December 2023; it was withdrawn in April 2026 after a review of commitments for 2028.
Mission LiFE is India's idea-level contribution centred on
individual behaviour change
The declaration was associated with the BRICS meeting at Rio in July 2025 and supported Global South demands.

secs.t: India's constraints, climate equity and CBAM → issues — Mitigation constraints

x: India argues that developed countries should provide clean, affordable technology and finance to support the transition.
Gevra is a coal mine in Chhattisgarh and Rajmahal is a coal mine in Jharkhand; both are on the LINGO list of carbon bombs.
India links its later net-zero target to development priorities, a large population needing growth and industrialisation, and continuing coal dependence.

secs.t: India's constraints, climate equity and CBAM → issues — Climate equity → terms

x: All four statements express the climate-equity position: historical responsibility lies mainly with developed countries, India's per capita emissions are lower, developing countries seek carbon space, and those least responsible may suffer most.
The Loss and Damage Fund associated with COP27 in 2022 was regarded as an ethical win in the context of climate justice.

secs.t: India's constraints, climate equity and CBAM → issues — EU CBAM

x: CBAM entered its transitional phase in 2023, its definitive phase on 1 January 2026, aims to prevent carbon leakage, and exempts firms subject to an equivalent domestic carbon price.
India argues that CBAM violates the principle of Common but Differentiated Responsibilities and Respective Capabilities (CBDR-RC) and amounts to green protectionism.
The 12th BRICS Environment Ministers' Meeting in New Delhi, during India's chairmanship, called CBAM
unilateral, punitive, discriminatory and protectionist

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Because the CMP and CMA work by consensus, every party can effectively block agreement, leading to the criticism that they resemble 'hop-on, hop-off buses'.
Climate refugees displaced by sea-level rise fall outside the legal scope of the
1951 Refugee Convention
Nepal's request after the August 2026 glacial-collapse flood was viewed as
an early test of the Fund
for Responding to Loss and Damage.
The agreed scientific baseline informs negotiations, and the 1.5°C and net-zero-by-2050 benchmarks rest on SR1.5 and AR6.
India's 2070 net-zero target is criticised as late, while India defends it using the principles of common but differentiated responsibilities and development needs.

rows.title: India's climate commitments - NDCs, Panchamrit, net-zero 2070, LiFE mission, ISA, CDRI, carbon market
sub: Group-II M2-B-99: India's climate commitments - NDCs, Panchamrit and net zero by 2070
Group-II M2-B-101: India's climate initiatives - International Solar Alliance, CDRI, LiFE and the carbon credit trading scheme

secs.t: NDCs and Panchamrit → targets, years and progress — NDC targets by version

x: India crossed the 50% non-fossil share in installed electric capacity in
June 2025
, five years ahead of the 2030 target timeline.
The 2015 INDC target was 33–35%, the 2022 target was 45%, and NDC 3.0 sets 47% emissions-intensity reduction and 60% non-fossil installed capacity.
The 2035 NDC includes a 47% intensity cut, 60% non-fossil power capacity and an additional sink of 3.5–4.0 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent.

secs.t: NDCs and Panchamrit → targets, years and progress — NDC versions → date and feature

x: Exam angle: the target is non-fossil
installed capacity
, not generation. UPSC notes say "40% of power generation", which is wrong.
India submitted its INDC to the UNFCCC in October 2015, before the Paris Climate Change Conference, COP21.
The updated NDC was communicated in August 2022, formalising the Panchamrit.
NDC 3.0 includes Mission LiFE, enhanced adaptation and demands for new, low-cost climate finance.

secs.t: NDCs and Panchamrit → targets, years and progress — Panchamrit — the five COP26 pledges

x: Exam angle: memory hook 500-50-1-45-2070. The trap is capacity versus generation.
The Panchamrit commitments were announced at Glasgow on
1 November 2021
during COP26.
The Panchamrit sequence is 500 GW, 50 percent, 1 billion tonnes, 45 percent and net zero by 2070.
The 45 percent emissions-intensity reduction commitment and the 50 percent renewable-energy commitment entered the August 2022 NDC.

secs.t: NDCs and Panchamrit → targets, years and progress — Progress data

x: Emissions intensity:
Fell
below 2005 levels by 2020.
Non-fossil capacity:
Generation gap:
Only ~
25% of power generated
is non-fossil, due to storage shortage (26-27 Mar 2026)

secs.t: Net zero 2070 — terms, LT-LEDS transitions and Net Zero Portal

x: India invokes the principle of Common but Differentiated Responsibilities (CBDR) and its development requirements to justify the 2070 target, later than the 2050 targets of most developed countries.

The seven transitions include low-carbon electricity systems, low-carbon transport, urban adaptation and efficient buildings, decoupling growth from industrial emissions, CO2 removal, forest and vegetation cover, and low-carbon finance.

secs.t: Energy and carbon-sink data — capacity, storage, forest cover

x: The Economic Survey 2025–26 places India
fourth
in installed renewable energy capacity; another cited source gives a third-place ranking.
The first utility-scale standalone BESS is a
180 MW
project developed by IndiGrid in Gujarat.
The identified pumped storage potential is 258 GW, with 7 GW operational and more than 17 GW additional capacity planned by 2030.

secs.t: Missions and programmes → objectives — Green Hydrogen, Nuclear, GIM, LiFE

x: The mission has an outlay of ₹19,744 crore and targets 5 MMT/year capacity by 2030, supporting energy independence by 2047 and net zero by 2070.
The official estimate for carbon sink addition during 2005–2019 was
1.97 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent
Mission LiFE seeks to move the focus from state action towards individual behaviour, especially mindful consumption.

secs.t: Carbon market — CCTS and Green Credit Programme: Acts, sections, administering bodies — Act / scheme → year → provision

x: The Green Credit Programme was introduced in October 2023 under the
Environment (Protection) Act, 1986
The Indian Council of Forestry Research and Education (ICFRE), Dehradun, administers the Green Credit Programme.
The CCTS was notified in June 2023 under Section 14AA of the Energy Conservation Act, 2001, as amended in 2022.

secs.t: Carbon market — CCTS and Green Credit Programme: Acts, sections, administering bodies — CCTS

x: The Indian Carbon Market combines a compliance mechanism for energy-intensive sectors with an offset mechanism for voluntary projects in ten sectors.
Entities that beat their notified GHG Emission Intensity targets earn tradeable Carbon Credit Certificates.
CCTS is a qualifying carbon price under the UK CBAM (from 1 Jan 2027), so Indian exports are not charged twice.

secs.t: Carbon market — CCTS and Green Credit Programme: Acts, sections, administering bodies — Green Credit Programme

x: The programme covers activities such as tree planting, water management, sustainable agriculture, waste management, air-pollution reduction, mangroves, ecomark and sustainable buildings.
The programme is a market-based incentive for voluntary environmental actions.
The Surat Emissions Trading Scheme reduced particulate-matter emissions by 20–30 percent.
The Khasi Hills Community REDD+ project is India’s first
Plan Vivo-certified REDD+ project

secs.t: Organisations → launch, HQ, members — ISA, CDRI and India-led coalitions — ISA vs CDRI
Organisations → launch, HQ, members — ISA, CDRI and India-led coalitions — International Solar Alliance (ISA)

x: Although the ISA initially began with the idea of bringing together sunshine countries between the tropics, its membership is now open to all UN member states.
The United States joined in 2021, announced withdrawal in January 2026, and had contributed about $2.1 million, or roughly 1 per cent of ISA funds.

secs.t: Organisations → launch, HQ, members — ISA, CDRI and India-led coalitions — Other India-led coalitions

x: The Global Biofuels Alliance was launched during India’s G20 Presidency; LeadIT was set up by India and Sweden in 2019; Mission Innovation began at COP21 in 2015; and the Big Cat Alliance was launched at Mysuru in April 2023.
LeadIT focuses particularly on low-carbon transitions in the
steel and cement
sectors and aligns heavy industry with the Paris goals.

secs.t: Index and reports — CCPI, BTR1; negotiating stance and finance

x: The CCPI is published by Germanwatch, the NewClimate Institute and Climate Action Network (CAN) International.
India was ranked
11th
in CCPI 2019 (released at COP24, December 2018); 9th was its rank in CCPI 2020. ⚠ APPSC key said 9th.
All three statements describe India’s stated negotiating position: equity, climate justice, CBDR-RC, and continuity with incremental advance within its equitable share.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The audit found weak convergence with CAMPA and MGNREGS and inadequate funding; it did not find excessive funding and complete convergence.
The plan expects
of the projected 1,121 GW capacity to be non-fossil by 2035–36.
The demand seeks to allow smaller firms to monetise avoided emissions through wider access to the carbon market.

rows.title: National Action Plan on Climate Change - the eight national missions; State Action Plans on Climate Change
sub: Group-II M2-B-100: National Action Plan on Climate Change - the eight missions; State Action Plans and AP's plan

secs.t: NAPCC — definitions, scope and FIRSTs

x: The NAPCC is India’s overarching domestic climate framework and covers both mitigation and adaptation.
NAPCC was released on 30 June 2008 by PM Dr Manmohan Singh.
Four
of the eight core missions focus on adaptation, while the NAPCC as a whole addresses both adaptation and mitigation.
India’s National Statement at COP30 in Belém, Brazil, was delivered on
17 November 2025

secs.t: Organisations → role — NAPCC governance and tracking tools

x: The India Climate Change Knowledge Portal was launched in 2020 and tracks ministry-wise climate actions; it is associated with the
Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
The Prime Minister’s Council on Climate Change sets policy, while the Executive Committee on Climate Change, under the Principal Secretary to the Prime Minister, coordinates it.
The MoEFCC Climate Change Division is the nodal unit for UNFCCC negotiations and coordination of the National Action Plan on Climate Change.

secs.t: The eight National Missions → nodal ministry and launch — Count of missions

x: The
Perform, Achieve and Trade
(PAT) scheme is included in the National Mission for Enhanced Energy Efficiency and is associated with the Ministry of Power and BEE.
NMSH is under MoHUA (a-ii), Green India Mission under MoEFCC (b-i), NMSA under the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers' Welfare (c-iv) and the National Water Mission under Jal Shakti (d-iii).

secs.t: The eight National Missions → nodal ministry and launch — DST missions

x: Exam angle: "Which is NOT a NAPCC mission?" - distractors are usually schemes such as Swachh Bharat, Ujjwala or AMRUT.
The Economic Survey 2025–26 uses a nine-mission description by adding health, while the officially tested count of core missions remains eight.
Nuclear and Green Hydrogen are newer initiatives that advance the net-zero-by-2070 objective but remain outside the original eight missions.

secs.t: Mission objectives → targets — GIM, NWM, PAT, NMSA

x: The three sub-missions concern forest quality, forest and tree cover with ecosystem restoration, and incomes of forest-dependent people.
The five goals include a public water database, impact assessment, citizen/state action, focus on over-exploited areas and better water-use efficiency.
PAT rewards industries that beat their energy-saving targets with tradable Energy Saving Certificates.

secs.t: Schemes and funds → year and implementing entity — CCAP, NAFCC, NCEF

x: CCAP (2014) is an MoEFCC scheme that builds assessment capacity, supports SAPCCs and strengthens the scientific base.
NAFCC was set up in 2015 as a central sector scheme to fund adaptation projects of States/UTs in vulnerable sectors (2017 is when the coal cess was folded into GST compensation cess).
The National Clean Energy Fund was created in 2010–11 from a clean energy cess on coal to fund clean-energy research and projects.

secs.t: State Action Plans on Climate Change (SAPCC) — framework, support, finance

x: States have moved from broad mitigation-centric plans in 2010–15 towards district-specific, risk-based adaptation plans from 2020 onwards, linked with social schemes and local institutions.
NDC implementation is pursued through the National Adaptation Plan, national missions and State Action Plans on Climate Change.
The proposal is to introduce climate budgeting through State Finance Departments by means of
a budget circular

secs.t: Andhra Pradesh climate action — Climate Change Cell, AP SAPCC 2025-30, FFF-AP

x: The revised AP SAPCC covers 2025–30, includes eight energy-sector adaptation measures and is based on vulnerability to rising temperatures, variable rainfall and extreme events.
The AP National Green Corps was established in
; the national programme began in 2001–02.
Heatwaves, droughts, floods and cyclones affect water, agriculture, food security and health.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The NAPCC Dashboard was launched in September 2026 to track the progress of the national climate missions.
The NAPCC is the domestic vehicle for implementing India’s
Nationally Determined Contributions
(NDCs).
Tamil Nadu has a Governing Council on Climate Change headed by the Chief Minister and also has a TN Green Climate Company.
