rows.title: Environmental pollution - types, sources and impacts (overview)
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I F-85

secs.t: Pollution — types, classification and terms

x: By source geometry: a chimney is a point source, a highway with vehicles is a line source, a mining area is an area source and farm runoff is a diffuse (non-point) source.
Xenobiotics are synthetic chemicals foreign to living systems, such as pesticides, PCBs and plastics, and they generally resist degradation.

secs.t: Toxic pollutants → sources and effects

x: Lead from vehicles and smelters causes brain damage.
Coal ash can contain heavy metals such as
arsenic, mercury, lead, cadmium and chromium
; its disposal can therefore pollute soil.
Brominated flame retardants are used in electronics, plastics, foam and textiles.
Such burning can release dioxins, furans, carbon monoxide, sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, lead, cadmium and mercury.

secs.t: Index and organisations → HQ — CEPI and monitoring bodies

x: CEPI was developed by the CPCB with IIT Delhi (2009), not IIT Bombay.
CEPI considers pollutant, pathway and receptor, with the receptor representing exposed people, and covers air, water and land pollution.
A CEPI score of 70 or above indicates a critically polluted cluster.
The 2009 assessment found
clusters critically polluted (CEPI ≥70).

secs.t: Major pollution disasters → year, place, pollutant

x: Exam angle: Bhopal = gas leakage / MIC / 1984 is asked almost every year.
The Los Angeles smog was photochemical smog, produced when sunlight acted on nitrogen oxides and hydrocarbons from vehicle exhaust, particularly at about 24–32°C.
The correct sequence is Los Angeles smog (1943), Minamata disease (1956), Bhopal gas tragedy (1984), and Chernobyl (1986).

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Environment Audit Rules 2025 introduced third-party auditors.
PARIVESH 3.0 is described as a single-window mechanism for environmental governance and approvals.
The Andhra Pradesh Common Zoning Regulations 2026 recognise
nine
land-use categories, including provisions noting white and green industries.

rows.title: Air pollution - sources, pollutants, NAAQS, AQI, National Clean Air Programme, stubble burning
sub: Group-II M2-B-74: Air pollution - pollutants, sources, standards (NAAQS), AQI and health impacts
Group-II M2-B-75: Air pollution control - National Clean Air Programme, stubble burning and vehicular emission measures
Group-II M2-B-91: Acid rain - causes, chemistry, effects and control measures

secs.t: Air pollution sources — types, terms and smog

x: Vehicles emit pollutants such as carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides, VOCs, particulate matter and unburnt hydrocarbons.
Ozone, PAN and ammonium sulphate are formed in the atmosphere and are secondary pollutants or products.
The Asian Brown Cloud is a dry-season layer of soot, black carbon and aerosols over South Asia and the Indian Ocean, arising mainly from biomass and fossil-fuel burning.
Forest fires
, volcanic eruptions and dust storms are natural sources (APPSC 2025 answer: forest fires).

secs.t: Pollutants → source and health effect; indoor pollution; bioindicators — Pollutant → health effect

x: Exam angle: "pollutant from vehicles that reduces O2 carrying capacity of blood" = carbon monoxide.

Carbon monoxide reduces the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity; sulphur dioxide irritates the eyes and respiratory system; lead damages the brain; and ground-level ozone causes asthma and eye irritation.
Carbon monoxide
combines functionally with blood haemoglobin and reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood, causing giddiness and potentially death.

secs.t: Pollutants → source and health effect; indoor pollution; bioindicators — SO2 and secondary particulates

x: Ammonium sulphate (SO2 + NH3) is a secondary particulate and makes up nearly 1/3 of India's PM2.5.
Lichens indicate
sulphur dioxide
pollution and disappear from areas with high SO2 levels.
Indoor air pollution is linked to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer and heart disease.
Indoor pollution also comes from dust, smoke, pesticides, gases and mosquito coils.

secs.t: Acid rain — definition, FIRST, causes and chemistry — Definition, pH and FIRST

x: The acid-rain threshold is pH 5.6, and normal rain (~5.6) is slightly acidic due to carbonic acid from CO2.
Robert Angus Smith
coined the term “acid rain” in 1872 while describing pollution associated with coal burning in Manchester.

secs.t: Acid rain — definition, FIRST, causes and chemistry — Causes

x: Exam angle: "which gases cause acid rain" and "excess of which causes acid rain" (RPSC: NOx + SO2 only).
Carbon monoxide and methane are not principal causes of acid rain; .
Volcanoes are a natural source of SOx, while lightning is a natural source of NOx.

secs.t: Acid rain — definition, FIRST, causes and chemistry — Chemistry

x: Atmospheric SO2 and NOx undergo oxidation and reaction with water to form sulphuric acid (H2SO4) and nitric acid (HNO3).
Sulphuric acid accounts for approximately two-thirds of acid-rain acidity, while nitric acid accounts for about one-third.
It is wet deposition that occurs in humid regions; dry deposition is acidic gases and particles settling on surfaces in dry areas.

secs.t: Acid rain — effects, Taj Mahal case and regions affected

x: The yellowing and loss of lustre of marble caused by pollution is popularly called “
marble cancer
.” Acid rain accelerates the decay of limestone and marble structures.
Sulphur dioxide is the principal pollutant identified in relation to the Taj Mahal, with industrial sources around Agra, notably the Mathura refinery.
Acid deposition leaches calcium and magnesium from soil and releases toxic aluminium, damaging roots.
Acid deposition corrodes limestone and marble, metals and paint, thereby damaging buildings and monuments.

secs.t: Acid rain — control, monitoring and conventions → year

x: Low-sulphur or cleaner fuels reduce emissions, and the International Maritime Organization imposes sulphur limits on ship fuel.
The
India Meteorological Department
monitors precipitation chemistry under the WMO Global Atmosphere Watch and BAPMoN.
The sequence is LRTAP Convention (1979), Helsinki Sulphur Protocol (1985), Sofia NOx Protocol (1988), and Gothenburg Protocol (1999).
The Helsinki Protocol sought a 30% sulphur-emission cut; the Sofia Protocol froze NOx emissions; Gothenburg imposed pollutant caps; and LRTAP was the first binding treaty.

secs.t: Air quality standards — NAAQS and WHO AQG 2021 data

x: India’s NAAQS cover 12 pollutants, including PM10, PM2.5, SO2, NO2, CO, O3, NH3, lead, benzene, benzo(a)pyrene, arsenic and nickel.
Benzene
is included in the 12-pollutant NAAQS set, but not among the eight pollutants used in the NAQI list stated here.
The specified SO2 limits are 80 µg/m³ for 24 hours, 50 µg/m³ annually in urban areas and 20 µg/m³ annually in ecologically sensitive areas.
NCR winter PM2.5 is reported at nearly
35 times
the WHO limit.

secs.t: Index and monitoring networks → launch and features — NAQI, NAMP, CAAQMS, SAFAR

x: The NAQI covers eight pollutants—PM10, PM2.5, NO2, SO2, CO, O3, NH3 and Pb—on a 0–500 scale.
The correct matches are 51–100—Satisfactory, 201–300—Poor, 301–400—Very poor and 401–500—Severe.
The
Severe
category, covering AQI values 401–500, is represented by maroon.
NAMP regularly monitors
SO2, NO2, PM10 and PM2.5
SAFAR is an MoES (IITM Pune) system with the SAFAR-AIR app.
NAMP now has
1,646 stations in 603 cities
(March 2026).

secs.t: Programmes → targets — NCAP, PRANA, Swachh Vayu Survekshan — NCAP launch and targets

x: Exam angle: NCAP is the answer for "government initiative to control industrial emissions".
The original NCAP target was a
20–30 per cent
reduction in PM10 and PM2.5 by 2024, using 2017 as the base year.
PRANA means
Portal for Regulation of Air-pollution in Non-Attainment cities
and is used to track NCAP progress.

secs.t: Programmes → targets — NCAP, PRANA, Swachh Vayu Survekshan — Progress data

x: SVS ranks the 130 NCAP cities annually since 2022-23, and Indore won among million-plus cities.
Varanasi
recorded the highest percentage reduction in PM10 during the period 2017–18 to 2023–24.
The NGT observed that 86 per cent of spending had gone to road dust and directed that funding be tied to measured PM reductions, while asking southern States to execute their plans.

secs.t: Control devices and fuels → what they remove — vehicles and industry — Vehicular control

x: Silver iodide is a cloud-seeding agent, not a catalytic-converter metal.
Cycling, walking, public transport, green belts, Miyawaki micro-forests and dust-free roads help control air pollution.
Fuel injection promotes more
complete combustion
, thereby reducing the formation of pollutants associated with incomplete combustion.
BS-III started from 1 April 2005 in NCR and 10 other cities.

secs.t: Control devices and fuels → what they remove — vehicles and industry — Cleaner fuels and programmes

x: The Methanol Economy concerns methanol fuel or blending; SATAT concerns compressed biogas; the National Green Hydrogen Mission concerns hydrogen; and the Ethanol Blending Programme requires support for E20 in new vehicles.
Bag filters use fabric filtration; cyclone separators use centrifugal force for coarse particles; wet scrubbers remove gases and particles; and FGD can remove up to 95% of SO2 from flue gas.

secs.t: Stubble burning, CAQM Act and GRAP — emergency measures

x: Cloud seeding may use silver iodide, potassium iodide, dry ice and common salt.
Paddy and wheat stubble is mainly burnt during
October–November in Punjab, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh
Stage I corresponds to poor AQI (201–300), Stage II to very poor (301–400), Stage III to severe (401–450), and Stage IV to severe-plus, above 450.
VAYU, or Wind Augmentation PurifYing Unit, is a roadside purifier developed by CSIR-NEERI.

secs.t: AP air quality action — APPCB network, Visakhapatnam, thermal clusters

x: Visakhapatnam emerged as Andhra Pradesh’s pollution hotspot; its PM2.5 increased by 33 per cent from January 2024 to April 2026 and exceeded national limits.
The burning of tyres, plastic and flex can release dioxins, furans, sulphur dioxide and heavy metals.
The school Eco-Clubs operate under the AP National Green Corps and have existed since 2002–03.
APPCB has 12 CAAQM stations (9 more coming), 19 AQI LED boards and 25 real-time noise stations.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: In January 2026, the Supreme Court, under Chief Justice Surya Kant, told CAQM that
the causes of air pollution were still unclear
The critique states that NCAP covers only about 4% of chronically polluted towns and that PM10, rather than PM2.5, may be an inappropriate yardstick.
The WHO annual PM2.5 guideline is 5 µg/m³, compared with India's NAAQS value of 40 µg/m³; thus, the WHO limit is eight times stricter.

rows.title: Bharat Stage emission norms - evolution from BS-I to BS-VI and their implications
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I F-86

secs.t: Bharat Stage norms → year — FIRSTs, Euro equivalence and notifying authority

x: Exam angle: "since when Euro norms under the BS name" = 2000; BS-I also called "India 2000".
First norms were 1991 (petrol) and 1992 (diesel), and Euro-based Bharat Stage norms began in 2000 (APPSC-GS 2019 key).
The norms are notified under the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 by the
Ministry of Road Transport and Highways
, on the advice of CPCB and MoEFCC.

secs.t: BS-V skipped — Supreme Court deadline and why

x: The leapfrog was intended to address urgent urban air pollution, particularly in the Delhi-NCR region, and to close the technology gap with Europe without two successive changeovers.
The Supreme Court ordered that no BS-IV vehicle could be sold or registered from 1 April 2020.
Registering authorities cannot register non-compliant vehicles after a norm takes effect.

secs.t: Vehicular pollutants → health effect; what Euro norms limit

x: CO binds haemoglobin (carboxyhaemoglobin); PM2.5 penetrates deep lungs/bloodstream; benzene is a carcinogen (leukaemia); NOx causes respiratory illness and forms ground-level ozone and acid rain.
Lead damages the nervous system, is particularly harmful to children’s brain development, and leaded petrol was phased out in India by 2000.
The covered list includes carbon monoxide, hydrocarbons and lead; therefore all three are correct.

secs.t: Data — fuel sulphur and emission limits per stage

x: The limits descend as BS-II—500 ppm, BS-III—350 ppm, BS-IV—50 ppm and BS-VI—10 ppm.
Euro II ultra-low sulphur diesel contains 0.05% sulphur or less, which is equivalent to 500 ppm.
BS-VI is expected to reduce NOx emissions by about 25% in petrol cars and 70% in diesel cars.

secs.t: Emission control technologies → function

x: SCR uses AdBlue (urea) to turn NOx into N2 + water; DPF traps soot and burns it off periodically; OBD-II monitors emissions continuously and alerts the driver.
RDE testing measures emissions on-road under real driving conditions and became applicable under BS-VI Phase 2 from April 2023.
During the BS-I era, catalytic converters converted CO to CO2.

secs.t: Implications and allied measures — CAFE III, E20, scrappage, PUC

x: The introduction of advanced emission-control technologies increased vehicle prices, while improved public health produced offsetting social savings.
The CAFE III third draft (16 July 2026) sets fuel-efficiency norms for cars from April 2027, gives credits for ethanol, CBG and biofuels, and uses a flatter weight curve.
The policy provides for fitness-based de-registration through
Automated Testing Stations and Registered Vehicle Scrapping Facilities

secs.t: Universal angles

x: BS-VII, planned for 2026–27, is expected to be equivalent to Euro 7.
Fuel sulphur declined from 500 ppm under BS-II to 10 ppm under BS-VI, a major reduction over approximately fifteen years.
The first Euro-based norm under the Bharat Stage name was BS-I, introduced in 2000, and BS-V was the only stage skipped.

rows.title: Water pollution - sources, eutrophication, Namami Gange, sewage treatment, groundwater contamination (arsenic, fluoride)
sub: Group-II M2-B-76: Water pollution - sources, eutrophication, effluent standards and groundwater contamination
Group-II M2-B-77: Water pollution control - Namami Gange, river action plans and sewage treatment

secs.t: Water pollution — sources and terms → meaning (DO, BOD, COD, solids)

x: Suspended solids such as silt and clay are retained on a filter, while dissolved solids such as sodium salts pass through it.
NTU is used for turbidity, TDS represents dissolved salts, and coliform count indicates faecal contamination.
BOD is the oxygen bacteria need to decompose organic matter, so high BOD means a heavily polluted water body.

secs.t: Water quality standards — CPCB best-use classes, BIS IS 10500 and WHO

x: The cited Ganga bathing standard for faecal coliform is
The CPCB Class A standard specifies total coliform not exceeding
50 MPN/100 ml
Under BIS IS 10500, fluoride has an acceptable limit of 1.0 mg/L and a permissible limit of 1.5 mg/L.
The BIS iron limit is 0.3 mg/L, whereas no WHO value is specified in the given standards table.

secs.t: Eutrophication — causes, process and stages

x: The progression is oligotrophic, mesotrophic, eutrophic and, where enrichment becomes extreme, hypereutrophic.
Nitrogen and phosphorus enrichment promotes algal blooms; decomposition of the algae consumes dissolved oxygen, causing hypoxia and fish kills.
Fertiliser runoff, sewage, detergents, aquaculture effluent and airborne nitrogen can trigger eutrophication.

secs.t: Groundwater contaminants → regions

x: The reported arsenic belt is in the Ganga-Brahmaputra plains, uranium above 30 ppb has been found in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana among other states, and 56% of districts exceed the nitrate level of 45 mg/L.
Nitrate contamination is mainly attributed to
fertiliser use
, and 56% of districts reportedly exceed 45 mg/L.
The Nalgonda technique uses
alum, lime and bleaching powder
for fluoride removal.

secs.t: Pollution-linked diseases → pollutant

x: Methyl mercury biomagnified in fish and caused neurological damage in Minamata disease.
Arsenicosis or blackfoot disease is associated with skin lesions and skin and lung cancer.
Excess nitrate in drinking water can cause
methaemoglobinaemia
, commonly called blue baby syndrome, in infants.
Itai-itai disease was caused by
cadmium from mining wastewater used for irrigation
, causing bone and joint pain (APPSC 2024).

secs.t: Sewage and effluent treatment — data, technologies, HAM, reuse, CETP — Treatment gap data

x: An SBR carries out treatment in batches within one tank, integrating the sequential stages of the treatment process.
The reported gap consists of piped sewerage access for only 33% of urban households, plant utilisation at 64% capacity and treatment of about 28% of urban sewage.
Raising the limit from 10 mg/L to 30 mg/L permits a higher BOD concentration in discharged effluent, which attracted criticism.

secs.t: Sewage and effluent treatment — data, technologies, HAM, reuse, CETP — Reuse policy

x: AMRUT 2.0 mandates 20 per cent reuse of treated urban wastewater.
A CETP is a shared treatment facility established for
clusters of small-scale industries
AP runs 9 CETPs and has directed industries to adopt ZLD (and banned non-biodegradable effluent discharge).

secs.t: River conservation programmes → year and scope — GAP, NRCP, YAP, NLCP

x: NRCP was launched in 1995 to improve the water quality of
rivers other than the Ganga and its tributaries
through a Centre-State cost-sharing Centrally Sponsored Scheme.
NRCP funds
interception and diversion of sewage, sewage treatment plants and low-cost sanitation
measures to reduce pollution loads in rivers.
GAP-I began in 1985 for 25 main-stem Ganga towns; GAP-II began in 1993 for 60 towns on specified tributaries and rivers; NRCP began in 1995 for rivers other than the Ganga.

secs.t: Ganga governance bodies → year — Central Ganga Authority to National Ganga Council

x: The sequence is 1985 Central Ganga Authority and GAP-I, 2009 NGRBA, 2011 NMCG, and 2016 National Ganga Council.
The legal base is the
River Ganga (Rejuvenation, Protection and Management) Authorities Order, 2016
, notified on 7 October 2016.
The five tiers are National Ganga Council, Empowered Task Force, NMCG, State Ganga Committees and District Ganga Committees.

secs.t: Namami Gange Mission — goals, pillars, results and GRCA — Mission basics

x: Namami Gange-II was approved in 2022 with ₹22,500 crore for
, up to 31 March 2026.

Sewerage, river-surface cleaning, afforestation, biodiversity, riverfront development, industrial effluent monitoring, Ganga Gram and public awareness are associated with the mission; uranium mining is not.
High faecal coliform is identified as the main Ganga problem, and there is a capacity mismatch between overloaded Haridwar STPs and under-used Devprayag facilities.

secs.t: Namami Gange Mission — goals, pillars, results and GRCA — Arth Ganga and people's participation — terms

x: GRCA was launched at COP28, Dubai (not New Delhi) and is led by NMCG (Jal Shakti).
Arth Ganga promotes a river-linked economy through natural farming, river tourism such as dolphin safaris, treated-water reuse and support for artisans.
JALAJ livelihood centres are associated with
NMCG and the Wildlife Institute of India
under the Arth Ganga approach.

secs.t: Reports and index — polluted river stretches, CWMI

x: India was ranked
120th among 122 countries
in the water quality index cited in the NITI Aayog CWMI 2018.
Priority-I stretches have BOD above
30 mg/L
. 3 mg/L is the BOD criterion for bathing (Class B) water, 10 mg/L was the earlier STP discharge limit (since relaxed to 30), and 6 mg/L is not a Priority-I threshold.

secs.t: AP water bodies under pollution stress — Kolleru and Godavari

x: Kolleru’s severe eutrophication is linked to conversion of the lake bed into aquaculture ponds and the inflow of farm runoff.
All three are identified sources or locations associated with pollution stress in Andhra Pradesh water bodies.
Andhra Paper Ltd. and the Nalla Channel
were identified as the main polluters.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The
Central Ground Water Board
's 2025 report flagged widespread groundwater contamination in Andhra Pradesh: uranium above 30 ppb, residual sodium carbonate above limit in 26.87% of samples, and nitrate, iron and fluoride alerts.
The main AP water polluters identified are Pharma City (Vizag), tanneries, paper mills and aquaculture.
All three are identified criticisms: capacity mismatch, top-down execution and inadequate attention to river-basin planning.

rows.title: Soil, noise, thermal, marine and radioactive pollution - sources, effects and control
sub: Group-II M2-B-78: Soil, noise, thermal, marine and radioactive pollution - sources, effects and control

secs.t: Soil pollution — definition, causes and heavy metals → source

x: Floods, acid rain and mineral deposition are natural causes, while industrial waste, farm runoff, urban waste, mining, e-waste and coal ash are human causes of soil pollution.

Mercury is associated with chlor-alkali effluent and fungicides; cadmium with mining effluent, phosphate fertilisers and batteries; copper, zinc and lead with smelting and industrial waste; and chromates with tanneries and industrial waste.

secs.t: Soil rules, control and bioremediation technologies

x: The Rules operate under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, test sites against 189 hazardous chemicals and apply the Polluter Pays principle.
Biofertilisers, integrated pest management, afforestation, scientific waste disposal, biomining and reduced chemical inputs are control measures.
Fly ash must be used in bricks, cement and roads within
300 km
of thermal plants.
Oil Zapper is a consortium of bacteria from TERI that consumes oily sludge and crude oil from oil spills.

secs.t: Noise pollution — unit, thresholds and data

x: dB(A) is an A-weighted decibel scale that approximates the sensitivity of human hearing at different frequencies.
A 10 dB rise roughly doubles loudness, exposure above 85 dB may cause permanent hearing loss, and around 80 dB is regarded as hazardous noise.
Prolonged noise exposure may constrict blood vessels, cause digestive spasms and impair night vision.

secs.t: Noise Rules 2000 → zone limits; monitoring and control

x: Exam angle: unit (decibel), the residential night limit, and which effects are linked to noise.
The prescribed daytime limits are 75 dB(A) for industrial areas, 65 for commercial areas, 55 for residential areas and 50 for silence zones.
The CPCB Real Time National Ambient Noise Monitoring Network has 70 stations in seven metros: Mumbai, Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai, Bengaluru, Lucknow and Hyderabad.
Both statements are true, and the stress response involving increased cortisol helps explain the effects of prolonged noise exposure on blood pressure and sleep.

secs.t: Thermal and marine pollution — sources, effects and terms → meaning

x: Sudden temperature changes can
stress or kill aquatic life
, while warmer water also holds less dissolved oxygen.
Cooling towers, cooling ponds, recirculating cooling water and regulated discharge temperatures help control thermal pollution.
The Gulf of Mexico is an example of a marine area affected by a hypoxic dead zone caused by nutrient runoff and eutrophication.

secs.t: Marine conventions, organisations and FIRSTs — MARPOL, GloLitter, SACEP

x: Samudra Pratap is
India’s first indigenously built Pollution Control Vessel
, built by Goa Shipyard Limited.
GloLitter Partnerships is a joint initiative of the International Maritime Organization and the Food and Agriculture Organization.
SACEP was established in 1982, has its secretariat in Colombo and comprises eight members including India.
Ballast water can carry invasive species, and the IMO Ballast Water Management Convention addresses this problem.

secs.t: Radioactive pollution — sources, radon, effects and units

x: Natural sources include cosmic rays and radon-222; building materials may contain thorium and radon from granite; medical sources include X-rays and isotopes; nuclear sources include reactor waste and accidents.
Becquerel and curie measure activity, gray and rad measure absorbed dose, and sievert and rem measure biological dose.
Radon
(Rn-222) is the radioactive noble gas used to treat cancer (APPSC-G1 2018); it is also a leading cause of lung cancer after smoking.

secs.t: Radiation safety bodies and places; dark sky FIRSTs

x: MRDS are given for metros and State capitals to detect unclaimed ('orphan') radioactive material (APPSC 2021, asked twice); the 2010 Mayapuri cobalt-60 incident is the precedent.
Hanle in Ladakh became India's first Dark Sky Reserve in 2022 within Changthang Wildlife Sanctuary, while Pench Tiger Reserve became India's first Dark Sky Park in 2024.
Dark sky reserves require very little artificial light, clear and dry skies, a protected core with a buffer and community light-management rules.

secs.t: Pollution type → major source and constitutional link — quick revision

x: Article 21 concerns life and personal liberty; Article 48A concerns environmental protection; Article 51A(g) is the environmental fundamental duty; SDG 6 concerns clean water and sanitation.
Marine pollution has several major sources, including land runoff, plastics, oil and sewage; it is not exclusively caused by radioactive hospital waste.
Per the APPSC-G2 2025 key: air → industrial emissions, water → sewage discharge, soil → chemical fertilisers and pesticides, noise → construction.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Andhra Pradesh Pollution Control Board operates 25 Real Time Noise Monitoring Stations, runs 9 Common Effluent Treatment Plants and promotes Zero Liquid Discharge.
Andhra Pradesh is identified as a frontrunner on SDG 14, which concerns marine conservation.
Both the assertion and the reason are true.
APPCB was set up in 1976 under the Water Act, 1974.

rows.title: Solid waste, plastic waste, e-waste, biomedical and construction waste - rules and management
sub: Group-II M2-B-67: Solid wastes - definition and classification: municipal, industrial, hazardous, biomedical, e-waste, agricultural
Group-II M2-B-68: Methods of disposal and management of solid waste in India - collection, segregation, landfill, composting, incineration
Group-II M2-B-69: Solid Waste Management Rules and the Swachh Bharat Mission (urban and rural)
Group-II M2-B-70: Plastic waste management - rules, single-use plastic ban and extended producer responsibility
Group-II M2-B-71: E-waste management - magnitude, rules and recycling; biomedical waste rules
Group-II M2-B-72: Construction and demolition waste; hazardous waste rules and management

secs.t: Waste — definitions, categories and biodegradable vs non-biodegradable — Definitions

x: Construction and demolition waste is generally inert and includes
concrete, dirt, rocks and debris
E-waste consists of discarded electrical and electronic equipment and parts that are not intended for reuse.
Blood, sharps, cultures and discarded or expired medicines are all examples of biomedical waste; anatomical and chemical waste are also included.
Approximately
of healthcare waste is general non-hazardous waste, while about 15% is hazardous, including infectious, chemical and radioactive waste.

secs.t: Waste — definitions, categories and biodegradable vs non-biodegradable — Biodegradable vs non-biodegradable

x: Exam angle: "which is NOT biodegradable" - tin/metal/glass/plastic; "which IS biodegradable" - wool, peels.
Tin scrap
is a metal and cannot normally be decomposed by microorganisms.
Microorganisms decompose biodegradable matter into simpler substances; oxygen-supported decomposition produces compost, while anaerobic decomposition produces methane or biogas.
Non-biodegradable waste is generally inorganic, is not broken down by microorganisms and accumulates in the environment.

secs.t: Waste management — FIRSTs, highest and records

x: India ranks third among dry municipal solid-waste generators of
textile waste
, producing approximately 7.8 million tonnes annually.
EPR first entered Indian waste law through the
E-waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 2011
New Zealand
banned thin plastic produce bags in supermarkets from July 2023 (APPSC-GS 2022 key).
Delhi’s Burari plant is recognised as
India’s first construction and demolition waste recycling plant

secs.t: Terms → meaning: waste hierarchy, 3R/5R and circular economy

x: Biomining of legacy waste supports the circular economy by recovering materials from old waste accumulations for reuse or further processing.
Expanded 5R versions may add
Refuse and Repurpose
or, in some versions, Recover.
Biomining
is used to clear legacy waste dumps by excavating, segregating and processing the accumulated waste.
Biomining involves excavation and separation of legacy waste into recyclables, RDF, bio-soil and inert fill.

secs.t: Disposal methods → process → waste type

x: Exam angle: APPSC-G2 2023 match - organic-II (composting), e-waste-IV (recycling), hazardous-I (incineration), glass-III (landfilling).
Composting
is an aerobic treatment method for biodegradable organic waste and produces manure.
Sanitary landfills use compacted cells, daily cover, liners and leachate collection, and rely on containment.
Howard systematised the Indore and Bangalore methods, while
Acharya and Subrahmanyam
developed them.

E-waste is sent for recycling, broken glass pieces are landfilled, biomedical waste is incinerated at a common biomedical waste treatment facility, and high-calorific dry waste is used as RDF or co-processed in cement kilns.
RDF is made by shredding and dehydrating high-calorific MSW, mainly non-recyclable plastic, paper and textiles, after recyclables and biodegradable material are removed.

secs.t: Source segregation — stream → items, and the collection chain

x: Wet waste includes food scraps, peels and garden waste; dry waste includes paper, plastics, metals, glass and wood; sanitary waste includes diapers and napkins; special-care waste includes batteries, chemicals and paint cans.
The chain begins with door-to-door collection, followed by segregated transport, transfer station, MRF, processing or recycling, and final residual landfill.

secs.t: Plastics → resin code, product and hazard; microplastics

x: An FSSAI study found microplastics in all tested sugar and salt samples; the PWM Rules ban microbeads in cosmetics; and microplastics in the Sundarbans drive plastic-degrading enzymes in microbes carrying AMR genes.
Microplastics are particles
up to 5 mm
(APPSC-GS 2023). 'Up to 5 micrometres only' is far too narrow, while 5-50 cm and above 5 mm describe larger debris.

secs.t: Hazardous constituents → harm: e-waste, PFAS and mercury lamps

x: Old computers can release beryllium, cadmium, chromium, mercury and lead, besides PCBs and PBBs.
Lead affects the nervous system and kidneys; mercury damages the brain and kidneys and bioaccumulates in fish; cadmium damages kidneys and bones; PBBs are persistent and have endocrine effects.
Improper disposal releases toxic substances into soil and water, thereby damaging ecosystems and biodiversity.

secs.t: Biomedical waste — colour code → waste → treatment

x: Sharps go to White (translucent), glassware and metallic implants to Blue, contaminated recyclable plastics to Red, and anatomical waste/expired medicines to Yellow, so
a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i
BMW is treated before disposal mainly to prevent infection spread and protect human health (APPSC-GS 2025) - killing pathogens, stopping syringe reuse and cutting volume and toxicity.

secs.t: Industrial solid wastes → source industry → reuse

x: Fly ash comes from coal-based thermal power plants, steel slag from steel plants, red mud from alumina refining, and phosphogypsum from phosphoric acid or phosphatic fertiliser plants.
The notification requires utilisation of fly ash for specified construction purposes within
300 km
of thermal plants, helping prevent dumping on soil.
Fly ash can be used to make building bricks and can partly replace Portland cement in concrete.

secs.t: Solid waste rules → year → provisions (MSW 2000, SWM 2016, SWM 2026)

x: The 2016 Rules cover all four categories, including urban agglomerations, census towns, industrial townships, transport facilities, SEZs and religious or historical places.
The 2016 Rules provided for user fees, spot fines, extended producer responsibility for producers and brand owners, and prohibited the disposal of untreated waste in landfills.
The four streams are
wet, dry, sanitary and special care
waste, the last category covering domestic hazardous waste.
The 2026 Rules require mapping of legacy dumpsites, time-bound biomining and submission of quarterly reports.
Bulk Waste Generators must process wet waste on site or obtain an EBWGR certificate as prescribed under the 2026 Rules.

secs.t: Plastic Waste Management Rules → year → provision; SUP ban 2022 — Timeline

x: Exam angle: APPSC-GS 2021 - 2021 Rules aimed at phasing out SUP by
; EPR guidelines effective
July 2022
The stated progression is
40 microns in 2011, 50 microns in 2016, 75 microns from 30 September 2021 and 120 microns from 31 December 2022

The PWM Rules, 2016 promoted plastic roads and energy recovery, and the PWM (Amendment) Rules, 2026 allow waste-to-oil as an end-of-life route and treat plastic waste as an advanced-biofuel feedstock.

secs.t: Plastic Waste Management Rules → year → provision; SUP ban 2022 — PWM (Amendment) Rules 2026

x: The 2026 amendment includes all four measures: classification into three categories, three-year carry-forward, tradable certificates and specified end-of-life options.
Compostable plastics must meet the
IS/ISO 17088
standard.

secs.t: Plastic Waste Management Rules → year → provision; SUP ban 2022 — Single-use plastic ban — 1 July 2022

x: HDPE milk bottles
are not included in that list.
Plastic-stemmed earbuds, straws, stirrers and PVC banners below 100 microns are among the identified banned items.
Enforcement involves State Pollution Control Boards or Pollution Control Committees and local bodies, along with a National Level Taskforce and State Special Task Forces.
The ban covers only about
of total plastic waste.

secs.t: Extended Producer Responsibility — plastic packaging and e-waste

x: EPR applies to Producers, Importers and Brand Owners, or PIBOs, for plastic packaging not covered by the SUP ban.
Rigid plastics have a 30% to 60% progression, flexible single-layer plastics 10% to 20%, and multi-layered plastics 5% to 10%.
On the centralised CPCB EPR portal,
recyclers generate EPR certificates and sell them to producers

secs.t: E-waste and battery rules → year → provisions

x: Notified Nov 2022, in force 1 April 2023.
The Rules permit
only registered producers, manufacturers, refurbishers and recyclers
to deal in e-waste.
The Rules prescribe RoHS limits for lead, mercury and cadmium.
The Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022 replaced the 2001 rules and cover electric-vehicle, portable, automotive and industrial batteries under EPR.

secs.t: Hazardous waste Acts and Rules; Bhopal gas tragedy

x: PIC means
Prior Informed Consent
, a control associated with the import and export of hazardous waste.
The Act provides no-fault insurance cover intended to give immediate relief to victims of accidents involving hazardous substances.
337 tonnes were incinerated, about 900 tonnes of toxic residual ash remained, and the Supreme Court directed the victims’ NGO to approach the Madhya Pradesh High Court.

secs.t: Biomedical waste and C&D waste rules → year → provisions

x: The BMW Management Rules, 2016 cover 100% of healthcare facilities, use four colour categories and provide for barcoding and GPS tracking.
The 2016 Rules cover waste arising from building, renovation, excavation, road, flyover, bridge and pipeline activities.
The 2016 framework covers collection, transport, storage and re-processing, permits charges on bulk generators and treats C&D waste as a resource.

secs.t: International conventions and the Global Plastics Treaty

x: The INC venues were Punta del Este, Paris, Nairobi, Ottawa, Busan and Geneva in that order.
Transboundary hazardous-waste movement involves the physical transfer of hazardous waste for reprocessing or storage, frequently to developing countries.
The
Hazardous Substances Management Division
(HSMD) of MoEFCC is the nodal body for hazardous substances management.

Basel (1989) covers transboundary movement of hazardous wastes, Rotterdam is the PIC convention for hazardous chemicals and pesticides, Stockholm (2001) covers POPs and Minamata (2013) covers mercury.

secs.t: Sanitation programmes → year → focus; Swachh Bharat Mission

x: Integrated Low Cost Sanitation dates to 1980–81, the Central Rural Sanitation Programme to 1986, the Total Sanitation Campaign to 1999 and Nirmal Gram Puraskar to 2003.
The Integrated Low Cost Sanitation programme focused on converting dry latrines into pour-flush latrines and freeing manual scavengers.
GOBARdhan promotes conversion of cattle dung, agricultural waste and solid waste into
biogas and bio-slurry
, supported by a unified portal.

secs.t: SBM-Grameen — ministry, Phase I, ODF Plus

x: ODF Plus combines sustained ODF status with management of greywater, faecal sludge and plastic waste, along with options such as biogas and composting.
The IHHL incentive under SBM-G is
. ₹6,000, ₹10,000 and ₹15,000 are not the stated amount; separately, greywater support is ₹280/capita (villages up to 5,000) and ₹660/capita (above 5,000).

secs.t: SBM-Urban 2.0 and waste-to-energy — targets and certifications

x: The cited figures are 21 operational WtE plants producing more than 170 MW and 133 biogas facilities.
The SATAT and GOBARdhan linkage targets 500 new waste-to-wealth compressed biogas plants.
SBM-Urban 2.0 includes source segregation, legacy-dump remediation and C&D waste management, but does not prescribe
privatisation of all municipal water supply systems
The Garbage Free City certification uses 1-star, 3-star, 5-star and 7-star ratings for waste management.

secs.t: Swachh Survekshan — index, organisers and cleanest cities

x: Swachh Survekshan is the world's largest annual urban cleanliness survey, conducted by the
Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs under SBM-Urban
Indore topped the 10 lakh-plus Super Swachh League for the
eighth time
in Swachh Survekshan 2024-25.
Indore
is identified as India’s model zero-waste or landfill-free city and has repeatedly ranked first in cleanliness assessments.

secs.t: Data — municipal solid waste and e-waste

x: The waste sector accounted for
of India's emissions in 2020 according to the Fourth Biennial Update Report.
The Global E-waste Monitor is published by the International Telecommunication Union and the United Nations Institute for Training and Research.
The Global E-waste Monitor uses
six
categories, including cooling equipment, screens, lamps, large equipment, small equipment and IT equipment.
MeitY put e-waste collected and processed in FY 2021 at about
3.54 lakh tonnes
(APPSC-GS 2021 key).

secs.t: E-waste recycling chain — dismantlers, recyclers, informal hubs, R2

x: The authorised chain begins with the consumer and collection or producer take-back, followed by dismantling, recycling and recovery of materials.
Citizens should use authorised recyclers or collection centres and wipe personal data before handing over old electronics.
Separate handling is required; Seelampur and Moradabad are informal hubs; and CPCB data mention 468 authorised recyclers with 1.6 million tonnes of capacity.

secs.t: Andhra Pradesh — agencies, policy, CLAP, places and rankings — Agencies, partnerships and policy

x: Operation Clean Sweep is the Municipal Administration Department’s campaign for
scientific solid-waste management in Tier-1 and Tier-2 corporations
The Re Sustainability MoU covers all 123 ULBs for scientific e-waste collection, disposal and material recovery facilities.
The stated urban set-up consists of
17 Municipal Corporations, 113 municipalities and 7 cantonment boards

secs.t: Andhra Pradesh — agencies, policy, CLAP, places and rankings — Clean Andhra Pradesh (CLAP)

x: Legacy waste can emit methane and pollute groundwater.
Ongole is biomining the Guthikondavaripalem yard (1.76 lakh t of 2.56 lakh t processed) and supplying RDF to cement plants.
The two CHWTSDFs identified for Andhra Pradesh are located in
Anakapalli and SPSR Nellore
CLAP was launched on 2 October 2021 under the name
Jagananna Swachha Sankalpam

secs.t: Andhra Pradesh — agencies, policy, CLAP, places and rankings — Urban profile and sanitation rankings

x: In SS 2022, Visakhapatnam was 'Top Impact Creator' (million-plus) and Tirupati came first in 'Safai Mitra Surakshit Shehar' (APPSC-G1 2022 key).

secs.t: Andhra Pradesh — data on collection, processing, biomedical waste and plastic curbs

x: The APPCB permitted 12 cement industries to co-process incinerable, plastic and municipal waste.
Biomedical waste is sent to Common Bio-Medical Waste Treatment Facilities for
incineration
The cited figures are 49.32% of wards with 100% source segregation and MRFs in 101 ULBs.
Andhra Pradesh bans single-use plastic and carry bags below
120 microns
, with enforcement involving the Revenue Department, Police and Pollution Control Board.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The 2026 campaign of Swachh Bharat Mission-Grameen was titled “
Swabhav Swachhata - Sanskaar Swachhata
Rural waste is shifting from predominantly biodegradable waste towards plastic, sanitary and other non-biodegradable waste.
More than 70% of recycled plastic is handled by informal workers, NAMASTE seeks to formalise them, and approximately 15 lakh waste-pickers remain outside formal systems.
Vapes, USB cables and LED accessories
are examples of ‘invisible e-waste’ that may be thrown into regular waste streams.
The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 serves as an umbrella for frameworks including the EIA, Hazardous Waste, Coastal Regulation Zone and Contaminated Sites Rules.
The Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026 have raised
questions concerning federalism and administrative design

rows.title: Carbon emissions, carbon footprint, carbon sequestration, carbon credits and carbon trading

secs.t: Carbon terms → meaning: footprints, scopes, sinks

x: The carbon footprint measures total greenhouse-gas emissions from human activities in tonnes of CO2 equivalent per year.
Direct emissions from owned sources are Scope 1, emissions from purchased electricity or heat are Scope 2, and the remaining value-chain emissions are Scope 3.
Blue carbon is stored in coastal ecosystems such as mangroves, seagrass beds and salt marshes.
Tropical peatlands
store more carbon per hectare than any other terrestrial ecosystem.

secs.t: Carbon capture, sequestration and removal → meaning and applications

x: CCS captures CO2 at stationary sources such as power plants and stores it in geological or ocean formations.
CCUS involves using captured CO2 or storing it permanently and can support coal gasification and hydrogen.
Capturing and storing CO2 from industrial processes is
carbon sequestration
(APPSC-GS 2024 key; carbon capture was also accepted).

secs.t: Carbon FIRSTs — panchayat, UT, market, tax

x: The railway siding is the world’s first
modal-shift project
registered with Verra’s Verified Carbon Standard.
New Zealand was the first country to propose a tax on agricultural emissions, while Denmark is to become the first to actually levy a livestock carbon tax from 2030.
Ladakh’s carbon-neutral effort includes solar water lifting, passive solar buildings, geothermal heating and electric vehicles.

secs.t: Carbon sinks and monitoring — programmes, pools, satellites

x: The National Carbon Project is implemented under the
ISRO Geosphere-Biosphere Programme
The project assesses carbon pools, fluxes and the net carbon balance of terrestrial biomes, with sub-projects on vegetation carbon, soil carbon and related fluxes.
The five pools are above-ground biomass, below-ground biomass, dead wood, litter and soil organic carbon.
NASA's OCO-2 and Japan's GOSAT
are CO2-observing satellites.

secs.t: Carbon markets — Kyoto, standards, CCTS 2023, Net Zero Portal

x: The programme follows the DST roadmap and concerns industrial carbon credits; it is not a farmer-only scheme.
India could earn 20–40 billion dollars from voluntary credits by 2030, and 242 agri-food projects are registered.
The CCTS was notified in June 2023 under Sec. 14AA of the Energy Conservation Act, 2001, and is administered by the BEE (Ministry of Power).

secs.t: Carbon pricing — EU and UK CBAM → provisions

x: Transitional phase 2023, definitive phase from 1 Jan 2026.
CBAM can place decarbonisation costs on exporters, while the resulting revenue is retained in Europe.
Article 9 permits deduction of a carbon price already paid, including a price paid under India's Carbon Credit Trading Scheme, from the CBAM liability.
The UK CBAM starts on 1 Jan 2027.

secs.t: Data — emitters, India's targets and carbon pricing

x: The roadmaps rely on renewable energy available round the clock, nuclear power and carbon capture, utilisation and storage.
The biomass co-firing requirement is 5% in FY 2024-25 and 7% from FY 2025-26, with monitoring by the SAMARTH mission.
A carbon bomb is a fossil project that could emit over 1 Gt CO2 in its lifetime.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The criticism of CBAM as potentially placing India in a rule-taker position is framed as a climate-justice issue.
Agricultural credits face
measurement and credibility gaps
, which affect the reliability of claimed reductions or removals.
All three developments are associated with the stated current carbon-market context: UK recognition, the EU CBAM definitive phase and the Net Zero Portal.

rows.title: Recent projects, acts and initiatives to reduce environmental pollution in India
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I F-90

secs.t: Pollution-control alternatives → meaning (terms)

x: Incineration is a conventional waste-treatment method and is not classified as an alternative pollution-control approach in this context.
Electrostatic precipitators, scrubbers and selective catalytic reduction are conventional end-of-pipe tools.
Research on CCS is ongoing for cement plants, and NITI Aayog published a report on a CCUS policy framework in 2022.

secs.t: Acts and rules → year → provision

x: The Fund may support monitoring, remediation of contaminated sites, laboratories and clean-technology R&D. Universal fossil-fuel subsidies are not a stated use.
The Supreme Court upheld PCB power under
Section 33A of the Water Act and Section 31A of the Air Act
The revised categories introduced a new Blue category, illustrated by compressed biogas, and replaced the mandatory 33% green belt requirement with pollution-potential norms.

secs.t: Programmes, schemes and clean-up tools → launch → objective

x: The CPCB made online continuous emission and effluent monitoring compulsory for highly polluting industries in the 17-category classification.
PM Ujjwala Yojana was launched in 2016 to provide free LPG connections to poor households, promoting clean cooking and reducing indoor smoke.
The assessment cites PMUY as a model clean-cooking programme and identifies
clean cooking
and heating as South Asia’s leading solution towards 2035.

secs.t: Eco-labels → organisation → scope (Ecomark, Blue Flag, PRAMAAN)

x: The 2024 Ecomark Rules replaced the 1991 scheme and aim to ensure accurate labelling, prevent misleading green claims and support informed purchases.
PRAMAAN is a voluntary third-party forest and wood certification initiative for sustainable forestry and agroforestry.
Blue Flag is an international beach eco-label of the Foundation for Environmental Education (FEE), Denmark.

secs.t: AP measures → year → feature (green tax, APPCB, BRAP)

x: APPCB issues siting guidelines for industries near habitations, water bodies and fragile areas.
Andhra Pradesh streamlined clearances through
digitisation and single-window systems
under BRAP.
In September 2019 AP decided to impose and collect a green tax from industrial houses (PYQ).

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The debates include concerns that decriminalisation and relaxed green-belt norms could reduce deterrence.
APPCB is associated with siting guidelines, while BRAP is associated with a single-window system.
The emerging approach moves beyond end-of-pipe control towards prevention, including clean fuels, eco-labels and market credits.

rows.title: Environmental hazards and disaster management - DM Act 2005, NDMA and NDRF, Sendai Framework, disaster types and mitigation

secs.t: Disaster terms → meaning and the DM cycle

x: Capacity comprises the strengths and resources available to individuals, communities and institutions to cope with hazards.
Resilience
is the ability to resist, absorb and recover quickly from the effects of a hazard.
Risk rises with hazard and vulnerability and falls as coping capacity rises, so
Risk = Hazard x Vulnerability / Capacity
Embankments, mangroves and zoning are pre-disaster
mitigation
measures.

secs.t: Disaster classification — types, notified disasters, Bhopal

x: Exam angle: "which category" questions - fire, gas leak, epidemic.

All four pairs match the classification: geological = earthquakes, volcanic eruptions; biological = epidemics, pest attacks; emerging = cyber attacks, space weather; man-made/industrial = chemical accidents, nuclear incidents.
Man-made disaster
s arise from human activity, negligence or technological failure (APPSC 2025 key), so a fire from careless gas-cylinder handling is man-made.

secs.t: Disaster types → criteria and mitigation

x: IMD warnings, shelters, evacuation, shelter belts and mangroves are cyclone-related measures.
Coringa and Krishna are associated with mangroves that help mitigate cyclones and storm surges.
Floods are mitigated through embankments and forecasting; landslides through zonation and warnings; and the stated thresholds define heat-wave and cold-wave conditions in plains.
ISRO's Disaster Management Support programme and the National Database for Emergency Management support all hazards, with NDEM functioning as a GIS database.

secs.t: Global frameworks → year → note (IDNDR, Hyogo, Sendai, CDRI)

x: The four priorities include understanding risk, strengthening risk governance, investing in risk reduction, and enhancing preparedness for effective response and Build Back Better.

The Sendai global targets include increasing the availability of and access to multi-hazard early-warning systems, along with reducing mortality, affected people, economic loss and infrastructure damage.
The three post-2015 frameworks are the Sendai Framework, the Sustainable Development Goals for 2015–2030 and the Paris Agreement.

secs.t: Institutions → chair → role (NDMA, MHA, NPDRR, NIDM, APSDMA, SACHET)

x: The disaster management division of the
Ministry of Home Affairs
undertakes overall coordination.
Fire services are a State subject, and the DG Fire Services, Civil Defence and Home Guards under MHA has an advisory role.
APSDMA is chaired by the Chief Minister, serves as the State’s chief nodal agency, runs the State Emergency Operations Centre and supports early warning.

secs.t: Community-based DRR — DM Act roles, PRI project, Aapda Mitra

x: Aapda Mitra is an NDMA scheme for training community volunteers to act as first responders.
Social media can support communication and community engagement, but it is a complementary tool rather than a replacement for official disaster-management systems.
The project has an outlay of Rs 507.37 crore, is run by MoPR with NDMA, and creates 20 Model GPs on 6 hazard themes.

secs.t: HADR operations → country → event

x: Operation Vanilla assisted Madagascar following Cyclone Diane in 2020.
Maitri assisted Nepal, Dost assisted Turkey and Syria, Karuna assisted Myanmar, and Sadbhav assisted Vietnam, Laos and Myanmar.
Operation Brahma assisted Myanmar following the 2025 earthquake.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Andhra Pradesh now has the third-longest coastline in India and the longest on the east coast. 'Second-longest' is the older figure, AP is on the east (not west) coast, and its long coast makes it highly exposed to cyclones and storm surges.
Andhra Pradesh released
Rs 277.63 crore
under SDRF/NDRF in 2025–26, compared with Rs 479.01 crore in 2026–27.

rows.title: Preparedness and response - surveillance, Epidemic Diseases Act, National Health Emergency framework
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I F-91

secs.t: Acts and regulations → year → provisions (1897 Act, DM Act, IHR 2005)

x: The Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897 provides the legal framework for dealing with biological disasters and epidemics and was used during COVID-19.
The draft Bill was intended to replace the 1897 Act and covered epidemics, bio-terrorism and disasters, but it has not been enacted.
All three are obligations under the IHR (2005): building surveillance and response capacities, reporting possible PHEICs to WHO within 24 hours, and naming a National IHR Focal Point.

secs.t: Institutions → role (MoHFW, NCDC, NDMA, DM Cell, labs)

x: NDMA is chaired by the Prime Minister, SDMAs by the Chief Ministers, and NDMA lays down guidelines and coordinates health emergencies under the DM Act, 2005 (e.g. its Biological Disaster Management guidelines of 2008).
INSACOG (Indian SARS-CoV-2 Genomics Consortium), set up in December 2020, is a network of genome-sequencing labs under DBT, ICMR, CSIR and MoHFW that tracks SARS-CoV-2 variants.

secs.t: DM cycle for epidemics → phase → measure

x: Pre-outbreak vaccine distribution reduces the potential impact of an epidemic and is therefore a
mitigation
measure.
All four pairs correctly associate epidemic measures with the mitigation, preparedness, response and recovery phases respectively.
The 2016 NDMP was India's first.
Epidemics are treated as
biological disasters
in disaster-management planning.

secs.t: Programmes — IDSP, IHIP, U-WIN, One Health, PM-ABHIM → year → scale

x: Under PM-ABHIM, MoHFW's DM Cell has 15 Health Emergency Operation Centres and 50 BHISHM Cubes, which were deployed during Operation Sindoor.
AP is preparing the plan under the One Health approach with NCDC, US CDC and Jhpiego.
At Vijayawada, 10 Critical Care Blocks and 12 Integrated Public Health Laboratories were opened at a cost of Rs 250 crore.

secs.t: Digital tools → application (geospatial tracing, war rooms, Covid Pharma app)

x: Geospatial technology supports contact tracing, hotspot and containment-zone mapping, and GIS-based real-time vaccine distribution planning.
The GIS-supported COVID war room was set up by the
Bruhat Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike
(BBMP).
The AP Medical and Health Department launched Covid Pharma on 25 April 2020 to track people buying over-the-counter
medicines for cough, cold and fever

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The BRICS New Delhi Declaration set up a sub-working group on an integrated early-warning system for infectious diseases.
The 1897 Act is criticised as colonial and for lacking both a definition of dangerous epidemic disease and adequate rights safeguards.
An
Ebola
advisory was issued to States in May 2026.

rows.title: Biotechnology - nature, scope, tools; applications in agriculture, medicine and industry
sub: Group-II M2-B-86: Bioremediation - meaning, types (in-situ and ex-situ), phytoremediation and bioaugmentation
Group-II M2-B-87: Scope and applications of bioremediation in India

secs.t: Biotechnology — definition, branches and FIRSTs

x: The CBD 1992 definition describes biotechnology as using biological systems to
make or modify products
The first indigenous haemophilia A gene-therapy trial was conducted at CMC Vellore with support from the Department of Biotechnology.
The first genetically engineered oil-eating bacterium was
Pseudomonas putida engineered by Ananda Mohan Chakrabarty
The case Diamond v. Chakrabarty, decided by the US Supreme Court in 1980, is associated with the first patenting of a living organism.

secs.t: Biotech tools and terms → meaning

x: PCR uses DNA polymerase (denaturation, annealing, extension); ligase only joins DNA.

secs.t: Persons → contributions

x: DNA fingerprinting uses variations in repetitive DNA, particularly variable number tandem repeats (VNTRs).
Alec Jeffreys developed DNA fingerprinting in 1984.
Hybridoma technology fuses antibody-producing B-cells with myeloma cells to create continuously multiplying antibody-producing cells.

secs.t: Agricultural biotechnology and animal cloning — organism → role

x: BARC
is associated with tissue-culture applications for banana and pineapple.
Sub1 flood-tolerant rice
is given as an example of marker-assisted selection.
Dolly was the first cloned mammal, a sheep produced at Roslin Institute in 1996; Garima was a buffalo cloned at NDRI in 2009; and Noori was a Pashmina goat cloned in 2012.

secs.t: Medical biotechnology — vaccine → developer → target; advanced therapies

x: Cervavac is developed by the Serum Institute of India against HPV and cervical cancer.
mRNA, viral-vector and protein-subunit platforms are all identified as indigenous vaccine platforms in India.
ZyCoV-D was developed by Zydus Cadila and is identified as the first DNA vaccine, targeting COVID-19.
R21/Matrix-M was developed by Oxford University and made by the Serum Institute of India for malaria.

secs.t: Industrial and environmental biotechnology → applications

x: Biotechnology uses genetically modified microbes and plants for pollution reduction and resource conservation, including oil degradation and plastic breakdown.

Engineered Pseudomonas and algae can target oil spills, PETase-producing bacteria break down plastic, engineered microbes can produce PLA and PHA, and biofilters use microbe-laden beds to treat air or gas streams.

secs.t: Policy, institutions and data — BioE3, DBT, BIRAC, Bio-RIDE, IBDC, AMTZ

x: The BioE3 policy, meaning Biotechnology for Economy, Environment and Employment, was approved by the Union Cabinet in
August 2024
Climate-resilient agriculture
is identified as a key thematic area of the BioE3 policy, whose full form is Biotechnology for Economy, Environment and Employment.
The bioeconomy is stated to have risen from $10 billion in 2014 to
$165.7 billion
in 2024, with a target of $300 billion by 2030.
DBT-BIRAC prioritises
Precision Biotherapeutics
under BioE3, which promotes high-performance biomanufacturing.

secs.t: Bioremediation — definition, agents, objective and what is NOT bioremediation

x: Exam angle: "Which is NOT bioremediation?" - burning contaminated soil; composting and bacterial oil clean-up are.
Bioremediation uses organisms such as bacteria, fungi, algae and plants, or their enzymes, to degrade or remove pollutants and restore a contaminated environment.
Bioremediation can be applied to soil, water and air and may address oil spills, heavy metals, pesticides, solvents and other organic pollutants.
The biological breakdown of organic waste by bacteria is microbial degradation and therefore constitutes
bioremediation

secs.t: In-situ vs ex-situ bioremediation — site, techniques, cost

x: Exam angle: in-situ vs ex-situ; match technique to agent.
Landfarming, composting and biopiles
require contaminated material to be treated outside its original location and are ex-situ techniques.
In-situ bioremediation
treats contamination at its original site and is generally cheaper and more passive than ex-situ treatment.
Ex-situ
bioreactors
can be the fastest option under optimised conditions because they permit rapid kinetics.

secs.t: Bioremediation techniques → how → pollutant

x: Phytoremediation uses plants, mycoremediation uses fungi, rhizoremediation uses root-zone microbes, and bioaugmentation adds microorganisms.
Water hyacinth is a standard example of phytoextraction, taking up heavy metals from water.
Oil spills and oily sludge may be treated through bioaugmentation with oil-degrading bacteria.

Mycoremediation uses fungi, rhizofiltration uses plant roots to remove contaminants from water, biosparging injects air below the water table, and rhizoremediation involves root–microbe interactions in the rhizosphere.
Biostimulation adds nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus, and may also supply oxygen, to enhance the activity of existing microbes in polluted water bodies.
Ideonella sakaiensis degrades PET plastic, Bacillus flexus acts on arsenate and Acinetobacter junii on arsenite.

secs.t: Phytoremediation — sub-types and hyperaccumulator plant → metal

x: Pteris vittata accumulates arsenic; Brassica juncea accumulates lead, cadmium and selenium; Thlaspi caerulescens accumulates zinc and cadmium; and Alyssum species accumulate nickel.

Sunflower accumulates heavy metals and uranium/other radionuclides, water hyacinth takes up heavy metals and toxic materials from water, and Indian mustard (Brassica juncea) accumulates lead, cadmium and selenium.

secs.t: Research bodies → product: Oilzapper, NEERI, Phytorid

x: Oilzapper and Oilivorous-S are bacterial consortia developed by TERI with Indian Oil.

TERI is associated with Oilzapper and Oilivorous-S; CSIR-NEERI undertakes nodal bioremediation R&D; CPCB is associated with oil-contaminated soils; and DBT-BIRAC funds relevant biotechnology start-ups.
Constructed wetlands may be natural or engineered systems where
plants and microbes break down and absorb pollutants
, especially in sewage treatment.

secs.t: Places and programmes — Vizag drain PIL, dumpsite remediation

x: Immediate bioremediation and decentralised STPs were proposed as a lower-cost alternative to pumping schemes.
The Dumpsite Remediation Accelerator is an initiative of the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs under Swachh Bharat Mission-Urban 2.0.
The target of the accelerator is described as “
Lakshya Zero Dumpsites
”, focusing on clearing legacy dumpsites through accelerated bioremediation.

secs.t: Bioremediation — advantages, limitations and debate vs conventional

x: Bioremediation is often slow, and its results vary with the pollutant, organism, site conditions and co-contaminants.
Bioremediation may require regulation and monitoring; introducing microbes does not make oversight unnecessary.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Synthetic biology is a current relevance area, precision biotherapeutics are linked with BioE3, Visakhapatnam was chosen for a marine biomaterials research facility, and AMTZ is associated with Vizag.

The US EPA Superfund bioremediation guidelines (the US programme for cleaning contaminated waste sites) are cited as the model for India's bioremediation push, which includes biomining and bioremediation of legacy dumpsites under SWM Rules 2026 and 'Lakshya Zero Dumpsites'.

rows.title: Eco-friendly technologies in agriculture - integrated pest management, biofertilisers, biopesticides, organic and natural farming
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I F-92

secs.t: Sustainable agriculture — definition, practices and FIRSTs

x: Sustainable agriculture seeks to
produce food while protecting the environment and conserving resources for future generations
Sustainable agriculture may use synthetic inputs judiciously, unlike the stricter approach generally associated with organic farming; .
The evergreen revolution approach is associated with
ZBNF, organic farming, water conservation and integrated pest management
Organic farming's main advantage is
reduced chemical input and improved soil health
(PYQ).

secs.t: Agrochemicals — impacts, restricted pesticides and remedies

x: Indiscriminate agrochemical use can cause secondary pest outbreaks, pesticide resistance, ecosystem contamination and contamination of soil and water.
Broadcasting granular fertiliser may lose
50–70 percent
of the applied nitrogen through ammonia loss or nitrate leaching into aquifers.
Pesticide residues can bioaccumulate in the food chain, leading to increasing concentration across feeding levels.

secs.t: Bio-inputs → composition / source → benefit (manures, biopesticides)

x: Vermicompost
is produced by the digestion of organic waste by earthworms and helps restore soil microbes and organic carbon.
Green manure consists of leguminous crops such as sunn hemp and dhaincha that are ploughed into the soil while green, adding nitrogen and organic matter.
Azadirachtin is derived from
neem
and acts against a wide range of insects, chiefly as an antifeedant.

secs.t: Integrated pest management — definition and components

x: IPM uses all suitable methods to keep pest populations below economic injury levels.
All four statements describe recognised IPM components: resistant varieties, cultural practices, mechanical or physical methods, and need-based chemical control.
Green lacewings act as natural enemies of aphids and therefore represent a biological IPM method.

secs.t: Schemes → launch → key facts (PKVY, MOVCDNER, NMNF, certification)

x: PKVY was launched in 2015–16 as the first comprehensive Centrally Sponsored Scheme for organic farming.
MOVCDNER
promotes organic value chains in the North-Eastern Region, whereas PKVY covers the rest of the country.
NMNF had an outlay of
Rs 2,481 crore
, comprising Rs 1,584 crore from the Centre and Rs 897 crore from the States, up to March 2026.

secs.t: Natural farming and permaculture — persons, inputs, terms

x: ZBNF was developed by
Subhash Palekar
Jeevamrutha is a microbial culture prepared from cow dung and urine.
Organic farming involves certification and approved organic inputs.
Permaculture involves designing ecological habitats and food systems in a site-specific manner.
The term permaculture was coined by
Bill Mollison and David Holmgren in Australia

secs.t: Andhra Pradesh — APCNF, green manure and organic clusters

x: APCNF was formerly ZBNF, uses jeevamrutham and ghanajeevamrutham, and covers over seven lakh farmers.
APCNF received the Gulbenkian Prize for Humanity in 2024.
NTR district was promoted as a natural-farming model with QR-based traceability for organic produce

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The scalability of Zero Budget Natural Farming has been questioned in debates concerning the wider adoption of natural farming.
Andhra Pradesh
has been described as a global pioneer in natural farming, and a Kenyan delegation undertook a study visit there.
Sikkim holds the distinction of being the first fully organic State, whereas PKVY was the first comprehensive Centrally Sponsored Scheme for organic farming.

src: Sources: CDI (Block07 Organic and Sustainable Agriculture; Govt policies - natural farming); APP (Environment Part 2 > Unit 4 Sustainable agriculture, IPM, biopesticides); UPSC (Environment p.259; Economy p.188); IYB 2026 (pp.309, 316); ES 2025-26 Summary p.54, Highlights p.23; APPCA Feb 2026 (AP CA - PKVY, APCNF, NTR district); LENS Aug 2025 p.68, May 2026 p.136, Aug 2026 p.150; LENSD 11 May, 21 May, 29 Aug 2026; TH 8 Mar, 23 May, 3 Jun, 8 Jul 2026

rows.title: Precision agriculture, drip irrigation and other resource-efficient technologies
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I F-92

secs.t: Micro-irrigation terms → meaning: drip vs sprinkler, fertigation

x: Exam angle: "which technology suits water-scarce regions?" - drip irrigation.
Drip systems require relatively higher initial investment, while sprinklers are useful on uneven terrain but are more exposed to wind and evaporation losses.
Drip irrigation
applies water directly to the root zone, reaching about 90% efficiency and cutting evaporation and runoff, so it suits water-scarce areas (APPSC-G2 2025).

secs.t: Resource-conserving technologies → benefit

x: Zero tillage is associated with sowing wheat without burning previous residue, direct planting of paddy without a nursery, and soil carbon sequestration.
Laser land levelling creates a uniform field surface, allowing water to spread evenly and thereby saving irrigation water.
All three are correct (UPSC 2022): SRI uses less seed, alternate wetting and drying cuts methane from flooded paddies, and less pumping saves electricity.

secs.t: Protected cultivation and soilless farming → technique → key point

x: Protected cultivation in greenhouses, polytunnels or shade nets provides a controlled environment and protection from adverse weather, pests and diseases.
Aeroponics
suspends plant roots in air and supplies them with a mist of nutrient solution.
Vertical farming
grows crops in stacked indoor layers under controlled conditions and can provide year-round output even in non-tropical or harsh settings.

secs.t: Precision agriculture tools → application; AI advisories

x: The
Mahalanobis National Crop Forecast Centre
has run the ISRO crop forecasting programme associated with FASAL since 2012 and monitors 29 double-risk districts through satellites.
The KISAN project uses space technology for planning Crop Cutting Experiments under the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana.
GPS, drones, AI and sensors form the technological core of
the Second Green Revolution and sustainable intensification

secs.t: Drones in agriculture — uses, rules, schemes

x: Kisan drones are used for crop assessment, soil health analysis and spraying, and can reduce human exposure to chemicals.
Agricultural drones are regulated by the Directorate General of Civil Aviation under the Drone Rules, 2021.
Drone Shakti supports the drone ecosystem through manufacturing and training for Remote Pilot Certificates.

secs.t: Schemes and missions → year → provisions (PDMC, PMKSY, MIF, DAM, PM-KUSUM) — Per Drop More Crop and PMKSY

x: PDMC was launched in 2015–16, remained part of PMKSY until 2021–22, and has operated under RKVY since 2022–23.
The priority areas are rainfed regions, water-stressed districts and critical groundwater blocks.
The reported area brought under micro-irrigation during 2015-16 to 2025-26 was 102 lakh hectares.
NMSA provides subsidy of up to 55% for micro-irrigation, subject to a ceiling of 5 hectares.

secs.t: Schemes and missions → year → provisions (PDMC, PMKSY, MIF, DAM, PM-KUSUM) — Digital Agriculture Mission

x: AgriStack is described as an Aadhaar-like digital public good developed through a federated Centre-State build.
Krishi DSS joins
satellite, weather, soil and crop data
The digital crop survey records plot-level, real-time crop acreage to improve the accuracy of production estimates.
Component A of PM-KUSUM covers decentralised grid-connected solar/renewable plants on barren or fallow land.

secs.t: Data — irrigated area, micro-irrigation coverage, soil health cards

x: The gross irrigated area increased from 41.7% in 2001-02 to
The reported number of Soil Health Cards issued as of November 2025 was
25.55 crore

secs.t: Andhra Pradesh — micro-irrigation rank, automation, drones

x: The Andhra Pradesh Micro Irrigation Project is implemented State-wide under the
Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchai Yojana
with financial assistance.
The newer automation-based system uses sensors and data analytics so that irrigation and fertiliser application are based
on precision rather than guesswork
APSES 2024-25 records large-scale drip and sprinkler irrigation and rainwater harvesting, and names precision farming, drones and IoT as key areas of focus.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The policy emphasis on higher output with lower ecological cost is described as the
Evergreen Revolution
, associated with M.S. Swaminathan.
The current relevance includes PMKSY at ten years, automation-based micro-irrigation in Andhra Pradesh and APDC drone services in all 26 districts.
APSES 2024-25 identifies
precision farming, drones, IoT, drip and sprinkler irrigation, and rainwater harvesting
as the way forward.

rows.title: Genetic engineering - recombinant DNA, GM crops (Bt cotton, Bt brinjal, GM mustard), gene editing/CRISPR
sub: Group-II M2-B-82: Impact of transgenics on the environment - gene flow, biodiversity and biosafety concerns

secs.t: Genetic engineering — rDNA steps, tools and FIRSTs

x: DNA is first isolated, then cut at specific sites, joined by DNA ligase to form recombinant DNA, and finally inserted into a host cell.
Polymerase chain reaction, or
PCR
, is used for isolation and amplification of the desired DNA fragment.
Agrobacterium tumefaciens is called nature's genetic engineer because T-DNA from its disarmed Ti plasmid can carry the desired gene into the plant nucleus.

secs.t: Bt technology → gene source, mode of action, versions

x: Bacillus thuringiensis forms crystal proteins called
delta-endotoxins
during sporulation.
The Bt protoxin is activated in the alkaline gut of the larva, binds to midgut cells, creates pores and ultimately kills the insect.
Bollgard I, introduced in 2002, contains Cry1Ac.
Although persistence of Bt proteins in soil was feared,
experiments have shown that they degrade in soil

secs.t: GM crops in India → developer, target, status

x: Exam angle: Bt brinjal "developed for" - insect resistance; "only GM crop cultivated" - Bt cotton.
Bt brinjal was recommended by the GEAC in October 2009, developed by the stated institutions for insect resistance, and placed under a moratorium in 2010 by Jairam Ramesh.
GM mustard DMH-11 received GEAC approval for environmental release in October 2022, although the matter remained under consideration by the Supreme Court.

secs.t: Bt cotton and stress-tolerant crops → outcomes and problems

x: The reported yield increased from
190 kg/ha in 2002 to 480 kg/ha in 2023
, although benefits varied by region.
The reported difficulties included pest resistance, failure to adopt refuges or recommended practices, high input costs and dependence on purchased seed.
The claimed benefits include reduced pesticide use in Bt cotton, herbicide tolerance, drought tolerance and stress tolerance achieved through genome editing.

secs.t: Other GM foods and transgenic animals → trait and gene

x: Golden Rice produces beta-carotene, which is a precursor of
Vitamin A
and is intended to help combat Vitamin A deficiency and blindness.
GM mosquitoes may be engineered either to suppress mosquito populations or to block transmission of diseases such as malaria, dengue and Zika.
Gene drives may spread a trait through wild populations, potentially causing population collapse or producing malaria-resistant mosquitoes.

secs.t: Gene editing — CRISPR discoverers, SDN categories, new tools

x: TnpB
is an indigenous, smaller alternative to CRISPR-Cas9 developed by ICAR and is considered easier to deliver.
Base editing converts one DNA base into another without producing double-strand breaks in the DNA.
ContactSeek uses AI with AlphaFold3 to help
cut off-target edits
, thereby improving the precision of gene editing.
Personalised medicine built on genetic make-up is associated with CRISPR (UKPSC 2025 key).

secs.t: Genetic medicine — terms → meaning

x: Genetic medicines are intended
to correct or compensate for faulty genes
Engineered viruses and lipid nanoparticles
are used as carriers for delivering genetic material in genetic medicine.
MRT is the 'three-parent baby' technique and raises ethical issues of germline editing and designer babies (A).
The recombinant vaccines specifically mentioned are those for hepatitis B, HPV and COVID-19.

secs.t: Environmental risks → effects

x: Movement of herbicide-tolerance genes into weedy relatives can create invasive superweeds and increase weediness.
Bt toxins or other engineered traits may affect beneficial insects such as pollinators and natural enemies, soil nematodes and microbes, and aquatic organisms.
Gene flow, the movement of transgenes by pollen into non-GM crops and wild relatives, is the primary environmental concern (PYQ).

secs.t: Health and biosafety risks → cases

x: The Brazil-nut gene was intended to improve methionine content, but the resulting soybean raised allergy concerns and was therefore never released.
Antibiotic-resistance marker genes may contribute to the spread of antibiotic resistance, which is a recognised biosafety concern.
Mon 863 was a Monsanto genetically modified pest-resistant maize variety directed against corn rootworm and was discussed in connection with feeding-study safety.

secs.t: Crop diversity, GURT and safeguards — issues and Acts

x: Genetic homogenisation results when uniform varieties are widely cultivated, reducing agro-biodiversity and increasing vulnerability to new pathogens and climate shocks.
Monoculture and concentration of seed production can displace traditional
landraces and farmer varieties
Terminator technology makes the next generation of seeds non-viable, preventing seed saving and replanting and potentially forcing annual purchases.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Pusa Rice DST1 is an edited version of MTU1010, an Andhra Pradesh-bred rice variety associated with Maruteru.
Stated in the debate.
The Cartagena Protocol was adopted in 2000, entered into force in 2003, governs transboundary movement of living modified organisms, and India is a party to it.
